mechanism.text:
Acts as an application-scoped registry and local provider wrapper for tools, UI components, resources and prompts — essentially the owner/manager that declares what an app exposes to a running FastMCP server. An instance holds the app identity (name) and a LocalProvider used as the on-disk / in-process component store; it is responsible for annotating components with app metadata (visibility, app name, and a deterministic tool hash) and registering them into that local store.

Construction is lightweight: you create it with an application name and it instantiates its internal LocalProvider. Typical usage is declarative: call its decorator-like methods (tool, ui) or add_tool to register callables or Tool objects. Those registration helpers resolve names, assemble UI/resource metadata (including visibility and renderer hints), compute addressing hashes, attach auth/timeout/meta, and hand the Tool to the internal provider. The instance itself is not a running server; it provides an async lifespan context that proxies to the LocalProvider’s lifespan for any async setup/teardown the provider requires. To actually serve the app’s tools, the instance is added to a FastMCP server (via run or server.add_provider).

Important lifecycle notes: the LocalProvider lifecycle is managed through the app’s lifespan context manager; for proper resource cleanup any async initialization/teardown should be driven by entering/exiting lifespan. run starts a server process and does not imply additional implicit disposal of the LocalProvider beyond its lifespan — callers should use lifespan when lifecycle control is required.

Key invariants and role in architecture:
- Every registered component will carry fastmcp.app metadata linking it to this app and a stable _tool_hash derived from (app, tool name).
- UI components are given renderer/resource URIs and appropriate visibility; tools default to app-only visibility unless explicitly exposed to model.
- The instance is a coordinator/builder: it doesn’t execute tools itself but prepares, annotates and stores them in a provider that the server will expose.

class AppConfig(BaseModel):
    resource_uri: str | None = Field(default=None, alias='resourceUri', description='URI of the UI resource (typically ui:// scheme). Tools only.')
    visibility: list[Literal['app', 'model']] | None = Field(default=None, description="Where this tool is visible: 'app', 'model', or both. Tools only.")
    csp: ResourceCSP | None = Field(default=None, description='Content Security Policy for the app iframe')
    permissions: ResourcePermissions | None = Field(default=None, description='Iframe sandbox permissions')
    domain: str | None = Field(default=None, description='Domain for the iframe')
    prefers_border: bool | None = Field(default=None, alias='prefersBorder', description='Whether the UI prefers a visible border')
    model_config = {'populate_by_name': True, 'extra': 'allow'}

# --- helper: fastmcp.apps.config.ResourceCSP ---
class ResourceCSP(BaseModel):
    connect_domains: list[str] | None = Field(default=None, alias='connectDomains', description='Origins allowed for fetch/XHR/WebSocket (connect-src)')
    resource_domains: list[str] | None = Field(default=None, alias='resourceDomains', description='Origins allowed for scripts, images, styles, fonts (script-src etc.)')
    frame_domains: list[str] | None = Field(default=None, alias='frameDomains', description='Origins allowed for nested iframes (frame-src)')
    base_uri_domains: list[str] | None = Field(default=None, alias='baseUriDomains', description='Allowed base URIs for the document (base-uri)')
    model_config = {'populate_by_name': True, 'extra': 'allow'}

# --- helper: fastmcp.apps.config.ResourcePermissions ---
class ResourcePermissions(BaseModel):
    camera: dict[str, Any] | None = Field(default=None, description='Request camera access')
    microphone: dict[str, Any] | None = Field(default=None, description='Request microphone access')
    geolocation: dict[str, Any] | None = Field(default=None, description='Request geolocation access')
    clipboard_write: dict[str, Any] | None = Field(default=None, alias='clipboardWrite', description='Request clipboard-write access')
    model_config = {'populate_by_name': True, 'extra': 'allow'}

mechanism.text:
Choice instances encapsulate a reusable provider that builds and exposes an interactive "choose an option" UI tool to the FastMCPApp ecosystem. Conceptually each instance is a small UI-builder and configuration holder: it stores presentation defaults (title, button variant) and registers a callable tool (choose) that constructs a PrefabApp view and a minimal local state for each invocation.

When constructed the instance registers its choose handler with the parent FastMCPApp (via _register_tools). The handler is the operational surface that the LLM or backend invokes to obtain a live UI: it composes cards, headings, prompt text and a column of buttons and returns a PrefabApp object containing the rendered view and a state dict with a single boolean flag (decided: False). Each button is wired to two actions — send a message reflecting the selection and flip the decided flag — so every invocation yields an independently scoped UI instance with its own state.

No external long-lived resources are opened by Choice; it neither holds sockets nor needs explicit disposal. Lifecycle is therefore: construct -> registers tool -> used repeatedly to produce PrefabApp instances -> garbage-collected when unreferenced. There is no close/cleanup API required.

Key invariants and architectural role: Choice guarantees that invocations produce a card-based choice UI with a consistent state key ("decided") and that provider-level configuration (title and variant) deterministically influences presented elements. Architecturally it acts as a provider/builder within the FastMCPApp pattern: separating a tool interface (what the model calls) from the UI implementation the backend returns, enabling repeatable, stateless UI construction while keeping per-invocation interactivity confined to the returned PrefabApp state.

mechanism.text:
Instances represent a small, self-contained form-collection application: they coordinate a Pydantic schema, register tool handlers, and assemble a UI prefab that validates and submits user input back into the system. Conceptually an instance is a builder/coordinator that maps a typed data model (the schema) into two runtime primitives — a tool that accepts validated data and a UI prefab that renders a validated form and calls that tool on submit.

Construction binds the instance to a specific Pydantic model and immediately registers two runtime artifacts with the FastMCP framework: (1) a submit tool that validates incoming dictionaries against the model and either calls a user-provided callback or returns a JSON-serialized payload, and (2) a UI tool that returns a PrefabApp containing a form built from the same model. After construction the instance is used by invoking its UI tool from agents or other app code: callers display the form, wait for the user to submit, and then the submit tool receives and validates the data. The PrefabApp keeps transient UI state (a submitted flag) but no external resources or long-running threads are owned by the instance, so explicit disposal or closing is not required.

Key invariants: an instance always has a valid Pydantic model and consistent tool names registered against that model; the submit tool will never pass a raw dict downstream without model validation; boolean fields absent from user input are deterministically backfilled (using the model’s default or False). Architecturally, the class sits at the integration layer between typed schema definitions and the FastMCP runtime: it automates UI generation, input validation, and submission wiring, reducing repeated boilerplate when collecting structured user input in MCP workflows.

mechanism.text:
Representations of single approval dialogs: each instance encapsulates the configuration and UI-building logic needed to present an approval request (summary, optional details, labels/variants for approve/reject) and to produce a small interactive PrefabApp that manages a simple "decided" boolean state and emits a message when the user chooses. It is both a lightweight configuration object (title and button text/variants) and a factory/coordinator that exposes one callable tool — request_approval — which constructs and returns a self-contained UI + state bundle when invoked.

Lifecycle and usage: an instance is constructed once with its desired defaults. During initialization it registers its UI tool with the FastMCPApp machinery so the language model or caller can invoke request_approval. Each invocation of that tool builds a transient PrefabApp: a view tree (card, header, content, footer with buttons) and an initial state {'decided': False}. The returned PrefabApp is the runtime artifact shown to an end-user; user actions send messages and flip the internal decided flag. The Approval object itself is long-lived and reusable — there is no per-invocation resource attached to it that requires explicit disposal. The PrefabApp and any UI runtime are managed by the surrounding framework and cleaned up when no longer needed.

Invariants and architectural role: Approval maintains the invariant that its registered tool will always produce a PrefabApp whose UI reflects either the instance defaults or any per-call overrides, and whose internal state accurately records whether an answer was sent. Architecturally it acts as a provider/adapter: it separates declarative UI construction from runtime message-sending logic, exposing a high-level approval interaction to the larger FastMCPApp ecosystem. It does not manage external resources (files, network sockets) nor lifecycle beyond registration and producing ephemeral PrefabApp instances.

implementation:
class Approval(FastMCPApp):

    def __init__(self, name: str='Approval', *, title: str='Approval Required', approve_text: str='Approve', reject_text: str='Reject', approve_variant: Literal['default', 'destructive', 'success', 'info']='default', reject_variant: Literal['default', 'outline', 'destructive', 'success', 'info']='outline') -> None:
        super().__init__(name)
        self._title = title
        self._approve_text = approve_text
        self._reject_text = reject_text
        self._approve_variant = approve_variant
        self._reject_variant = reject_variant
        self._register_tools()

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        return f'Approval({self.name!r})'

    def _register_tools(self) -> None:
        provider = self

        @self.ui()
        def request_approval(summary: str, details: str | None=None, title: str | None=None, approve_text: str | None=None, reject_text: str | None=None, approve_variant: str | None=None, reject_variant: str | None=None) -> PrefabApp:
            _title = title or provider._title
            _approve = approve_text or provider._approve_text
            _reject = reject_text or provider._reject_text
            _approve_v = approve_variant or provider._approve_variant
            _reject_v = reject_variant or provider._reject_variant
            approve_msg = f'"{summary}" — I selected: {_approve}'
            reject_msg = f'"{summary}" — I selected: {_reject}'
            with Card(css_class='max-w-lg mx-auto') as view:
                with CardHeader():
                    H3(_title)
                with CardContent(), Column(gap=3):
                    Text(summary, css_class='font-medium')
                    if details:
                        Muted(details)
                with CardFooter():
                    with If(STATE.decided):
                        Muted('Response sent.')
                    with If(~STATE.decided):
                        with Row(gap=2, css_class='w-full justify-end'):
                            Button(_reject, variant=_reject_v, on_click=[SendMessage(reject_msg), SetState('decided', True)])
                            Button(_approve, variant=_approve_v, on_click=[SendMessage(approve_msg), SetState('decided', True)])
            return PrefabApp(view=view, state={'decided': False})

mechanism.text:
Instances act as an on-demand provider that registers and exposes UI-generation tools and the static renderer resource into the FastMCP provider system. Conceptually each object coordinates three concerns: (1) a local component registry (LocalProvider) where tools and resources are added, (2) a lazily-initialised sandbox used by the generative execution engine, and (3) application/resource configuration (CSP and AppConfig) that controls what the renderer can load and what origins it may contact.

Lifecycle: construction is lightweight — it sets up identity, flags and placeholders (local provider and sandbox reference) but does not register any tools or resources yet. Registration is deferred until the first interaction that requires available tools or resources: methods such as _list_tools, _get_tool, _list_resources, or entering lifespan call _ensure_setup which builds CSP/AppConfig, creates tool wrappers around the generative execution/search functions, and adds a renderer TextResource to the local provider. The public lifespan() is an async context manager that ensures setup and delegates to the local provider’s lifespan for any runtime orchestration; callers should use it when they need a managed runtime window. There is no separate close API on the instance — lifecycle cleanup is delegated to the local provider’s lifespan and any sandbox finalisation it performs.

Key invariants and role in the architecture:
- Setup is idempotent: _ensure_setup runs once and sets _setup_done to prevent duplicate registration.
- The LocalProvider always holds the definitive set of tools/resources exposed to the rest of the system after setup.
- The sandbox reference is a single lazily-created execution environment reused for subsequent generations.
- The provider mediates security/config by building and attaching CSP/AppConfig to renderer resources so the UI runs with the intended resource/connect restrictions.

Role: it bridges prefab-ui’s generative renderer and FastMCP’s tool/resource model, presenting interactive UI generation as first-class tools and a renderer resource while encapsulating sandboxing and CSP configuration.

class GenerativeUI(Provider):

    def __init__(self, *, tool_name: str='generate_prefab_ui', include_components_tool: bool=True, components_tool_name: str='search_prefab_components') -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self._tool_name = tool_name
        self._components_tool_name = components_tool_name
        self._include_components_tool = include_components_tool
        self._local = LocalProvider(on_duplicate='error')
        self._sandbox: Any = None
        self._setup_done = False

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        return f'GenerativeUI(tool_name={self._tool_name!r})'

    def _get_sandbox(self) -> Any:
        if self._sandbox is None:
            from prefab_ui.sandbox import Sandbox
            self._sandbox = Sandbox()
        return self._sandbox

    def _ensure_setup(self) -> None:
        if self._setup_done:
            return
        csp = _build_csp()
        app_config = AppConfig(resource_uri=_gen.RESOURCE_URI, csp=csp)
        from prefab_ui.app import PrefabApp
        sandbox_ref = self

        async def generate_ui(code: str, data: str | dict[str, Any] | None=None) -> PrefabApp:
            parsed_data: dict[str, Any] | None
            if isinstance(data, str):
                parsed_data = json.loads(data) if data.strip() else None
            else:
                parsed_data = data
            return await _gen.execute(code, data=parsed_data, sandbox=sandbox_ref._get_sandbox())
        tool = Tool.from_function(generate_ui, name=self._tool_name, description=_gen.execute.__doc__ or '', meta={'ui': app_config_to_meta_dict(app_config)})
        self._local._add_component(tool)
        if self._include_components_tool:
            components_tool = Tool.from_function(_gen.search_components, name=self._components_tool_name, description=_gen.search_components.__doc__ or '')
            self._local._add_component(components_tool)
        from fastmcp.resources.types import TextResource
        resource_config = AppConfig(csp=csp)
        resource = TextResource(uri=_gen.RESOURCE_URI, name='Prefab Generative Renderer', text=get_generative_renderer_html(), mime_type=UI_MIME_TYPE, meta={'ui': app_config_to_meta_dict(resource_config)})
        self._local._add_component(resource)
        self._setup_done = True

    async def _list_tools(self) -> Sequence[Tool]:
        self._ensure_setup()
        return await self._local._list_tools()

    async def _get_tool(self, name: str, version: Any=None) -> Tool | None:
        self._ensure_setup()
        return await self._local._get_tool(name, version)

    async def _list_resources(self) -> Sequence[Any]:
        self._ensure_setup()
        return await self._local._list_resources()

    async def _get_resource(self, uri: str, version: Any=None) -> Any | None:
        self._ensure_setup()
        return await self._local._get_resource(uri, version)

    async def _list_resource_templates(self) -> Sequence[Any]:
        return []

    async def _get_resource_template(self, uri: str, version: Any=None) -> Any | None:
        return None

    async def _list_prompts(self) -> Sequence[Any]:
        return []

    async def _get_prompt(self, name: str, version: Any=None) -> Any | None:
        return None

    @asynccontextmanager
    async def lifespan(self) -> AsyncIterator[None]:
        self._ensure_setup()
        async with self._local.lifespan():
            yield

# --- helper: fastmcp.apps.generative._build_csp ---
def _build_csp() -> ResourceCSP:
    csp = get_generative_renderer_csp()
    return ResourceCSP(resource_domains=csp.get('resource_domains'), connect_domains=csp.get('connect_domains'))

mechanism.text:
Orchestrates launching an application server by deciding between direct in-process execution, spawning an external "uv" environment, or running a Python module in a subprocess with optional file-watch reload. The control flow is a decision tree that first distinguishes module-mode vs object/import mode, then determines whether an external environment builder is required (by probing an environment.build_command for a no-op), and finally either executes directly (awaiting an async runner) or constructs and runs a subprocess command (optionally wrapped by an env builder) — with a special code path that replaces the current process when an external environment is needed.

1) Algorithm / computational approach
- Decision-tree orchestration: choose execution strategy based on flags and environment state (module flag, skip_env marker, reload flag, whether already inside a uv subprocess).
- Capability probing: determine whether an environment wrapper (UV) is necessary by comparing environment.build_command(test_cmd) to the identity test_cmd; if different, the environment must be used.
- Command synthesis: build a list of CLI tokens representing an inner runner, optionally wrap it via the environment builder, and either spawn it with subprocess.run or start a hot-reload loop via a specialized run_with_reload helper.
- Special-case handling: module mode ignores server-specific options (transport/host/port/path), reload mode injects stateless/no-reload markers and refuses reload for transports that lose session state.

2) Domain knowledge required
- Familiarity with Python process models (importing modules vs python -m), async vs sync execution, and subprocess invocation.
- Understanding of virtual/isolated environment tooling that can wrap commands (a build_command abstraction).
- Server transports and their semantics (stdio, HTTP, SSE), and why some transports break on restart (session loss for SSE).
- Hot-reload mechanics: watching directories, respawning worker processes, and preserving CLI arguments.

3) Key constraints and assumptions
- The env.build_command identity check reliably indicates whether wrapping is needed; build_command is expected to be deterministic and return the same sentinel for "no wrapping".
- A marker environment variable (FASTMCP_UV_SPAWNED) and is_already_in_uv_subprocess() are used to avoid recursive wrapping.
- Reload is incompatible with SSE (session loss), and module-mode delegates server lifecycle entirely to the module.
- Command-line composition assumes downstream tools understand the constructed token sequence and separators (e.g., "--").
- Error handling ramps to sys.exit on failures; this is intended for CLI contexts.

4) When appropriate to use
- Running or developing a fastmcp-managed server from the CLI where you may need environment isolation, hot-reload during development, or the option to run a module instead of importing an object.
- When you need transparent spawning of an environment wrapper (for example, to use a different Python version or install dependencies) while preserving original CLI semantics.
- Not appropriate for library code that expects to embed server lifecycle without process spawning or for transports that require continuity of in-memory session state (e.g., SSE with reload).

mechanism.text:
Resolves a user-specified server target and routes a high-level "call" operation (tool, resource, or prompt) through an asynchronous client, handling argument parsing, output formatting, authentication selection, and controlled process exit on errors.

1. Underlying algorithm / computational approach
- Deterministic dispatch: the code resolves a server spec into a concrete transport (HTTP/SSE endpoint, stdio command, JSON-config, or named server), constructs a Client with chosen auth/timeout/elicitation hooks, then selects one of three handlers based on the target form: prompt, resource URI (contains "://"), or tool name.  
- Input normalization: CLI key=value arguments and optional JSON are merged and validated against a tool’s input schema before a call. For prompts, the arguments are coerced to an expected object.  
- Output modes: results are either pretty-printed text (with sanitization and summaries for blobs/images) or emitted as raw JSON. Errors from remote calls are surfaced but controlled (raise_on_error=False), allowing CLI to decide exit codes.  
- Heuristics & fallbacks: when resolving server specs, the code infers transport, recognizes file paths by extension, optionally appends '/sse' for SSE transport, and suggests close matches for missing tools/prompts using string similarity.

2. Domain knowledge required
- Familiarity with client-server interaction patterns (HTTP vs SSE vs stdio transports).  
- Understanding of schema-driven tool interfaces (JSON Schema-like inputSchema, required fields).  
- Knowledge of CLI UX expectations (suggestions for close names, JSON vs human-readable output) and basic security hygiene (sanitizing untrusted text).

3. Key constraints and assumptions
- Target must be provided and unambiguous; prompt flag switches semantics.  
- File heuristics rely on extensions (.py/.js/.json) and filesystem checks.  
- Default auth is inferred (HTTP → 'oauth') unless overridden; 'none' explicitly disables it.  
- Handlers expect specific Client APIs: list_tools/list_prompts, call_tool/get_prompt/read_resource.  
- Exit-on-error behavior is intentional for CLI use (sys.exit).

4. When appropriate to use
- Use this when invoking a remote or local MCP-compatible server from a CLI to call named tools, fetch resources by URI, or run named prompts—especially when schema validation, human-friendly output, or JSON export is needed. Not intended for embedding as a library-returning-value function because it performs process exits and console I/O.

mechanism.text:
Lists the capabilities (tools, resources, prompts) offered by a running MCP-style server by resolving a server specification to an executable transport, opening an async client session, retrieving metadata endpoints, and rendering them either as JSON or as a human-readable console summary.

Algorithmically it combines four phases. First it normalizes the "server spec": a URL, local file (Python/JS/JSON), a named resolver, or a stdio command; HTTP URLs may be rewired to an SSE endpoint when requested. Second it selects an authentication policy (explicit, disabled, or a simple heuristic that defaults to OAuth for HTTP targets) and constructs a client object. Third, within an async context it concurrently calls list_tools/list_resources/list_prompts as requested, maps tool input/output JSON Schemas into short signatures (converting property types, required lists and defaults), and optionally returns full JSON-serialized metadata. Fourth it sanitizes any untrusted text for safe console output and prints formatted summaries, or emits JSON for machine consumption.

Domain knowledge needed: familiarity with the MCP protocol or whatever RPC/metadata API the server exposes; basic understanding of JSON Schema (properties, required, defaults) to interpret tool signatures; concepts of transports (HTTP vs SSE vs stdio) and how local executables can be used as transports; async I/O patterns for opening and closing network/stdio clients; and terminal-safety concerns when printing untrusted text.

Key constraints and assumptions: server spec resolution assumes specific filename conventions (.py/.js/.json), a resolve_name registry, and that a JSON spec file contains the transport description; HTTP endpoints imply OAuth unless overridden; schema printing is minimal (only prints full schema if properties exist); error handling is CLI-oriented (prints and exits); sanitization reduces non-printable characters and escapes rich-markup. The implementation expects the client API to provide list_tools/list_resources/list_prompts and that tools expose inputSchema/outputSchema shaped like JSON Schema.

Appropriate use: as a CLI utility to inspect what an MCP-compatible server exposes (for discovery, debugging, or scripting). Use when you need a quick human-readable inventory or machine-friendly JSON export of server capabilities before invoking tools programmatically.

mechanism.text:
Takes command-line-like inputs (a tuple of key=value strings plus an optional raw JSON body) and builds a dict of typed arguments by parsing JSON where supplied and coercing scalar strings to primitive types according to a lightweight input schema.

Algorithmically it combines two sources of input: an explicit JSON blob and zero-or-more key=value tokens. If a single raw token looks like a JSON object and no separate JSON blob was given, that token is treated as the JSON body. Any JSON body is parsed into a dict and merged into the result. Remaining key=value tokens are split on the first '='; each value string is coerced to a target Python type based on the property's declared "type" in input_schema (integer → int, number → float, boolean → specific true/false strings → bool, array/object → JSON-decoded structure, otherwise left as string). Errors (invalid JSON, malformed tokens, failed coercion) are reported and cause immediate process exit.

Required domain knowledge: understanding of JSON and its distinctions from plain strings; typical simple JSON Schema-style typing (string, integer, number, boolean, array, object); and expectations of command-line argument conventions (key=value and the use of a single JSON argument). Also useful is familiarity with the host application's error-reporting conventions (console printing and sys.exit).

Key constraints and assumptions: input_schema provides a 'properties' mapping with per-key 'type' hints; no deep schema validation (no required/enum/format/constraints enforcement); JSON decoding is the authority for arrays/objects; boolean parsing accepts only specific textual forms ('true','1','yes' and 'false','0','no'); single-token JSON detection uses a simple startswith('{') heuristic; errors terminate the process. Locale, numeric formats, or more complex coercions (dates, nested validation) are not handled.

Appropriate use cases: small CLI tools or RPC wrappers that need quick, predictable coercion from user-typed arguments into structured types guided by a minimal schema. Not appropriate when you need full JSON Schema validation, sophisticated error recovery, complex type inference, or safe handling of untrusted JSON beyond simple parsing.

implementation:
def generate_skill_content(server_name: str, cli_filename: str, tools: list[mcp.types.Tool]) -> str:
    skill_name = server_name.replace(' ', '-').lower().replace('\\', '').replace('"', '')
    safe_name = server_name.replace('\\', '').replace('"', '')
    description = f'CLI for the {safe_name} MCP server. Call tools, list resources, and get prompts.'
    lines = ['---', f'name: "{skill_name}-cli"', f'description: "{description}"', '---', '', f'# {server_name} CLI', '']
    if tools:
        tool_bodies = '\n\n'.join((_tool_skill_section(tool, cli_filename) for tool in tools))
        lines.extend(['## Tool Commands', '', tool_bodies, ''])
    lines.extend(['## Utility Commands', '', '```bash', f'uv run --with fastmcp python {cli_filename} list-tools', f'uv run --with fastmcp python {cli_filename} list-resources', f'uv run --with fastmcp python {cli_filename} read-resource <uri>', f'uv run --with fastmcp python {cli_filename} list-prompts', f'uv run --with fastmcp python {cli_filename} get-prompt <name> [key=value ...]', '```', ''])
    return '\n'.join(lines)

# --- helper: fastmcp.cli.generate._tool_skill_section ---
def _tool_skill_section(tool: mcp.types.Tool, cli_filename: str) -> str:
    schema = tool.inputSchema
    properties: dict[str, Any] = schema.get('properties', {})
    required = set(schema.get('required', []))
    flag_parts_list: list[str] = []
    for p, p_schema in properties.items():
        flag = _param_to_cli_flag(p)
        schema_type = p_schema.get('type')
        is_bool = schema_type == 'boolean' or (isinstance(schema_type, list) and 'boolean' in schema_type)
        if is_bool:
            flag_parts_list.append(flag)
        else:
            flag_parts_list.append(f'{flag} <value>')
    flag_parts = ' '.join(flag_parts_list)
    invocation = f'uv run --with fastmcp python {cli_filename} call-tool {tool.name}'
    if flag_parts:
        invocation += f' {flag_parts}'
    rows: list[str] = []
    for prop_name, prop_schema in properties.items():
        flag = f'`{_param_to_cli_flag(prop_name)}`'
        type_label = _schema_type_label(prop_schema).replace('|', '\\|')
        is_required = 'yes' if prop_name in required else 'no'
        description = prop_schema.get('description', '')
        _, needs_json = _schema_to_python_type(prop_schema)
        if needs_json:
            description = f'{description} (JSON string)' if description else 'JSON string'
        description = description.replace('\n', ' ').replace('|', '\\|')
        rows.append(f'| {flag} | {type_label} | {is_required} | {description} |')
    param_table = ''
    if rows:
        header = '| Flag | Type | Required | Description |\n|------|------|----------|-------------|'
        param_table = f'\n{header}\n' + '\n'.join(rows) + '\n'
    lines: list[str] = [f'### {tool.name}']
    if tool.description:
        lines.extend(['', tool.description])
    lines.extend(['', '```bash', invocation, '```'])
    if param_table:
        lines.extend(['', param_table.strip('\n')])
    return '\n'.join(lines)

mechanism.text:
Generates a standalone shell command that will run a Python-based FastMCP server inside a reproducible environment and either prints it or copies it to the clipboard.

1) Algorithm / computational approach
- Normalize inputs (empty lists for optional repeated flags).
- Resolve a server file path and optional object name into a server specification string (path[:object]).
- Create an environment specification (UVEnvironment) encoding Python version, dependencies, editable packages, requirements file, and project directory. This object encapsulates how to install or invoke the runtime.
- Ask that environment object to build the concrete command (list of program + args) to install dependencies and run fastmcp run <server_spec>. Convert the list into a shell-quoted string with shlex.join.
- Either copy the quoted command to the clipboard (pyperclip) or print it to stdout. Return success/failure, catching OS, value, and clipboard-related errors.

2) Domain knowledge required
- How Python virtual environments and dependency installation work (editable installs, requirements files, package lists).
- Shell command quoting and why commands are assembled as argv lists then joined safely (shlex).
- Cross-platform clipboard semantics (pyperclip can fail on systems without clipboard backends).
- How FastMCP expects a server spec (file path and optional object) and what running fastmcp run implies.

3) Key constraints and assumptions
- UVEnvironment.build_command produces a complete, runnable command; correctness depends on that implementation.
- Paths are resolved to absolute paths; user filesystem layout matters.
- Clipboard operations may fail; failures are caught but mean no command copied.
- The routine does not execute the generated command—it only prints or copies it.
- Error handling is coarse: it returns False and prints an error on common exceptions but doesn’t provide structured diagnostics.

4) When appropriate to use
- When you need a reproducible one-line command to install dependencies and run a FastMCP server (for sharing, documentation, CI, or manual shell execution).
- When you want to assemble complex environment options (editable projects, explicit Python versions, requirements files) into a single user-visible command.
- Not appropriate if you want to programmatically execute the server immediately, require detailed failure handling, or depend on UVEnvironment internals rather than a human-copyable command.

mechanism.text:
Runs a child process under an asyncio loop and automatically restarts it when files change, using an asynchronous file-watcher and cooperative shutdown. The core algorithm is an event-driven loop that concurrently waits for three events: a file-change notification, the child process exiting, or an external shutdown signal. When a file change is observed the child is terminated and restarted; if the child exits on its own, the loop waits for the next file change before restarting (logging the exit code). Shutdown handlers and careful task cancellation ensure clean termination.

Key mechanisms:
- asyncio concurrency: create_subprocess_exec, asyncio.wait with FIRST_COMPLETED, and cancellation of pending tasks to coordinate multiple asynchronous waiters without blocking the event loop.
- File-watching: awatch (async iterator) yields change sets; anext/aiter are used to await the next change asynchronously.
- Process-group termination on POSIX: child processes are started in a new session to allow killing the whole group (os.killpg) with SIGTERM/SIGKILL if needed; Windows uses Process.kill.
- Signal management: loop.add_signal_handler is used on non-Windows platforms to translate OS signals into an asyncio.Event that triggers graceful shutdown.

Domain knowledge required:
- Familiarity with asyncio patterns (tasks, cancellation, wait_for, event loop behavior).
- Understanding of OS process semantics (sessions, process groups, signals) and platform differences between POSIX and Windows.
- Awareness of file-watching semantics (what is or isn’t reported by the watcher library) and the implications for restart behavior.

Key constraints and assumptions:
- Relies on an external async file-watcher (awatch) and a predefined filter of watched extensions.
- No debouncing or aggregation beyond awaiting the next change; rapid successive changes may cause multiple restarts.
- Signal handlers are not installed on Windows; process-group termination uses POSIX APIs and requires permission to signal child processes.
- When is_stdio is False, bidirectional features that require persistent connections are not available (stateless HTTP mode).

Appropriate usage:
- Development-time hot-reload for servers or CLI tools where automatic restarts on source changes are desired.
- Not suitable for production workloads where restarts must be orchestrated, or when fine-grained restart control, debouncing, or preservation of long-lived bidirectional sessions is required.

mechanism.text:
Detects whether the configured Docket backend is an in‑memory (single‑process) store and aborts CLI execution with a user message if so.

1. Underlying algorithm / computational approach
- Simple configuration check: read a stored URL string (fastmcp.settings.docket.url) and test whether it begins with the "memory://" scheme. If it does, emit a detailed explanatory error to the console and terminate the process (sys.exit(1)). There is no iterative or heavy computation — it’s a guard clause that enforces a runtime invariant before any multi‑process CLI workflows run.

2. Domain knowledge required
- Understanding the difference between single‑process (in‑memory) and distributed backends: in‑memory backends keep state inside one process’ memory and cannot be shared across processes. Distributed backends (Redis, Valkey, etc.) provide a networked, persistent coordination layer. Knowledge of how CLI commands spawn separate processes (or run in environments separate from the server process) is necessary to see why shared state is required. Familiarity with running and configuring services like Redis and environment‑variable based configuration is also needed.

3. Key constraints and assumptions
- The configuration value is available and represented as a URL-like string whose prefix accurately indicates backend type.
- The CLI operations require coordination across processes, so an in‑memory backend is insufficient.
- The code assumes the presence of a console printing utility and that exiting the process is an acceptable way to stop execution and inform the user.
- It assumes users can and will install/start a distributed broker and set FASTMCP_DOCKET_URL appropriately.

4. When to use it
- Use this check early in CLI entry points that perform task dispatching, inspection, or other operations that rely on cross‑process coordination. It is inappropriate for purely local, single‑process tooling (e.g., development servers or unit tests that intentionally use an in‑memory backend). The guard prevents subtle, hard‑to‑debug failures by enforcing a correct runtime environment for distributed task workflows.

implementation:
def check_distributed_backend() -> None:
    import fastmcp
    docket_url = fastmcp.settings.docket.url
    if docket_url.startswith('memory://'):
        console.print('[bold red]✗ In-memory backend not supported by CLI[/bold red]

Your Docket configuration uses an in-memory backend (memory://) which
only works within a single process.

To use [cyan]fastmcp tasks[/cyan] CLI commands (which run in separate
processes), you need a distributed backend:

[bold]1. Install Redis or Valkey:[/bold]
   [dim]macOS:[/dim]     brew install redis
   [dim]Ubuntu:[/dim]    apt install redis-server
   [dim]Valkey:[/dim]    See https://valkey.io/

[bold]2. Start the service:[/bold]
   redis-server

[bold]3. Configure Docket URL:[/bold]
   [dim]Environment variable:[/dim]
   export FASTMCP_DOCKET_URL=redis://localhost:6379/0

[bold]4. Try again[/bold]

The memory backend works great for single-process servers, but the CLI
commands need a distributed backend to coordinate across processes.

Need help? See: [cyan]https://gofastmcp.com/docs/tasks[/cyan]')
        sys.exit(1)

mechanism.text: Runs an asynchronous FastMCP 1.x server bound to the given host and port using the specified transport. It starts listening for and handling incoming connections within the current asyncio event loop and typically awaits until the server is stopped or the coroutine is cancelled; it does not return a useful value (completes when shutdown occurs, generally returning None). Call it from your program’s main async routine or entry-point to start serving during application runtime.

implementation:
async def run_v1_server_async(server: FastMCP1x, host: str | None=None, port: int | None=None, transport: TransportType | None=None) -> None:
    if host is not None:
        server.settings.host = host
    if port is not None:
        server.settings.port = port
    match transport:
        case 'stdio':
            await server.run_stdio_async()
        case 'http' | 'streamable-http' | None:
            await server.run_streamable_http_async()
        case 'sse':
            await server.run_sse_async()

mechanism.text:
Acts as the OAuth client coordinator for an MCP server: an instance encapsulates the client metadata, token storage adapter, redirect/callback plumbing, and flow orchestration needed to perform authorization-code and refresh-token exchanges on behalf of higher-level HTTP requests. It is both stateful (holds current client info, configured redirect port, and bound server URL) and a thin resource manager for the temporary callback server and HTTP client use during the interactive flow.

Lifecycle and usage:
- Construction collects configuration (scopes, client name, optional client_id/secret, token storage backend, HTTPX factory) but does not contact the server until bound. Binding happens automatically if an mcp_url is passed or when used inside a Client that supplies the server URL. _bind establishes the redirect URI, creates client metadata (or a static client info object when client_id is provided), and wraps the provided AsyncKeyValue into a TokenStorageAdapter keyed by server URL.
- At runtime it participates in the auth negotiation via async_auth_flow, an async generator that yields httpx.Request objects and consumes httpx.Response objects while driving the authorization-code flow. redirect_handler opens the authorization URL (and checks for basic server errors); callback_handler runs a short-lived local HTTP server to receive the OAuth redirect and returns the code/state.
- Initialization (_initialize) injects static client_info into the internal context and restores token expiry state from storage. The TokenStorageAdapter persists tokens, client info, and a separate token expiry entry.

Resources and cleanup:
- The class starts transient resources (an anyio task group and callback HTTP server, httpx client sessions created from httpx_client_factory). These are managed with async context managers and task-group cancellation; there is no separate close method to call. Persistent state lives in the provided AsyncKeyValue backend (or an in-memory fallback warned about at bind time).

Invariants and role in architecture:
- Once _bound is True, mcp_url, redirect_port, client metadata, and token_storage_adapter must be set and consistent.
- Token storage keys are namespaced by server URL so tokens/client info are per-MCP server.
- It acts as the auth provider implementation for higher-level Client code, orchestrating DCR, browser-based authorization, token persistence, expiry tracking, and a retry path when the server rejects cached client credentials.

implementation:
class OAuth(OAuthClientProvider):
    _bound: bool

    def __init__(self, mcp_url: str | None=None, scopes: str | list[str] | None=None, client_name: str='FastMCP Client', token_storage: AsyncKeyValue | None=None, additional_client_metadata: dict[str, Any] | None=None, callback_port: int | None=None, httpx_client_factory: McpHttpClientFactory | None=None, client_metadata_url: str | None=None, client_id: str | None=None, client_secret: str | None=None):
        self._scopes = scopes
        self._client_name = client_name
        self._token_storage = token_storage
        self._additional_client_metadata = additional_client_metadata
        self._callback_port = callback_port
        self._client_metadata_url = client_metadata_url
        self._client_id = client_id
        self._client_secret = client_secret
        self._static_client_info = None
        self.httpx_client_factory = httpx_client_factory or httpx.AsyncClient
        self._bound = False
        if mcp_url is not None:
            self._bind(mcp_url)

    def _bind(self, mcp_url: str) -> None:
        if self._bound:
            return
        mcp_url = mcp_url.rstrip('/')
        self.redirect_port = self._callback_port or find_available_port()
        redirect_uri = f'http://localhost:{self.redirect_port}/callback'
        scopes_str: str
        if isinstance(self._scopes, list):
            scopes_str = ' '.join(self._scopes)
        elif self._scopes is not None:
            scopes_str = str(self._scopes)
        else:
            scopes_str = ''
        client_metadata = OAuthClientMetadata(client_name=self._client_name, redirect_uris=[AnyHttpUrl(redirect_uri)], grant_types=['authorization_code', 'refresh_token'], response_types=['code'], scope=scopes_str, **self._additional_client_metadata or {})
        if self._client_id:
            metadata = client_metadata.model_dump(exclude_none=True)
            if 'token_endpoint_auth_method' not in metadata:
                metadata['token_endpoint_auth_method'] = 'client_secret_post' if self._client_secret else 'none'
            self._static_client_info = OAuthClientInformationFull(client_id=self._client_id, client_secret=self._client_secret, **metadata)
        token_storage = self._token_storage or MemoryStore()
        if isinstance(token_storage, MemoryStore):
            from warnings import warn
            warn(message='Using in-memory token storage -- tokens will be lost when the client restarts. For persistent storage across multiple MCP servers, provide an encrypted AsyncKeyValue backend. See https://gofastmcp.com/clients/auth/oauth#token-storage for details.', stacklevel=2)
        self.token_storage_adapter: TokenStorageAdapter = TokenStorageAdapter(async_key_value=token_storage, server_url=mcp_url)
        self.mcp_url = mcp_url
        super().__init__(server_url=mcp_url, client_metadata=client_metadata, storage=self.token_storage_adapter, redirect_handler=self.redirect_handler, callback_handler=self.callback_handler, client_metadata_url=self._client_metadata_url)
        self._bound = True

    async def _initialize(self) -> None:
        await super()._initialize()
        if self._static_client_info is not None:
            self.context.client_info = self._static_client_info
            await self.token_storage_adapter.set_client_info(self._static_client_info)
        if self.context.current_tokens and self.context.current_tokens.expires_in:
            stored_expiry = await self.token_storage_adapter.get_token_expiry()
            if stored_expiry is not None:
                self.context.token_expiry_time = stored_expiry
            else:
                self.context.update_token_expiry(self.context.current_tokens)

    async def redirect_handler(self, authorization_url: str) -> None:
        async with self.httpx_client_factory() as client:
            response = await client.get(authorization_url, follow_redirects=False)
            if response.status_code == 400:
                raise ClientNotFoundError('OAuth client not found - cached credentials may be stale')
            if response.status_code not in (200, 302, 303, 307, 308):
                raise RuntimeError(f'Unexpected authorization response: {response.status_code}')
        logger.info(f'OAuth authorization URL: {authorization_url}')
        webbrowser.open(authorization_url)

    async def callback_handler(self) -> tuple[str, str | None]:
        result = OAuthCallbackResult()
        result_ready = anyio.Event()
        server: Server = create_oauth_callback_server(port=self.redirect_port, server_url=self.mcp_url, result_container=result, result_ready=result_ready)
        async with anyio.create_task_group() as tg:
            tg.start_soon(server.serve)
            logger.info(f'🎧 OAuth callback server started on http://localhost:{self.redirect_port}')
            TIMEOUT = 300.0
            try:
                with anyio.fail_after(TIMEOUT):
                    await result_ready.wait()
                    if result.error:
                        raise result.error
                    return (result.code, result.state)
            except TimeoutError as e:
                raise TimeoutError(f'OAuth callback timed out after {TIMEOUT} seconds') from e
            finally:
                server.should_exit = True
                await anyio.sleep(0.1)
                tg.cancel_scope.cancel()
        raise RuntimeError('OAuth callback handler could not be started')

    async def async_auth_flow(self, request: httpx.Request) -> AsyncGenerator[httpx.Request, httpx.Response]:
        if not self._bound:
            raise RuntimeError('OAuth provider has no server URL. Either pass mcp_url to OAuth() or use it with Client(auth=...) which provides the URL automatically.')
        try:
            async with aclosing(super().async_auth_flow(request)) as gen:
                response = None
                while True:
                    try:
                        yielded_request = await gen.asend(response)
                        response = (yield yielded_request)
                    except StopAsyncIteration:
                        break
        except ClientNotFoundError:
            if self._static_client_info is not None:
                raise ClientNotFoundError('OAuth server rejected the static client credentials. Verify that the client_id (and client_secret, if provided) are correct and that the client is registered with the server.') from None
            logger.debug('OAuth client not found on server, clearing cache and retrying...')
            self._initialized = False
            await self.token_storage_adapter.clear()
            async with aclosing(super().async_auth_flow(request)) as gen:
                response = None
                while True:
                    try:
                        yielded_request = await gen.asend(response)
                        response = (yield yielded_request)
                    except StopAsyncIteration:
                        break

# --- helper: fastmcp.client.auth.oauth.ClientNotFoundError ---
class ClientNotFoundError(Exception):
    pass

# --- helper: fastmcp.client.auth.oauth.TokenStorageAdapter ---
class TokenStorageAdapter(TokenStorage):
    _server_url: str
    _key_value_store: AsyncKeyValue
    _storage_oauth_token: PydanticAdapter[OAuthToken]
    _storage_client_info: PydanticAdapter[OAuthClientInformationFull]

    def __init__(self, async_key_value: AsyncKeyValue, server_url: str):
        self._server_url = server_url
        self._key_value_store = async_key_value
        self._storage_oauth_token = PydanticAdapter[OAuthToken](default_collection='mcp-oauth-token', key_value=async_key_value, pydantic_model=OAuthToken, raise_on_validation_error=True)
        self._storage_client_info = PydanticAdapter[OAuthClientInformationFull](default_collection='mcp-oauth-client-info', key_value=async_key_value, pydantic_model=OAuthClientInformationFull, raise_on_validation_error=True)

    def _get_token_cache_key(self) -> str:
        return f'{self._server_url}/tokens'

    def _get_client_info_cache_key(self) -> str:
        return f'{self._server_url}/client_info'

    def _get_token_expiry_cache_key(self) -> str:
        return f'{self._server_url}/token_expiry'

    async def clear(self) -> None:
        await self._storage_oauth_token.delete(key=self._get_token_cache_key())
        await self._storage_client_info.delete(key=self._get_client_info_cache_key())
        await self._key_value_store.delete(key=self._get_token_expiry_cache_key(), collection='mcp-oauth-token-expiry')

    @override
    async def get_tokens(self) -> OAuthToken | None:
        return await self._storage_oauth_token.get(key=self._get_token_cache_key())

    @override
    async def set_tokens(self, tokens: OAuthToken) -> None:
        await self._storage_oauth_token.put(key=self._get_token_cache_key(), value=tokens, ttl=60 * 60 * 24 * 365)
        if tokens.expires_in is not None:
            expires_at = time.time() + int(tokens.expires_in)
            await self._key_value_store.put(key=self._get_token_expiry_cache_key(), value={'expires_at': expires_at}, collection='mcp-oauth-token-expiry', ttl=60 * 60 * 24 * 365)

    async def get_token_expiry(self) -> float | None:
        raw = await self._key_value_store.get(key=self._get_token_expiry_cache_key(), collection='mcp-oauth-token-expiry')
        if raw is not None:
            return float(raw['expires_at'])
        return None

    @override
    async def get_client_info(self) -> OAuthClientInformationFull | None:
        return await self._storage_client_info.get(key=self._get_client_info_cache_key())

    @override
    async def set_client_info(self, client_info: OAuthClientInformationFull) -> None:
        ttl: int | None = None
        if client_info.client_secret_expires_at:
            ttl = client_info.client_secret_expires_at - int(time.time())
        await self._storage_client_info.put(key=self._get_client_info_cache_key(), value=client_info, ttl=ttl)

mechanism.text:
Spawns a separate process to run a Python module and then terminates the current interpreter with that child's exit code. The implementation builds a command list, optionally rewrites it through an "environment builder", invokes subprocess.run synchronously with check=True, and calls sys.exit with the resulting return code. That approach treats the module as an external program: it executes independently, streams I/O to the same terminal, and forces the caller to stop once the child finishes.

Conceptually it is a simple process hand-off pattern: construct argv, run a new process (no shell interpolation because a list of args is used), detect nonzero exit via exceptions, log failures, and propagate the child’s exit code up to the parent process’s caller. The use of subprocess.run with check=True centralizes error detection (it raises CalledProcessError on nonzero exit), and sys.exit ensures consistent propagation of status to the operating system or a supervising process.

Using this correctly requires domain knowledge about process models, exit codes, and interpreter selection. Users must understand the difference between spawning a new interpreter (here sometimes the literal "python" binary vs the current sys.executable), how command lists avoid shell quoting issues, and that running is blocking and inherits standard streams. You should also be aware of platform PATH semantics, permission/executable availability, and how virtual environments affect which Python binary runs.

Key constraints and assumptions: it is synchronous and will terminate the caller (non-returning in normal use), env_command_builder must return a safe argv list, the chosen Python executable must exist, and no signal forwarding or advanced I/O handling is provided. Not suitable inside libraries or long-lived processes that must continue after delegation. Appropriate when implementing CLI dispatchers or thin wrappers whose whole purpose is to invoke another module and exit, and where simple, direct propagation of exit codes and terminal I/O is desired.

import importlib
import importlib.util
import sys

server_spec = "examples/tasks/server.py"

# Try the regular import path first; fall back to loading the module by file path.
try:
    mod = importlib.import_module("fastmcp.cli.tasks.worker")
except Exception:
    # If the package layout in the environment doesn't allow dotted import,
    # attempt to locate the module file and load it directly.
    # This keeps the call semantics identical: we obtain an object with a
    # callable attribute named `worker` and invoke it with a string path.
    module_path = "./venv/lib/python/site-packages/fastmcp/cli/tasks/worker.py"
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("fastmcp.cli.tasks.worker", module_path)
    if spec is None:
        raise
    mod = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
    sys.modules[spec.name] = mod
    spec.loader.exec_module(mod)

# Call the function exactly as named in the API: worker(server_spec: str)
mod.worker(server_spec)

mechanism.text:
Starts a long-running worker process that attaches to a FastMCP server's lifespan and keeps a separate process alive to run background/task work while validating that a distributed task backend is configured. The routine loads and merges a server configuration (from a provided Python spec or auto-detected fastmcp.json), ensures the configured Docket backend is not the single-process in-memory backend, then creates the server instance and enters its lifespan context while printing status and idling in an asyncio loop until interrupted.

1. Underlying algorithm / computational approach
- Configuration resolution: loads config (with potential spec resolution) and constructs a server object.
- Backend validation: inspects the docket URL and rejects memory:// since CLI workers run in separate processes and cannot coordinate through in-memory backends.
- Lifespan management: uses an async context manager (server._lifespan_manager()) to start and stop server resources (startup/shutdown hooks, connections).
- Worker loop: runs an asyncio-run event loop that enters the lifespan and then sleeps in a long-lived loop (sleep 3600s repeatedly) to keep the process alive so any background tasks or worker coordination can run. KeyboardInterrupt is caught to exit cleanly.

2. Domain knowledge required
- Understanding of distributed task systems and the need for a networked broker (Redis or Valkey) versus an in-process backend.
- Familiarity with asyncio event loops, async context managers for application lifespan, and how background tasks/workers interact with a running server.
- Knowledge of FastMCP’s configuration structure and Docket settings.

3. Key constraints and assumptions
- Requires a distributed backend reachable by URL (not memory://).
- Assumes server.source.load_server() returns an object with a working async lifespan manager.
- The idle loop is used solely to keep the process alive; it does not poll for work itself — task dispatch/processing is handled by the external Docket system.
- Exits on configuration file not found or invalid backend; minimal error handling otherwise.

4. When appropriate to use
- Use when launching a CLI-based worker process that must share a server’s lifecycle and participate in distributed task execution (e.g., background jobs) in a multi-process deployment. Not appropriate for single-process development with an in-memory backend or when you need the worker to actively poll for tasks inside the loop (that responsibility belongs to the task backend).

examples.code:
from fastmcp.client.auth.oauth import TokenStorageAdapter
import asyncio

# Minimal in-memory AsyncKeyValue implementation used for testing.
class InMemoryAsyncKeyValue:
    def __init__(self):
        self._store = {}

    async def get(self, key: str):
        return self._store.get(key)

    async def set(self, key: str, value):
        self._store[key] = value

    async def delete(self, key: str):
        self._store.pop(key, None)

# Instantiate and use the TokenStorageAdapter with a server URL namespace.
async def main():
    async_kv = InMemoryAsyncKeyValue()
    server_url = "https://mcp.example.com"

    adapter = TokenStorageAdapter(async_key_value=async_kv, server_url=server_url)

    # adapter is now available for storing tokens (usage depends on adapter methods).
    print(type(adapter), adapter)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

mechanism.text: A protocol describing a token storage adapter that manages persistence, retrieval, and lifecycle metadata for authentication tokens (access and refresh tokens, expiry, scopes). Instances represent concrete storage strategies (in-memory, filesystem, secure enclave, database) that guarantee how tokens are saved, loaded, and cleared. Typical use: a client component asks the store for a token before requests, saves tokens returned by an auth flow, updates expiry/refresh state, and clears tokens on logout or credential rotation.

mechanism.text: Stores the mutable session state for a Client instance, grouping runtime fields such as connection/session identifiers, authentication tokens, retry/backoff counters, active transport or socket handles, and other ephemeral flags. It separates per-instance state from shared configuration so each Client gets a fresh record. Created when a new Client is instantiated (or when a session is reset) and consumed by client methods, request handling, connection management, and lifecycle/cleanup logic.

mechanism.text: An OAuth-style authorization callback payload with four optional string fields: code (authorization code), state (client-provided state value), error (error identifier), and error_description (human-readable error details). It represents the structured result returned to a client application at an OAuth/OIDC redirect/callback endpoint after an authorization attempt. Produced by authorization servers and consumed by client callback handlers to continue token exchange or to handle and report authorization errors.

examples.code:
import anyio
from fastmcp.client.oauth_callback import OAuthCallbackResult

# Simple synchronous creation and inspection
res = OAuthCallbackResult()
print('Created OAuthCallbackResult instance:', type(res))

import anyio
from fastmcp.client.oauth_callback import OAuthCallbackResult

# Use OAuthCallbackResult together with anyio.Event for async coordination.
# One task will populate the container and notify the waiter via an Event.
async def producer(result_container, ev):
    # attach a payload attribute dynamically and notify
    result_container.payload = {'access_token': 'token123'}
    ev.set()

async def consumer(result_container, ev):
    await ev.wait()
    # read the payload that the producer attached
    print('Received payload:', getattr(result_container, 'payload', None))

async def main():
    result = OAuthCallbackResult()
    event = anyio.Event()
    async with anyio.create_task_group() as tg:
        tg.start_soon(producer, result, event)
        tg.start_soon(consumer, result, event)

anyio.run(main)

mechanism.text: Holds the data extracted from an OAuth authorization redirect: the authorization response parameters (for example, authorization code, state, and any error/error_description values) together with any metadata needed to resume the flow. It is created by the HTTP callback/redirect handler that receives the browser’s response from the authorization server, and is consumed by the awaiting coroutine or task (coordinated via an anyio.Event) that continues token exchange and application logic.

mechanism.text: Routes server log messages to corresponding logging levels (e.g., info, warning, error) and returns a ready-to-use handler/callback that forwards incoming server log records to the application's logger. The returned handler normalizes server-specific severities and message formats, ensuring they appear at the correct level in the configured logging backend. Use it when integrating or replacing a server’s built-in logging pipeline—install the handler into the server or framework so all runtime messages are routed into your application logger.

implementation:
async def default_log_handler(message: LogMessage) -> None:
    data = message.data
    level_map = {'debug': from_server_logger.debug, 'info': from_server_logger.info, 'notice': from_server_logger.info, 'warning': from_server_logger.warning, 'error': from_server_logger.error, 'critical': from_server_logger.critical, 'alert': from_server_logger.critical, 'emergency': from_server_logger.critical}
    log_fn = level_map.get(message.level.lower(), logger.info)
    msg_prefix: str = f'Received {message.level.upper()} from server'
    if message.logger:
        msg_prefix += f' ({message.logger})'
    log_fn(msg=f'{msg_prefix}: {data}')

mechanism.text:
Logs a concise textual representation of incremental work and an optional human-readable message to a debug logger. Conceptually it formats three possible progress models: a ratio with percentage when a nonzero total is known, a ratio without percentage when the total is explicitly zero, and a bare progress value when total is unknown. The output is always a single debug-level string prefixed with "Progress:" so downstream consumers (logs, monitors) get a consistent, parseable tag.

Algorithmically this is pure formatting and conditional branching: choose formatting branch based on the presence and value of total, compute percent only when division is defined and meaningful, and assemble an optional trailing message. The percent computation uses floating-point arithmetic to produce a one-decimal percentage, which is appropriate for human-readable monitoring but not for precise accounting. The function is asynchronous only to match async caller conventions; it performs no I/O other than the synchronous logging call.

Domain knowledge: understand progress reporting semantics—what it means for total to be unknown, zero, or finite—and the implications for interpreting percent. In streaming or incremental tasks, total may be unknown (e.g., live feeds), zero may indicate an empty task (avoid divide-by-zero), and a known positive total enables progress percent and ETA estimates elsewhere. Familiarity with logging levels and consumers is useful so that debug-level output is visible where intended.

Key constraints and assumptions: progress and total are numeric (floatable), total being None signals unknown, total == 0 is treated specially to avoid division, and percent precision is fixed to one decimal. The function assumes callers manage units and normalization (e.g., bytes vs. items) and that logging at debug granularity is acceptable. It is inappropriate for high-frequency tight loops where logging cost or allocation of formatted strings would be a performance problem, or where machine-parseable structured telemetry is required instead of human-readable text.

Appropriate usage: lightweight progress callbacks in CLI tools, background jobs, or async workflows where human debugging output suffices and totals may be unknown or zero. Avoid for high-volume telemetry or where precise metering/structured metrics are needed.

import asyncio
import fastmcp.client.oauth_callback as oauth_callback

async def main():
    # Create a callback server bound to 127.0.0.1:8080 listening on /callback
    server = oauth_callback.create_oauth_callback_server(port=8080)

    # Run the server as a background task (uvicorn.Server.serve() is a coroutine)
    serve_task = asyncio.create_task(server.serve())

mechanism.text:
Listens on a loopback HTTP port for a single OAuth redirect, parses the query string into a typed response object, and atomically records the authorization outcome for the rest of the application to consume.

1. Algorithm / computational approach
- A minimal HTTP server (Starlette + Uvicorn Server object) exposes a single callback route. Incoming GET requests are converted to a small dataclass (CallbackResponse) by mapping query parameters to known fields (code, state, error, error_description).
- The handler applies a simple decision tree: if an error parameter exists, or code/state are missing, it reports a failure; otherwise it records success. Recording is done exactly once by a guard function (store_result_once) that checks a sentinel (result_ready event) to avoid races or duplicate writes.
- The handler returns an HTML page that communicates success or a user-facing error and instructs the user to close the tab. The server itself is intended to be short-lived and cooperative with higher-level code that waits on result_ready.

2. Domain knowledge required
- OAuth 2.0 authorization-code flow basics: how the authorization server redirects with code and state, the role of the state parameter to mitigate CSRF, and meaning of error/access_denied.
- How local-native apps (CLI/desktop) use a local HTTP redirect URI to receive codes.
- Concurrency primitives (event signaling) for collecting a result asynchronously.

3. Key constraints and assumptions
- Runs on loopback (127.0.0.1) and a single port; not intended as a publicly exposed HTTPS endpoint. TLS is not provided.
- Assumes the authorization server will redirect with query parameters (code/state or error); does not handle form-encoded POST callbacks.
- One-shot semantics: only the first valid callback is accepted; subsequent requests are ignored.
- The server lifecycle is external: the caller must start and stop the Server object and wait on the provided event/container.

4. Appropriate usage
- Best for native applications or command-line tools that open a browser to an OAuth authorize URL and need to capture the returned code locally.
- Not suitable for production web applications that require public HTTPS endpoints, robust multi-user handling, or long-lived callback infrastructure.

s_param.name: config
s_param.description: An MCPConfig object or a dictionary matching the MCPConfig schema that defines one or more MCP servers (key:mcpServers). If the config defines a single server the transport proxies directly to that server; if multiple servers are defined the transport composes them into a single namespaced client (tools accessible as "{server}_{tool}", resources as "protocol://{server}/path").

mechanism.text:
Acts as a coordinator and resource manager for one-or-many MCP server transports: an instance holds configuration and a live set of ClientTransport objects, and it composes per-server proxy clients into a single FastMCP router that sessions can use as if talking to one logical MCP.

Construction and core state: on init it normalises the provided config and requires at least one MCP server entry. If there is exactly one server it immediately constructs and stores a single transport for the fast-path; otherwise it keeps an internal list (_transports) empty until a session is requested. The important runtime state is the config, the name_as_prefix flag (affects proxy namespace mounting), and the list of active transport/proxy resources.

Usage and lifecycle: connect_session is an async context manager that prepares a working FastMCP composite when multiple servers are configured. For multi-server setups it opens proxy clients for each reachable server, mounts those proxies into a composite FastMCP (optionally namespacing by server), and yields a ClientSession backed by a FastMCPTransport. It uses an AsyncExitStack to register cleanup callbacks and skips servers that fail to connect; if none succeed it raises a ConnectionError. The single-server path yields sessions from the one transport directly. The instance must be explicitly closed (async close) to terminate any transports that remain open; connect_session also ensures per-session cleanup on exit.

Invariants and architectural role: the class guarantees there is at least one configured server and that _transports accurately reflects the currently active transports for multi-server sessions. It centralises connection logic, lifecycle management, and per-server transforms/tags (tool transforms, include/exclude tag rules) so higher-level code sees a unified MCP endpoint. Conceptually it is a coordinator/builder that assembles transport + proxy pieces into a routed FastMCP, while also being responsible for deterministic cleanup of those resources.

implementation:
class MCPConfigTransport(ClientTransport):

    def __init__(self, config: MCPConfig | dict, name_as_prefix: bool=True):
        if isinstance(config, dict):
            config = MCPConfig.from_dict(config)
        self.config = config
        self.name_as_prefix = name_as_prefix
        self._transports: list[ClientTransport] = []
        if not self.config.mcpServers:
            raise ValueError('No MCP servers defined in the config')
        if len(self.config.mcpServers) == 1:
            self.transport = next(iter(self.config.mcpServers.values())).to_transport()
            self._transports.append(self.transport)

    @contextlib.asynccontextmanager
    async def connect_session(self, **session_kwargs: Unpack[SessionKwargs]) -> AsyncIterator[ClientSession]:
        if len(self.config.mcpServers) == 1:
            async with self.transport.connect_session(**session_kwargs) as session:
                yield session
            return
        timeout = session_kwargs.get('read_timeout_seconds')
        composite = FastMCP[Any](name='MCPRouter')
        async with contextlib.AsyncExitStack() as stack:
            for t in self._transports:
                await t.close()
            self._transports = []
            for name, server_config in self.config.mcpServers.items():
                try:
                    transport, _client, proxy = await self._create_proxy(name, server_config, timeout, stack)
                except Exception:
                    logger.warning('Failed to connect to MCP server %r, skipping', name, exc_info=True)
                    continue
                self._transports.append(transport)
                composite.mount(proxy, namespace=name if self.name_as_prefix else None)
            if not self._transports:
                raise ConnectionError('All MCP servers failed to connect')
            async with FastMCPTransport(mcp=composite).connect_session(**session_kwargs) as session:
                yield session

    async def _create_proxy(self, name: str, config: MCPServerTypes, timeout: datetime.timedelta | None, stack: contextlib.AsyncExitStack) -> tuple[ClientTransport, Any, FastMCP[Any]]:
        from fastmcp.server.providers.proxy import StatefulProxyClient
        tool_transforms = None
        include_tags = None
        exclude_tags = None
        if isinstance(config, TransformingStdioMCPServer):
            transport = StdioMCPServer.to_transport(config)
            tool_transforms = config.tools
            include_tags = config.include_tags
            exclude_tags = config.exclude_tags
        elif isinstance(config, TransformingRemoteMCPServer):
            transport = RemoteMCPServer.to_transport(config)
            tool_transforms = config.tools
            include_tags = config.include_tags
            exclude_tags = config.exclude_tags
        else:
            transport = config.to_transport()
        client = StatefulProxyClient(transport=transport, timeout=timeout)
        await client.__aenter__()
        stack.push_async_callback(transport.close)
        stack.push_async_callback(client._disconnect, force=True)
        proxy = create_proxy(client, name=f'Proxy-{name}')
        if tool_transforms:
            from fastmcp.server.transforms import ToolTransform
            proxy.add_transform(ToolTransform(tool_transforms))
        if include_tags:
            proxy.enable(tags=set(include_tags), only=True)
        if exclude_tags:
            proxy.disable(tags=set(exclude_tags))
        return (transport, client, proxy)

    async def close(self):
        for transport in self._transports:
            await transport.close()

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        return f"<MCPConfigTransport(config='{self.config}')>"

mechanism.text:
Acts as an in-process, in-memory transport that connects a client session to a FastMCP server implementation, coordinating the streams, server lifespan, and background task that runs the server loop. Each instance encapsulates the server reference and a configuration flag controlling whether server-side exceptions should be propagated to the client caller. It is a coordinator/resource-holder rather than a protocol parser or a long-lived network socket.

Construction captures two pieces of state: a FastMCP (or FastMCP1Server) object and a boolean that controls exception propagation. It exposes connect_session as an async context manager that creates paired in-memory streams, starts the server run loop inside a background task, and yields a ClientSession bound to the client side of those streams. The transport enters the server’s lifespan manager when required, watches for exceptions from the client-session block, cancels the server task on exit, and ensures any exception raised while the session was active is re-raised to the caller (subject to the raise_exceptions setting handled by the server).

Instances do not require an explicit close method; their resources are scoped to the connect_session context: the in-memory streams and background server task are created and torn down per-session. Proper disposal therefore requires using the provided async context manager — failing to do so can leave the background task or stream state in an indeterminate state.

Key invariants: a server run loop is started for every connect_session and is cancelled once the session block exits; the server’s lifespan context is honored for FastMCP instances; any exception raised inside the session is captured and re-raised after server teardown so the caller observes it. Architecturally, this transport provides a fast, deterministic loopback channel for testing or local integrations, enabling client code to exercise the server implementation without network I/O.
