Map numerical image channels into 8-bit RGB pixel values while enforcing per-channel minima and an intensity-scaling invariant. Instances encapsulate the mapping configuration (per-channel minimums, an optional maximum or inferred range from a reference image) and small immutable state derived from that configuration (the computed range, the constant uint8 maximum). They do not hold large external resources—only references to the provided image array when present—so they act as lightweight configuration/transform objects rather than resource managers.

Construction fixes the mapping invariants: minimum must be one or three values; if maximum is absent it can be inferred from the supplied image; minimum and maximum must not be equal for any channel. From these invariants the object derives a positive range (or leaves it None if maximum is not set), and a fixed scalar representing the uint8 peak value. These invariants guarantee valid scale factors and prevent divide-by-zero during intensity scaling.

Usage is stateless aside from that configuration: callers feed channel arrays to make_rgb_image, which subtracts minima, computes a combined intensity, converts that intensity to a per-pixel scaling factor (map_intensity_to_uint8), multiplies channels by that factor, clamps negatives to zero, and performs a normalization step to keep any channel within the 0–255 bounds while preserving relative color. The Mapping base implements the general pipeline and intensity handling; LinearMapping specializes how intensity maps to uint8 (linear scaling with clipping).

No explicit disposal or closing is required—instances can be garbage-collected when no longer referenced. In the library architecture these objects function as mapping/transform components used by visualization utilities (e.g., creating Lupton-style RGB composites), separating configuration/parameter handling from the pixel-wise conversion logic so different mapping strategies can be substituted by subclassing.

mechanism.text:
Mapping astronomical image intensities into display-ready values requires compressing very large dynamic ranges while preserving faint detail and bright structure. The modified asinh stretch implemented here combines Lupton-style inverse-hyperbolic-sine (asinh) softening with an automatic linear contrast range chosen by zscale, producing an intensity mapping that is powerful for astronomical CCD images.

At its core the mapping is
y = asinh(Q * x / stretch) * (frac / asinh(frac * Q)),
with frac = 0.1 and stretch = z2 − z1. Here x is the input intensity after optionally forming an intensity image from RGB inputs. zscale is an algorithm that inspects the image histogram and fits a linear range [z1, z2] that represents the visually informative span (it resists outliers and adapts to background/feature level). Dividing x by stretch normalizes intensities to that adaptive linear span. The asinh(Q··) then compresses high values smoothly: for small arguments asinh(u) ≈ u (linear response near background), while for large u it grows logarithmically, compressing bright peaks. The multiplicative factor frac/asinh(frac·Q) normalizes the mapping so that input values at x = frac·stretch map to y = frac, anchoring mid-level contrast and making the visual scale predictable across images.

Key design choices and rationale
- Use zscale for stretch: automatic, robust selection of a useful linear interval avoids hand-tuning of display limits and reduces sensitivity to outliers.
- Lupton asinh core with parameter Q: Q controls the softening—the transition between linear and logarithmic behavior—so users can emphasize faint structure (small Q) or compress highlights more (larger Q).
- Fixed frac = 0.1: provides a consistent normalization point near background/low-signal levels so images from different data share perceptual scaling.
- Symmetric asinh: handles negative values naturally (important for background-subtracted or noise-dominated pixels).

When to use vs alternatives
- Use this stretch when you need both preserved faint detail and controlled bright-region compression in astronomical images, and you want automatic contrast limits (zscale).
- Alternatives: plain linear stretch for quantitative plots; logarithmic stretch for stronger compression but poorer faint-feature linearity; a pure asinh with manually chosen stretch when you need full control instead of zscale autoscaling.
Important constraints and assumptions
- Q must be > 0. zscale assumes a mostly well-behaved background with limited pathological outliers—very sparse bright-saturated pixels or extreme artifacts can still distort z1,z2. Handle NaNs appropriately (mask or ignore). The mapping preserves sign, so negative-valued pixels map consistently but may need careful interpretation in display contexts.
references: Preparing Red-Green-Blue Images from CCD Data

s_param.name: stretch
s_param.description: Linear stretch of the image; must be greater than 0. Controls the width of the linear region in the asinh mapping.

s_param.name: Q
s_param.description: Asinh softening parameter; must be greater than 0. Controls the transition from linear to asinh behaviour (softening).

mechanism.text:
Mapping wide dynamic-range CCD intensities into the limited 0–1 display range while preserving both faint detail and bright structure is solved here by a soft-asymptotic compression: an inverse-hyperbolic-sine (asinh) transform that behaves nearly linear for small signals and logarithmically for large signals.

Mathematical core
y = asinh(Q * x / stretch) * frac / asinh(frac * Q), where frac = 0.1.
x is the input (normally non‑negative, linear image intensity), stretch sets the linear scaling, and Q controls the softening between the linear and logarithmic regimes. For x ≪ stretch/Q the argument of asinh is small and y ≈ (Q*x/stretch) * frac / asinh(frac*Q) — approximately linear. For large x the asinh saturates like log(x), compressing highlights. The multiplicative normalization by frac / asinh(frac*Q) fixes the output scale so that x = frac * stretch maps to y = 1 (or another chosen reference), giving predictable normalization across images.

Key design decisions and rationale
- Use of asinh: preserves small-signal linearity (so faint features are not exaggerated) while compressing bright pixels smoothly, reducing banding and clipping compared with a pure log.
- Two-parameter control (stretch, Q): separates an overall linear scale (stretch) from the curvature/softening (Q), letting users tune low-end visibility and high-end compression independently.
- Fixed frac = 0.1 and the specific normalization: enforces a consistent mapping point rather than unitless arbitrary scaling; the component modifies constants from the canonical Lupton prescription to produce a slightly different normalization behavior.
- Safety constraints (stretch>0, Q>0): ensure monotonic, well-behaved transform.

When to use vs alternatives; constraints
Use this transform for RGB composition or single-channel display when you want faithful representation of faint structure without blowing out highlights — particularly for astronomical CCD data after background subtraction and per-channel scaling. Alternatives: gamma or sqrt for simpler contrast boosts, pure log for stronger compression but non-linear low end, and linear for scientific analysis. Important assumptions: inputs should be nonnegative and pre-scaled (zero-centered/background removed); identical exposure/scaling across color channels if preserving color; stretch and Q must be tuned per dataset. This implementation is a Lupton-inspired variant with modified constants to alter normalization behavior compared with Astropy’s AsinhStretch.
references: Preparing Red-Green-Blue (RGB) Images from CCD Data

mechanism.text:
Maps raw image pixel values to a 0–1 display range by first choosing numeric bounds from the image distribution and then applying a monotonic intensity stretch. The two-step approach separates "interval estimation" (how to pick vmin and vmax from the data) from "stretching" (how to remap values between those limits). Interval selection can be percentile-based, min/max, asymmetric percentiles, or manual limits; stretching can be linear, power-law, square-root, logarithmic, inverse-hyperbolic-sine, or hyperbolic-sine. The result is an ImageNormalize-like object suitable for matplotlib imshow, so values outside the chosen interval can be clipped or represented as an "invalid" color.

Understanding this requires basic image-display and visualization concepts: dynamic range, outliers, contrast, and the human-eye sensitivity that motivates nonlinear stretches (e.g., log for high-dynamic-range scenes, power or sqrt for subtle fades). Percentile-based intervals are robust to outliers because they ignore extreme tails; min/max uses full data range and is sensitive to noise and artifacts. Stretches are monotonic transforms that preserve order but reshape contrast — e.g., emphasizing faint structure (asinh/log) or bright cores (power>1). The mapping assumes numeric arrays (including NaNs) and that monotonic mapping to [0,1] is acceptable for display.

Key constraints and assumptions: the algorithm assumes a single-channel (grayscale) intensity image or per-channel normalization applied separately; it does not attempt spatial adaptive normalization. Percentile methods require enough samples to estimate statistics reliably. Nonlinear stretches may compress or expand specific value ranges and are not reversible without parameters. Invalid (NaN) handling and clipping behavior are explicit choices and affect color mapping. Use this approach when you need consistent, reproducible display normalization that balances robustness to outliers with flexible contrast shaping — for exploratory visualization, publication figures, or preparing images for color mapping in matplotlib. Avoid it for tasks requiring physically calibrated radiometry or adaptive local contrast enhancement.

a = np.array([1.0, 2.0]) * u.m

mechanism.text:
Compares two numerical quantities for approximate equality while correctly handling physical units and tolerances. Under the hood it converts inputs into unit-aware Quantity objects, coerces the desired value and absolute tolerance into the same units as the “actual” quantity, enforces that relative tolerance is dimensionless, then delegates the numeric comparison to numpy.allclose using the raw numeric arrays and the converted rtol/atol values.

Algorithmically this is a two-step process: (1) unit normalization — map all operands to a common unit system so magnitudes are directly comparable, raising errors if units are incompatible; (2) elementwise approximate-equality checking — use the standard criterion |a - b| <= atol + rtol * |b| on the underlying numeric arrays (with optional NaN-equality behavior) implemented by numpy.allclose. The role of rtol and atol remains the usual relative/absolute tradeoff after unit stripping.

Correct use requires familiarity with dimensional analysis: inputs should represent quantities with meaningful units (or be unitless), tolerances must be provided in compatible units (atol in the same units as the data, rtol dimensionless). You should understand when relative vs absolute tolerances dominate (rtol scales with signal magnitude; atol sets a floor for small-magnitude cases). Be aware of broadcasting rules for array shapes and how NaNs are handled if equal_nan=True.

Key constraints and assumptions: units must be convertible (conversion errors are raised); quantities are converted to a single “actual” unit so that precision and round-off of conversion may affect results; rtol must be dimensionless; atol defaults to zero in the same units as actual. Appropriate when comparing arrays of physical measurements where unit consistency matters — e.g., test assertions or numeric checks that must respect units — and when you need the familiar numpy approximate-equality semantics but with correct unit handling.

mechanism.text:
Converting continuous graph structure into a compact set of discrete bond tokens so a transformer can predict and reason about local chemistry. The builder takes SMILES, computes per-bond feature descriptors and a bond-context string that concatenates the bond’s own features with summarized features of neighboring bonds (for both end atoms), then clusters or enumerates these context strings into a fixed vocabulary used by GROVER-style pretraining.

Algorithmically, the module implements deterministic feature extraction and tokenization rather than learned embedding construction. For each bond it computes categorical features (bond type, conjugation, ring membership, stereo, etc.) and counts or short summaries of adjacent bond features on the two incident atoms. It encodes the context as atomSymbol–bondFeature–Count tuples, combined in a fixed order to produce a canonical context string for the bond. The output is a mapping from unique context strings to integer token IDs (the “bond vocabulary”), optionally limited to the most frequent contexts and with special handling for rare/unknown contexts.

Key design decisions: (1) Use of local context rather than global graph embedding — keeps tokens interpretable and stable across datasets and enables masked-token pretraining targets. (2) Concatenation of neighbor summaries (atomSymbol-bondFeature-Count) captures first-order chemical environment without exploding combinatorial variety; counts compress neighborhood structure while preserving multiplicity information. (3) Deterministic string keys allow reproducible vocabularies and straightforward frequency-based pruning (keep top-K contexts) to control vocabulary size and rare-case handling. (4) Use of chemically meaningful categorical features aligns tokens with domain semantics and simplifies downstream masking/objectives.

Use this builder when preparing GROVER-style self-supertraining inputs where discrete bond tokens are required for masked-bond prediction or contextual contrastive tasks. It assumes input molecules in SMILES/rdkit-parsable form and that first-order neighborhood suffices to represent bond contexts; if richer spatial or learned continuous encodings are needed (e.g., 3D geometry, learned codebooks), prefer pretrained graph encoders or vector quantization approaches instead.
references: Self-Supervised Graph Transformer on Large-Scale Molecular Data

mechanism.text:
Representing an atom's local chemical context as a discrete token simplifies the self-supervised pretraining objective used by GROVER: predict masked atom tokens from graph context. The Atom Vocabulary Builder converts each atom in a molecule (from SMILES) into a short, discrete context string that captures the one-hop neighborhood in terms of neighbor element type, bond class, and multiplicity; the set of all distinct context strings across a corpus becomes the atom vocabulary used for masked-token prediction.

Algorithmically, for each molecule the builder:
- parses the SMILES into a molecular graph (atom nodes, labeled bonds);
- for each atom i, forms the multiset S_i = { (element(j), bond_type(i,j)) : j ∈ N(i) };
- counts identical (element, bond_type) pairs to produce entries like (C, SINGLE, 2);
- canonicalizes and sorts these entries into a deterministic string token (e.g., "C-SINGLE1;O-DOUBLE1");
- accumulates token frequencies across the dataset, applies a frequency cutoff (or maps rare tokens to an UNK token), and emits a vocabulary mapping token ↔ integer id.

Key design choices and rationale:
- One-hop neighborhood only: balances chemical specificity and combinatorial explosion; most valence-related chemistry is captured locally and this keeps vocabulary tractable.
- Discrete counts rather than continuous descriptors: enables a straightforward masked-token classification objective analogous to language-modeling, simplifying pretraining and leveraging categorical cross-entropy loss.
- Bond-type grouping (single/double/aromatic/etc.) and canonical token formatting: reduces token sparsity and ensures consistent hashing across SMILES permutations.
- Frequency thresholding / UNK mapping: controls vocabulary size, prevents overfitting to rare contexts, and keeps memory/softmax costs manageable.

When to use vs alternatives:
- Use this builder when training or evaluating GROVER-style masked-atom prediction objectives or when you want compact, interpretable atom tokens for graph transformers.
- Alternatives include continuous atom embeddings (learned from atom features), subgraph fingerprints (e.g., Morgan), or higher-radius substructure tokens; those capture longer-range or continuous variation but lose the simple discrete pretraining target and may increase model complexity.

Important constraints/assumptions: requires correct molecular parsing (RDKit/SMILES), treats only local (1-hop) context so long-range stereoelectronic effects are not encoded, and vocabulary quality depends on corpus diversity and chosen frequency cutoff.
references: Self-Supervised Graph Transformer on Large-Scale Molecular Data

import numpy as np
import torch
from deepchem.feat.graph_data import GraphData
from torch_geometric.nn import global_mean_pool
from deepchem.models.losses import DeepGraphInfomaxLoss

# Create a small graph with 4 nodes belonging to 2 graphs
x = np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1], [0, 0]])
edge_index = np.array([[0, 1, 2, 0, 3], [1, 0, 1, 3, 2]])
graph_index = np.array([0, 0, 1, 1])

# Convert to torch Geometric compatible GraphData
data = GraphData(node_features=x, edge_index=edge_index, graph_index=graph_index).numpy_to_torch()

# Instantiate DeepGraphInfomaxLoss and obtain the pytorch loss callable
graph_infomax_loss = DeepGraphInfomaxLoss()._create_pytorch_loss()

# Random node embeddings (num_nodes x embedding_dim)
num_nodes = data.num_nodes
embedding_dim = 8
node_emb = torch.randn(num_nodes, embedding_dim)

# Compute per-graph pooled summary embeddings (num_graphs x embedding_dim)
summary_emb = global_mean_pool(node_emb, data.graph_index)

# Expand the summary to each node according to its graph membership
positive_expanded_summary_emb = summary_emb[data.graph_index]

# Create a negative summary by shifting graph summaries (simple corruption)
negative_summary_emb = torch.roll(summary_emb, shifts=1, dims=0)
negative_expanded_summary_emb = negative_summary_emb[data.graph_index]

# Compute similarity scores (one score per node)
positive_score = torch.sum(node_emb * positive_expanded_summary_emb, dim=1)
negative_score = torch.sum(node_emb * negative_expanded_summary_emb, dim=1)

# Compute the Deep Graph Infomax loss
loss = graph_infomax_loss(positive_score, negative_score)
print('DGIM loss:', loss.item())

mechanism.text:
Encouraging node embeddings to be similar to a graph-level summary while dissimilar to summaries from corrupted graphs, the loss implements a contrastive mutual-information objective: it trains a discriminator to score pairs of (node embedding, summary embedding) high when they come from the same graph and low when either the node or the summary is from a corrupted example.

Mathematical core: given node embeddings {h_i} and a pooled summary s (usually a nonlinear readout of all h_i), the loss uses a binary classification objective over positive pairs (h_i, s) and negative pairs (h_i, s̃) where s̃ is a summary of a corrupted graph. If f(h, s) is a scalar compatibility score (commonly a bilinear form or dot product), the per-node contribution is
  L_i = - log σ( f(h_i, s) ) - log (1 - σ( f(h_i, s̃) )),
and the loss averages over nodes (and possibly over multiple corruptions). This approximates maximizing mutual information between local and global representations via a Jensen–Shannon-style estimator implemented by a logistic discriminator. In practice the component accepts precomputed positive_score (f(h_i, s)) and negative_score tensors and applies the sigmoid/logistic cross-entropy aggregation above.

Key design decisions and rationale:
- Use of a discriminator-based objective rather than explicit MI estimators: practical, stable, and scalable to many nodes because it reduces MI maximization to a binary classification problem.
- Local-versus-global contrast: pairing each node with a pooled summary encourages embeddings to capture features that are both discriminative locally and coherent globally (promotes nearby nodes having similar embeddings).
- Corruption mechanism for negatives: generating negatives by perturbing features or graph structure yields challenging negatives that improve representation quality.
- Per-node loss and pooling: averaging over nodes ties global summary learning to node-level structure, rather than only global graph classification.

When to use vs alternatives / constraints:
- Use for unsupervised pretraining of GNNs when node/graph labels are scarce and you want node embeddings that reflect graph context. It’s especially helpful when local structure matters.
- Alternatives: supervised objectives when labels exist, or other contrastive graph methods (GraphCL, InfoGraph) that use different augmentation/contrast schemes; those may outperform DGI if you can design stronger augmentations or need graph-level invariance instead of local-global MI.
- Important assumptions/constraints: requires a meaningful corruption strategy for negatives, relies on the pooled summary capturing useful global context, and can be sensitive to the choice of discriminator parametrization and negative sampling.
references: Deep Graph Infomax

mechanism.text:
Maps a compact parameter vector to an orthonormal set of molecular-orbital coefficients via a unitary rotation and exposes the inverse mapping expected by the surrounding orbital-parameter API. Conceptually, instances act as a stateless parameterization strategy: they do not hold data or resources but implement the rules that translate optimization parameters into usable orbital coefficient matrices and back.

The forward direction (params2orb) interprets the parameter vector as the independent entries of an upper-triangular generator of an antisymmetric (skew-Hermitian) matrix, embeds those entries into a full square generator, and exponentiates it to produce a unitary rotation. That rotation is applied to an input coefficient matrix to produce rotated, orthonormal orbitals. Because the mapping is constructed from a matrix exponential of an antisymmetric generator, orthonormality of orbitals is preserved by design—this is the primary invariant. The implementation also preserves batch shape, dtype, and device, and optionally returns a differentiable scalar "penalty" placeholder to fit optimizer interfaces.

The reverse direction (orb2params) is effectively a lightweight placeholder that calculates the expected parameter vector length from the orbital dimensions and returns a zero-filled parameter vector together with the provided coefficients. In a full implementation this would extract independent rotation parameters (for example via a logarithm of the unitary), but here it signals the intended contract: an optimizer sees a parameter vector and a canonical coefficient tensor.

Lifecycle is trivial: no construction, no disposal, and no internal state to manage—methods are static and intended to be called whenever conversion between parameter space and orbital space is required during optimization or model evaluation. In the library architecture this class serves as a "builder/representation" component for orbital parameterizations: it enforces orthonormality through a unitary parameter map and provides the interface that higher-level DFT/HF optimization routines expect for generating and consuming orbital coefficients.

mechanism.text:
Representations are learned by pulling together embeddings of chemically equivalent inputs (different conformers of the same molecule) and pushing apart embeddings of different molecules using a temperature-scaled softmax over cosine similarities. Concretely, the implemented loss is the NT-Xent / InfoNCE-style contrastive objective used in SimCLR, modified so a sample can have multiple positive examples instead of exactly one.

Mathematical core
- Let z be the network output (embedding) for each conformer; when norm=True embeddings are L2-normalized so cosine similarity = dot product. For a given anchor i, let P(i) be the set of indices that are positive examples (other conformers of the same molecule). With temperature τ, the loss for anchor i is
  L_i = − log ( sum_{j∈P(i)} exp(sim(z_i,z_j)/τ) / sum_{k≠i} exp(sim(z_i,z_k)/τ) ).
- sim(·,·) is typically cosine similarity; the denominator runs over all other samples in the batch (negatives plus positives). The overall loss is the average over anchors (and sometimes averaged symmetrically over both directions of pairs).

Key design decisions and rationale
- Allowing multiple positives per anchor: multiple conformers capture meaningful 3D variability; treating them all as positives increases invariance to conformational changes and uses additional supervision per molecule.
- L2 normalization (norm flag): makes cosine similarity numeric-stable and places embeddings on a hypersphere so the temperature τ directly controls concentration. Normalization often improves training stability and quality.
- Using batch-level negatives: efficient and simple, but requires sufficiently large and diverse batches (or a memory bank/queue) for good negative sampling.
- Softmax/InfoNCE formulation: converts pairwise similarities into a probabilistic discrimination task that scales well and has theoretical links to mutual information maximization.

When to use vs alternatives; constraints
- Use this loss for unsupervised pretraining of GNNs when you have multiple conformers per molecule and want conformer-invariant molecular embeddings. It is preferable when contrastive invariance (not explicit property prediction) is the goal.
- Alternatives: triplet or margin losses (simpler but less stable and require mining), supervised regression/classification when labels exist, or generative/self-predictive objectives (different inductive biases).
- Important assumptions/constraints: you must know which conformers belong to the same molecule; performance depends on batch size and negative diversity; computational cost grows with batch size and number of positives; embedding normalization and choice of τ materially affect outcomes.
references: A Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning of Visual Representations
3D Infomax improves GNNs for Molecular Property Prediction

implementation:
class NTXentMultiplePositives(Loss):

    def __init__(self, norm: bool=True, tau: float=0.5, uniformity_reg=0, variance_reg=0, covariance_reg=0, conformer_variance_reg=0) -> None:
        super(NTXentMultiplePositives, self).__init__()
        self.norm = norm
        self.tau = tau
        self.uniformity_reg = uniformity_reg
        self.variance_reg = variance_reg
        self.covariance_reg = covariance_reg
        self.conformer_variance_reg = conformer_variance_reg

    def _create_pytorch_loss(self):
        import torch
        from torch import Tensor

        def std_loss(x: Tensor) -> Tensor:
            std = torch.sqrt(x.var(dim=0) + 0.0001)
            return torch.mean(torch.relu(1 - std))

        def uniformity_loss(x1: Tensor, x2: Tensor, t=2) -> Tensor:
            sq_pdist_x1 = torch.pdist(x1, p=2).pow(2)
            uniformity_x1 = sq_pdist_x1.mul(-t).exp().mean().log()
            sq_pdist_x2 = torch.pdist(x2, p=2).pow(2)
            uniformity_x2 = sq_pdist_x2.mul(-t).exp().mean().log()
            return (uniformity_x1 + uniformity_x2) / 2

        def cov_loss(x: Tensor) -> Tensor:
            batch_size, metric_dim = x.size()
            x = x - x.mean(dim=0)
            cov = x.T @ x / (batch_size - 1)
            off_diag_cov = cov.flatten()[:-1].view(metric_dim - 1, metric_dim + 1)[:, 1:].flatten()
            return off_diag_cov.pow_(2).sum() / metric_dim

        def loss(z1: Tensor, z2: Tensor) -> Tensor:
            batch_size, metric_dim = z1.size()
            z2 = z2.view(batch_size, -1, metric_dim)
            z2 = z2.view(batch_size, -1, metric_dim)
            sim_matrix = torch.einsum('ik,juk->iju', z1, z2)
            if self.norm:
                z1_abs = z1.norm(dim=1)
                z2_abs = z2.norm(dim=2)
                sim_matrix = sim_matrix / torch.einsum('i,ju->iju', z1_abs, z2_abs)
            sim_matrix = torch.exp(sim_matrix / self.tau)
            sim_matrix = sim_matrix.sum(dim=2)
            pos_sim = torch.diagonal(sim_matrix)
            loss = pos_sim / (sim_matrix.sum(dim=1) - pos_sim)
            loss = -torch.log(loss).mean()
            if self.variance_reg > 0:
                loss += self.variance_reg * (std_loss(z1) + std_loss(z2))
            if self.conformer_variance_reg > 0:
                std = torch.sqrt(z2.var(dim=1) + 0.0001)
                std_conf_loss = torch.mean(torch.relu(1 - std))
                loss += self.conformer_variance_reg * std_conf_loss
            if self.covariance_reg > 0:
                loss += self.covariance_reg * (cov_loss(z1) + cov_loss(z2))
            if self.uniformity_reg > 0:
                loss += self.uniformity_reg * uniformity_loss(z1, z2)
            return loss
        return loss

# --- helper: deepchem.models.losses.Loss ---
class Loss:

from deepchem.metalearning.torch_maml import MAML

# Minimal MetaLearner implementation following the docstring pattern.
class SineLearner(dc.metalearning.torch_maml.MetaLearner):
    def __init__(self):
        # model parameters as torch.nn.Parameter
        self.w1 = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(np.random.normal(size=(1, 40)), dtype=torch.float32))
        self.w2 = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(np.random.normal(size=(40, 40)), dtype=torch.float32))
        self.w3 = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(np.random.normal(size=(40, 1)), dtype=torch.float32))
        self.b1 = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(40, dtype=torch.float32))
        self.b2 = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(40, dtype=torch.float32))
        self.b3 = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1, dtype=torch.float32))
        self.batch_size = 10

    # Provide variables as a read-only property (MetaLearner expects this)
    @property
    def variables(self):
        return [self.w1, self.w2, self.w3, self.b1, self.b2, self.b3]

    # Minimal compute_model implementation: forward pass using provided variables
    def compute_model(self, inputs, variables, training):
        x, _ = inputs
        w1, w2, w3, b1, b2, b3 = variables
        x = torch.matmul(x, w1) + b1
        x = torch.relu(x)
        x = torch.matmul(x, w2) + b2
        x = torch.relu(x)
        x = torch.matmul(x, w3) + b3
        return x

# Instantiate the learner and the MAML wrapper
learner = SineLearner()
maml = MAML(learner=learner, learning_rate=0.01, optimization_steps=1, meta_batch_size=5, model_dir=None, device=torch.device("cpu"))

mechanism.text:
Rapidly adapting a neural model to new tasks from only a handful of examples by learning an initialization that is easy to fine-tune. MAML trains a single set of parameters θ so that a small number of gradient steps on a new task's small training set produces parameters θ' that perform well on that task's validation set.

Algorithmic core implemented
- Inner (task) update: for each task T, compute adapted parameters via one or more gradient steps on the task's support set:
  θ_T' = θ − α ∇_θ L_T(support; θ).
- Meta (outer) objective: minimize the post-adaptation loss across tasks' query sets:
  min_θ ∑_T L_T(query; θ_T').
- Meta-update: compute gradients of the outer loss w.r.t. θ (this requires differentiating through the inner update) and apply an optimizer step (learning rate β).
DeepChem’s component implements this loop: sampling batches of tasks, performing inner optimization per task, backpropagating the query-set loss through the inner steps to update the shared initialization θ. It therefore supports multi-step inner updates, tunable inner/outer learning rates (α, β), and batching over tasks.

Key design decisions and rationale
- Differentiating through inner steps (full MAML) vs. omitting second-order terms (first-order approximations): full differentiation yields more accurate meta-gradients but incurs higher memory and compute; exposing both options lets users trade fidelity for speed.
- Task batching and few-shot splits (support/query): necessary to estimate meta-objective robustly while mimicking low-data adaptation at test time.
- Model-agnostic interface: any differentiable DeepChem model can be wrapped, enabling reuse across prediction heads and architectures.
- Configurable number of inner steps and optimizers: controls adaptation depth and stability.

When to use and constraints
Use MAML when you have many related tasks and need a model that quickly adapts to new tasks with very few labeled examples. Constraints: tasks must be differentiable supervised objectives; training is compute- and memory-intensive (especially with higher-order gradients); meta-training requires a sizeable collection of tasks representative of the deployment tasks. If tasks are scarce, highly heterogeneous, or you need cheaper training, consider simpler fine-tuning baselines or metric-based few-shot methods. Also watch for inner-loop issues (batch norm/statistics, catastrophic overfitting) and tune inner-step count and learning rates accordingly.
references: Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning for Fast Adaptation of Deep Networks

mechanism.text:
Estimating a contrastive/divergence objective requires separately reducing the contribution of "negative" (product-of-marginals) samples to a scalar divergence estimate; get_negative_expectation implements that reduction as a small library of variational transforms. Concretely, given critic scores T(x) computed on negative samples q (i.e., samples drawn from the marginal/product distribution), the function returns Ep = E_{q}[h(T)] where h is the specific transform that yields the negative part of a chosen variational bound or f‑divergence estimator.

Mathematical/algorithmic core
- The abstraction is: a critic produces scalar scores T; the negative expectation for a chosen measure is the sample average (or sum) of a measure-specific function h(T). Different measures correspond to different variational representations:
  - f‑divergence / f‑GAN style: h(T) = f^*(T) where f^* is the convex conjugate of the chosen f. This maps to transforms used in f‑GAN estimators.
  - Donsker–Varadhan (DV) bound: h(T) = exp(T) (with normalization in the full bound).
  - Jensen–Shannon (JSD) / GAN-style: h(T) is implemented via log-sigmoid / softplus variants that match the JSD variational form.
  - KL, χ^2 and others use their corresponding convex-conjugate transforms or direct forms (e.g., KL's negative term is simply E_q[T]).
- The implementation is a dispatcher: measure name → numerically stable elementwise transform (uses softplus/log-sum-exp patterns where necessary) → optional averaging across batch.

Key design decisions and rationale
- Single, small API that separates "critic scoring" from "measure-specific reduction" so losses can reuse the same critic outputs with multiple divergence estimators.
- Vectorized, elementwise transforms for efficiency and GPU compatibility.
- Numerical stability: use softplus/log-sum-exp patterns for transforms involving log(1+exp(·)) or log-sigmoid to avoid overflow.
- Option to average preserves flexibility: return per-sample terms for weighted losses or mean for direct scalar losses.

When to use vs alternatives; assumptions
- Use this when implementing mutual-information or adversarial-style losses that need the negative/marginal contribution (e.g., GlobalMutualInformationLoss). It’s appropriate when you have scores from a learned critic and want a particular variational bound or f‑divergence estimate.
- Choose the estimator based on bias/variance and robustness: DV tends to be high-variance but tight, JSD/GAN-style is more stable, f‑GAN/KL variants give different sensitivities. 
- Assumes negative samples are drawn from the marginal/product distribution and that critic outputs are appropriate (unconstrained scalar or in a domain expected by the chosen transform). Some transforms assume positivity or operate on log-space — pick measures consistent with your critic parametrization.
references: InfoGraph: Unsupervised and Semi-supervised Graph-Level Representation Learning via Mutual Information Maximization

mechanism.text: Computes the numerically stable log of the sum of exponentials of input values along a specified axis: y = log sum(exp(x), axis=axis), typically implemented with a max-shift to avoid overflow. It returns a tensor with the given axis reduced (broadcastable to the original shape if needed). Use it when aggregating logits or log-probabilities (e.g., log-likelihoods, log-sum for mixture models) or when implementing softmax/partition functions while preserving numerical stability.

implementation:
def log_sum_exp(x, axis=None):
    import torch
    x_max = torch.max(x, axis)[0]
    y = torch.log(torch.exp(x - x_max).sum(axis)) + x_max
    return y

mechanism.text:
Computes a scalar (or per-sample) contribution corresponding to the "positive" expectation term used in several variational divergence / objective estimators by applying a measure-specific nonlinear transform to critic scores sampled from the joint (positive) distribution.

Conceptually, many mutual-information estimators and adversarial/divergence objectives express a divergence or lower bound as a difference of expectations: E_{p}[\phi(T(x,y))] − E_{q}[\psi(T(x̃,y))], where T is a learned critic (log-density-ratio proxy) and φ/ψ are measure-dependent maps. This routine implements the φ part for a variety of measures (GAN, JSD, X2, KL, reverse-KL, Donsker–Varadhan, H2, W1) by applying element-wise transforms such as softplus-based forms (stable approximation to log(1+exp(·))), exponentials, squares, or identity. The average_loss flag optionally reduces the per-sample values to their mean.

Domain knowledge required: familiarity with variational divergence estimation, choice of f-divergence or lower bound (e.g., f-GANs, MINE/DV, JSD-based estimators), and the interpretation of critic outputs as (unnormalized) log-density ratios or logits. You must know which transform pair (positive vs negative expectation) corresponds to a mathematically consistent objective for the chosen measure and maintain consistent sign/conventions for critic outputs.

Key constraints and assumptions: p_samples should be torch tensors of critic scores coming from the joint distribution (positive pairs). The implemented transforms assume specific analytic forms of φ for each measure; they are not interchangeable without adjusting the negative term. Numerical stability is partially handled by softplus, but large-magnitude inputs can still overflow for exp. The function does not compute the full loss — the negative expectation counterpart is required.

Appropriate usage: when implementing training objectives that explicitly separate positive and negative expectations (e.g., contrastive/MINE-style estimators, f-GAN objectives). Use it as the positive-side term only, paired with the correct negative-side transform for the same divergence, and ensure critic output semantics match the derivation.

mechanism.text:
Capturing pairwise, content‑based interactions between elements in a sequence by a simple, differentiable kernel: scaled dot‑product attention scores each query against all keys, turns those scores into a distribution via softmax, and uses that distribution to aggregate value vectors into context-aware outputs.

Mathematical core implemented
- Given query matrix Q ∈ R^{n_q×d_k}, key matrix K ∈ R^{n_k×d_k}, and value matrix V ∈ R^{n_k×d_v}, compute raw scores S = Q K^T (shape n_q×n_k).
- Scale: S' = S / sqrt(d_k). Scaling stabilises gradients and prevents softmax from saturating when d_k is large.
- Normalize: A = softmax(S', dim=-1). Optionally apply an additive mask (e.g., causal mask or padding mask) before softmax.
- Aggregate: Output = A V, returning both Output ∈ R^{n_q×d_v} and attention weights A (often returned for inspection or loss terms).

Key design decisions and rationale
- Scaling by sqrt(d_k): maintains variance of dot products roughly constant with dimensionality, preventing extremely small softmax gradients and improving training stability.
- Softmax normalization: converts similarity scores into a convex weighting over values, letting the model perform soft selections.
- Matrix-multiplication formulation: expresses the whole operation as a few batched GEMMs for GPU efficiency (O(n^2 d_k) time, O(n^2) memory for weights).
- Optional masking and dropout: masks impose structural constraints (causal attention or ignore padded tokens); dropout on A regularizes attention.
- Single‑head vs multi‑head: DeepChem’s ScaledDotProductAttention implements the atomic per‑head operation; multi‑head attention composes several independent SDPA instances with lower-dimensional subspaces.

When to use vs alternatives; constraints and assumptions
- Use SDPA when you need content-dependent, parallelizable interactions (e.g., Transformer encoder/decoder blocks). It excels at modeling long-range dependencies compared with local convs or RNNs.
- Alternatives: additive (Bahdanau) attention can perform better for small d_k or when cosine/dot similarity is inappropriate; sparse or linearised attention variants reduce O(n^2) cost for very long sequences.
- Important constraints: assumes dot product is a meaningful similarity (so inputs should be in compatible vector spaces), requires comparable d_k across Q and K, and needs positional information externally if order matters. Memory/time scale quadratically with sequence length, and numerical stability requires the sqrt(d_k) scaling (and often masking and attention dropout).
references: Attention Is All You Need

mechanism.text:
Predicting an energy-like scalar (e.g., protein–ligand binding affinity or per-molecule energy) directly from 3D atomic coordinates by learning local geometric interactions. Atomic convolutional networks (ACNNs) extend graph convolution ideas to continuous 3D space: atoms are nodes, edges are defined by spatial proximity, and learnable radial filters operate on interatomic distances to produce per-atom feature updates that are pooled to a global energy score.

Algorithmic core implemented
- Neighborhood construction: for each atom i, gather neighbors j within a cutoff R_c (often via a neighbor list) and record pairwise distances r_ij and discrete atom types.
- Continuous convolution: each neighbor j contributes through learnable radial basis/filters g_k(r_ij) that are functions of distance (e.g., Gaussian or learned MLPs). Atom-type-specific channels modulate these contributions. A typical update has the form
  h_i = concat_a Sum_{j in N(i), type(j)=a} w_a * phi(r_ij),
  where phi are radial filter responses and w_a are learnable weights or embeddings for atom types.
- Local aggregation and stacking: per-atom vectors pass through pointwise nonlinearities and additional convolutional layers that mix information across neighbor-aggregated channels.
- Readout for energy: per-atom outputs are passed through shared dense layers to produce scalar per-atom energy contributions; the molecular energy is the sum (or sum plus global fc) of those contributions, enforcing extensivity.

Key design decisions and rationale
- Distance-based continuous filters (instead of discrete adjacency) preserve 3D geometric information and rotational invariance while being permutation equivariant across atoms.
- Atom-type channels let the model learn different interaction patterns depending on element types without hand-designing pair potentials.
- A cutoff radius limits computational cost and encodes locality of physical interactions.
- Summation readout enforces that total energy decomposes into local atomic contributions, a physically motivated inductive bias that helps generalization.

When to use vs alternatives; constraints
- Use ACNNs when accurate 3D geometry is available and the target is an energy-like scalar sensitive to spatial arrangement (binding affinity, formation energy). They outperform purely 2D graph models when 3D structure matters.
- Alternatives: message-passing GNNs on graphs when only connectivity is known; equivariant networks (SE(3)-equivariant models, SchNet/PhysNet variants) if preserving full rotational behavior or modeling forces is required.
- Important assumptions/constraints: requires reliable 3D coordinates (noisy/missing coordinates degrade performance), choice of cutoff and radial basis affects expressivity and compute, neighbor-list construction and batching can be memory/compute intensive for large complexes.
references: Atomic Convolutional Networks for Predicting Protein-Ligand Binding Affinity

implementation:
class AtomConvModel(TorchModel):

    def __init__(self, n_tasks: int, frag1_num_atoms: int=70, frag2_num_atoms: int=634, complex_num_atoms: int=701, max_num_neighbors: int=12, batch_size: int=24, atom_types: Sequence[float]=[6, 7.0, 8.0, 9.0, 11.0, 12.0, 15.0, 16.0, 17.0, 20.0, 25.0, 30.0, 35.0, 53.0, -1.0], radial: Sequence[Sequence[float]]=[[1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5, 4.0, 4.5, 5.0, 5.5, 6.0, 6.5, 7.0, 7.5, 8.0, 8.5, 9.0, 9.5, 10.0, 10.5, 11.0, 11.5, 12.0], [0.0, 4.0, 8.0], [0.4]], layer_sizes=[100], weight_init_stddevs: OneOrMany[float]=0.02, bias_init_consts: OneOrMany[float]=1.0, weight_decay_penalty: float=0.0, weight_decay_penalty_type: str='l2', dropouts: OneOrMany[float]=0.5, activation_fns: OneOrMany[ActivationFn]=['relu'], residual: bool=False, learning_rate=0.001, **kwargs) -> None:
        self.n_tasks = n_tasks
        self.complex_num_atoms = complex_num_atoms
        self.frag1_num_atoms = frag1_num_atoms
        self.frag2_num_atoms = frag2_num_atoms
        self.max_num_neighbors = max_num_neighbors
        self.batch_size = batch_size
        self.atom_types = atom_types
        self.model = AtomicConv(n_tasks=n_tasks, frag1_num_atoms=frag1_num_atoms, frag2_num_atoms=frag2_num_atoms, complex_num_atoms=complex_num_atoms, max_num_neighbors=max_num_neighbors, batch_size=batch_size, atom_types=atom_types, radial=radial, layer_sizes=layer_sizes, weight_init_stddevs=weight_init_stddevs, bias_init_consts=bias_init_consts, dropouts=dropouts, activation_fns=activation_fns, residual=residual, learning_rate=learning_rate)
        regularization_loss: Optional[Callable]
        if weight_decay_penalty != 0:
            weights = [layer.weight for layer in self.model.layers]
            if weight_decay_penalty_type == 'l1':
                regularization_loss = lambda: weight_decay_penalty * torch.sum(torch.stack([torch.abs(w).sum() for w in weights]))
            else:
                regularization_loss = lambda: weight_decay_penalty * torch.sum(torch.stack([torch.square(w).sum() for w in weights]))
        else:
            regularization_loss = None
        loss = L2Loss()
        super(AtomConvModel, self).__init__(self.model, loss=loss, batch_size=batch_size, regularization_loss=regularization_loss, **kwargs)

    def default_generator(self, dataset: Dataset, epochs: int=1, mode: str='fit', deterministic: bool=True, pad_batches: bool=True) -> Iterable[Tuple[List, List, List]]:
        batch_size = self.batch_size

        def replace_atom_types(z):
            np.putmask(z, np.isin(z, list(self.atom_types), invert=True), -1)
            return z
        for epoch in range(epochs):
            for ind, (F_b, y_b, w_b, ids_b) in enumerate(dataset.iterbatches(batch_size, deterministic=True, pad_batches=pad_batches)):
                N = self.complex_num_atoms
                N_1 = self.frag1_num_atoms
                N_2 = self.frag2_num_atoms
                M = self.max_num_neighbors
                batch_size = F_b.shape[0]
                num_features = F_b[0][0].shape[1]
                frag1_X_b = np.zeros((batch_size, N_1, num_features))
                for i in range(batch_size):
                    frag1_X_b[i] = F_b[i][0]
                frag2_X_b = np.zeros((batch_size, N_2, num_features))
                for i in range(batch_size):
                    frag2_X_b[i] = F_b[i][3]
                complex_X_b = np.zeros((batch_size, N, num_features))
                for i in range(batch_size):
                    complex_X_b[i] = F_b[i][6]
                frag1_Nbrs = np.zeros((batch_size, N_1, M))
                frag1_Z_b = np.zeros((batch_size, N_1))
                for i in range(batch_size):
                    z = replace_atom_types(F_b[i][2])
                    frag1_Z_b[i] = z
                frag1_Nbrs_Z = np.zeros((batch_size, N_1, M))
                for atom in range(N_1):
                    for i in range(batch_size):
                        atom_nbrs = F_b[i][1].get(atom, '')
                        frag1_Nbrs[i, atom, :len(atom_nbrs)] = np.array(atom_nbrs)
                        for j, atom_j in enumerate(atom_nbrs):
                            frag1_Nbrs_Z[i, atom, j] = frag1_Z_b[i, atom_j]
                frag2_Nbrs = np.zeros((batch_size, N_2, M))
                frag2_Z_b = np.zeros((batch_size, N_2))
                for i in range(batch_size):
                    z = replace_atom_types(F_b[i][5])
                    frag2_Z_b[i] = z
                frag2_Nbrs_Z = np.zeros((batch_size, N_2, M))
                for atom in range(N_2):
                    for i in range(batch_size):
                        atom_nbrs = F_b[i][4].get(atom, '')
                        frag2_Nbrs[i, atom, :len(atom_nbrs)] = np.array(atom_nbrs)
                        for j, atom_j in enumerate(atom_nbrs):
                            frag2_Nbrs_Z[i, atom, j] = frag2_Z_b[i, atom_j]
                complex_Nbrs = np.zeros((batch_size, N, M))
                complex_Z_b = np.zeros((batch_size, N))
                for i in range(batch_size):
                    z = replace_atom_types(F_b[i][8])
                    complex_Z_b[i] = z
                complex_Nbrs_Z = np.zeros((batch_size, N, M))
                for atom in range(N):
                    for i in range(batch_size):
                        atom_nbrs = F_b[i][7].get(atom, '')
                        complex_Nbrs[i, atom, :len(atom_nbrs)] = np.array(atom_nbrs)
                        for j, atom_j in enumerate(atom_nbrs):
                            complex_Nbrs_Z[i, atom, j] = complex_Z_b[i, atom_j]
                inputs = [frag1_X_b, frag1_Nbrs, frag1_Nbrs_Z, frag1_Z_b, frag2_X_b, frag2_Nbrs, frag2_Nbrs_Z, frag2_Z_b, complex_X_b, complex_Nbrs, complex_Nbrs_Z, complex_Z_b]
                y_b = np.reshape(y_b, newshape=(batch_size, 1))
                yield (inputs, [y_b], [w_b])

import torch

    return x.mean(dim=1)

mechanism.text: Acts as the prediction head for a modular graph neural network: it manages pooling of node- or graph-level representations and applies a downstream prediction module configured for regression or classification tasks. Instances encapsulate task type, task count, and class count and produce final outputs (scalars or logits) after pooling. Typical lifecycle: instantiate with a pooling function/module and a head, plug into a GNN pipeline, receive pooled features during training or inference, and output per-task predictions.

implementation:
class GNNHead(torch.nn.Module):

    def __init__(self, pool, head, task, num_tasks, num_classes):
        super().__init__()
        self.pool = pool
        self.head = head
        self.task = task
        self.num_tasks = num_tasks
        self.num_classes = num_classes

    def forward(self, data):
        node_representation, input_batch = data
        pooled = self.pool(node_representation, input_batch.graph_index)
        out = self.head(pooled)
        if self.task == 'classification':
            out = torch.reshape(out, (-1, self.num_tasks, self.num_classes))
        return out

mechanism.text:
Solving the many-electron Schrödinger equation by direct parametrisation of the antisymmetric wavefunction: Ferminet implements a neural network ansatz for the electronic ground-state wavefunction that is trained with Variational Monte Carlo (VMC). It represents orbitals as learned functions of electron coordinates and learned inter-electron / electron–nucleus features, builds antisymmetry by placing those orbitals into spin-specific determinants, and then minimises the expected quantum energy via stochastic sampling.

Mathematical / algorithmic core implemented
- Wavefunction ansatz: psi(X) = A(X) · exp(B(X)) where A(X) is a linear combination of Slater determinants of learned single-particle orbitals and B(X) is an envelope (symmetric) factor. Orbitals are not fixed basis functions but outputs of deep networks that take both single-electron inputs (r_i relative to nuclei) and permutation-equivariant pairwise features (functions of r_i - r_j).
- Permutation equivariance: electron features are constructed with layers that aggregate pairwise information so outputs transform correctly under electron permutations; determinants then enforce antisymmetry across spin channels.
- Training loop: pretrain the network to a Hartree–Fock (HF) baseline (matching orbital values) to stabilise optimisation, then run VMC: sample electron configurations by Metropolis-type moves, compute local energy E_loc(x) = H psi / psi, and backpropagate gradients of the Monte Carlo-estimated energy (or variance-regularised objectives) to update network parameters.

Key design decisions and rationale
- Learned orbitals + determinants: combining deep feature learning with determinants captures complex correlation while guaranteeing fermionic antisymmetry.
- Pairwise, permutation-equivariant layers: explicitly model electron–electron correlations (backflow-like) rather than relying solely on one-electron basis expansions.
- Envelope functions: enforce correct asymptotic and cusp behaviour and stabilise optimisation.
- HF pretraining: reduces optimisation difficulty and improves sampling efficiency by starting near a physically sensible mean-field solution.

When to use vs alternatives; constraints
- Use Ferminet when high-accuracy ab initio energies and correlated wavefunctions are needed for few- to moderate-size molecules where traditional quantum-chemistry methods (e.g., coupled-cluster) are costly or insufficient, and when one can afford heavy compute for VMC sampling and gradient-based training.
- Not ideal for very large systems due to cubic-to-worse scaling (determinants, sampling) and heavy sample requirements; assumes fixed nuclei (Born–Oppenheimer), nonrelativistic Hamiltonian, and needs careful hyperparameter / sampler tuning.
references: Better, Faster Fermionic Neural Networks

implementation:
class Ferminet(torch.nn.Module):

    def __init__(self, nucleon_pos: torch.Tensor, nuclear_charge: torch.Tensor, spin: tuple, n_one: List=[256, 256, 256, 256], n_two: List=[32, 32, 32, 32], determinant: int=16, batch_size: int=8) -> None:
        super(Ferminet, self).__init__()
        if len(n_one) != len(n_two):
            raise ValueError('The number of layers in one-electron and two-electron stream should be equal')
        else:
            self.layers = len(n_one)
        self.nucleon_pos = nucleon_pos
        self.determinant = determinant
        self.batch_size = batch_size
        self.spin = spin
        self.total_electron = spin[0] + spin[1]
        self.nuclear_charge = nuclear_charge
        self.n_one = n_one
        self.n_two = n_two
        self.ferminet_layer: torch.nn.ModuleList = torch.nn.ModuleList()
        self.ferminet_layer_envelope: torch.nn.ModuleList = torch.nn.ModuleList()
        self.running_diff: torch.Tensor = torch.zeros(self.batch_size)
        self.nuclear_nuclear_potential: torch.Tensor = self.calculate_nuclear_nuclear()
        self.ferminet_layer.append(FerminetElectronFeature(self.n_one, self.n_two, self.nucleon_pos.size()[0], self.batch_size, self.total_electron, [self.spin[0], self.spin[1]]))
        self.ferminet_layer_envelope.append(FerminetEnvelope(self.n_one, self.n_two, self.total_electron, self.batch_size, [self.spin[0], self.spin[1]], self.nucleon_pos.size()[0], self.determinant))

    def forward(self, input: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        eps = torch.tensor(1e-36)
        self.input = input.reshape((self.batch_size, -1, 3))
        two_electron_vector = self.input.unsqueeze(1) - self.input.unsqueeze(2)
        two_electron_distance = torch.linalg.norm(two_electron_vector + eps, dim=3).unsqueeze(3)
        two_electron = torch.cat((two_electron_vector, two_electron_distance), dim=3)
        two_electron = torch.reshape(two_electron, (self.batch_size, self.total_electron, self.total_electron, -1))
        one_electron_vector = self.input.unsqueeze(1) - self.nucleon_pos.unsqueeze(1)
        one_electron_distance = torch.linalg.norm(one_electron_vector, dim=3)
        one_electron = torch.cat((one_electron_vector, one_electron_distance.unsqueeze(-1)), dim=3)
        one_electron = torch.reshape(one_electron.permute(0, 2, 1, 3), (self.batch_size, self.total_electron, -1))
        one_electron_vector_permuted = one_electron_vector.permute(0, 2, 1, 3).float()
        self.ferminet_layer[0].batch_size = self.batch_size
        self.ferminet_layer_envelope[0].batch_size = self.batch_size
        one_electron, _ = self.ferminet_layer[0].forward(one_electron.to(torch.float32), two_electron.to(torch.float32))
        self.psi, self.psi_up, self.psi_down = self.ferminet_layer_envelope[0].forward(one_electron, one_electron_vector_permuted)
        return self.psi

    def loss(self, psi_up_mo: List[Optional[np.ndarray]]=[None], psi_down_mo: List[Optional[np.ndarray]]=[None], pretrain: List[bool]=[True]):
        criterion = torch.nn.MSELoss()
        if pretrain[0]:
            psi_up_mo_torch = torch.from_numpy(psi_up_mo).unsqueeze(1)
            psi_down_mo_torch = torch.from_numpy(psi_down_mo).unsqueeze(1)
            self.running_diff = self.running_diff.float() + criterion(self.psi_up.float(), psi_up_mo_torch.float()).float() + criterion(self.psi_down.float(), psi_down_mo_torch.float()).float()
        else:
            energy = self.calculate_electron_electron() - self.calculate_electron_nuclear() + self.nuclear_nuclear_potential + self.calculate_kinetic_energy()
            return energy.detach()

    def calculate_nuclear_nuclear(self) -> torch.Tensor:
        potential = torch.nan_to_num(self.nuclear_charge * 1 / torch.cdist(self.nucleon_pos.float(), self.nucleon_pos.float()) * self.nuclear_charge.unsqueeze(1), posinf=0.0, neginf=0.0)
        potential = (torch.sum(potential) / 2).unsqueeze(0)
        return potential.detach()

    def calculate_electron_nuclear(self):
        potential = torch.sum(torch.sum(1 / torch.cdist(self.input.float(), self.nucleon_pos.float()) * self.nuclear_charge, axis=-1), axis=-1)
        return potential.detach()

    def calculate_electron_electron(self):
        potential = torch.sum(torch.sum(torch.nan_to_num(1 / torch.cdist(self.input.float(), self.input.float()), posinf=0.0, neginf=0.0), axis=-1), axis=-1) / 2
        return potential.detach()

    def calculate_kinetic_energy(self):
        i = torch.arange(self.batch_size).view(self.batch_size, 1, 1, 1, 1)
        j = torch.arange(self.total_electron).view(1, self.total_electron, 1, 1, 1)
        k = torch.arange(3).view(1, 1, 3, 1, 1)
        input = torch.clone(self.input).detach()
        jac = torch.func.jacrev(lambda x: torch.log(torch.abs(self.forward(x))))
        hess = torch.func.jacrev(jac)
        tmp_batch_size = self.batch_size
        self.batch_size = 1
        jacobian_square_sum = torch.sum(torch.pow(torch.func.vmap(jac)(input).detach().squeeze(1), 2), axis=(1, 2))
        vectorized_hessian = torch.func.vmap(hess)
        hessian_sum = torch.sum(vectorized_hessian(input).detach().squeeze(1)[i, j, k, j, k], axis=(1, 2)).squeeze(1).squeeze(1)
        self.batch_size = tmp_batch_size
        kinetic_energy = -1 * 0.5 * (jacobian_square_sum + hessian_sum)
        return kinetic_energy.detach()

Typical use is as an attention pooling or aggregation layer in sequence, set, or graph models—initialized with dimension sizes, trained by gradient descent, and invoked repeatedly during forward passes to produce fixed- or variable-length attended representations.

mechanism.text:
Representing molecules as graphs of atoms and bonds, the Directed Message Passing Neural Network (D-MPNN) encodes information on directed bonds (edges) and propagates messages along those directed edges to learn per-bond hidden states that are later pooled to a molecular representation for property prediction. The class implements this edge-centric message-passing scheme used in the referenced paper: initial bond hidden vectors are computed from atom and bond features; during each message-passing step, a bond’s hidden state is updated from incoming messages on other bonds that terminate at its source atom (excluding the reverse bond), yielding directed, path-sensitive propagation that better captures bond-local chemical context than purely node-centric updates.

Algorithmically, the implementation follows these core steps:
- Featurization: compute per-atom and per-bond feature vectors (e.g., atom type, formal charge, bond type, ring flags).
- Initialization: for each directed bond (i→j) form an initial hidden vector h_{i→j}^{(0)} = ReLU(W_init [x_i; e_{i,j}]) (or equivalent linear + nonlinearity), where x_i is source-atom features and e_{i,j} bond features.
- Message passing (T steps): at step t, compute incoming message m_{i→j}^{(t)} = Σ_{k∈N(i)\k≠j} h_{k→i}^{(t-1)}; update hidden state h_{i→j}^{(t)} = ReLU(h_{i→j}^{(0)} + W_msg m_{i→j}^{(t)}) or similar gated/MLP update.
- Readout: aggregate per-bond (or derived per-atom) representations into a fixed-size molecular embedding (sum/mean/attention over atoms or bonds), optionally apply feedforward layers to predict properties.

Key design decisions implemented in the class:
- Edge-centric (directed bond) representation rather than node-only updates: reduces information leakage from reverse edges and emphasizes path directionality.
- Use of initial bond embeddings conditioned on source-atom features: grounds bond states in local atomic context.
- Exclusion of the reverse bond during incoming-message sum: enforces directionality and avoids trivial back-and-forth message amplification.
- Configurable number of message steps, hidden sizes, and readout MLPs so users can trade depth/capacity vs. overfitting.
- Reliance on precomputed featurizer (DMPNNFeaturizer) and batch graph objects for efficient batching.

When to use D-MPNN vs alternatives:
- Prefer D-MPNN for molecular property tasks where bond context and directed path information matter (reaction centers, electronic effects, connectivity-sensitive properties). It often outperforms simple node-based GCNs on small-molecule benchmarks.
- Choose node-centric GNNs (GCN, GAT) when simpler node aggregation suffices or when recent equivariant/3D-aware models (SchNet, PaiNN, GemNet) are needed for geometry-sensitive properties (conformational energies, interactions).
Important constraints/assumptions:
- The default implementation uses 2D graph topology and handcrafted atom/bond features — it does not use 3D coordinates unless extended.
- Accuracy depends on quality of the featurizer and chosen hyperparameters (message steps, hidden dims).
- Graphs are assumed molecular (sparse, relatively small); very large graphs or non-molecular domains may require adaptation.
references: Analyzing Learned Molecular Representations for Property Prediction

class DMPNN(nn.Module):

    def __init__(self, mode: str='regression', n_classes: int=3, n_tasks: int=1, global_features_size: int=0, use_default_fdim: bool=True, atom_fdim: int=133, bond_fdim: int=14, enc_hidden: int=300, depth: int=3, bias: bool=False, enc_activation: str='relu', enc_dropout_p: float=0.0, aggregation: str='mean', aggregation_norm: Union[int, float]=100, ffn_hidden: int=300, ffn_activation: str='relu', ffn_layers: int=3, ffn_dropout_p: float=0.0, ffn_dropout_at_input_no_act: bool=True):
        super(DMPNN, self).__init__()
        self.mode: str = mode
        self.n_classes: int = n_classes
        self.n_tasks: int = n_tasks
        self.encoder: nn.Module = layers.DMPNNEncoderLayer(use_default_fdim=use_default_fdim, atom_fdim=atom_fdim, bond_fdim=bond_fdim, d_hidden=enc_hidden, depth=depth, bias=bias, activation=enc_activation, dropout_p=enc_dropout_p, aggregation=aggregation, aggregation_norm=aggregation_norm)
        ffn_input: int = enc_hidden + global_features_size
        if self.mode == 'regression':
            ffn_output: int = self.n_tasks
        elif self.mode == 'classification':
            ffn_output = self.n_tasks * self.n_classes
        self.ffn: nn.Module = layers.PositionwiseFeedForward(d_input=ffn_input, d_hidden=ffn_hidden, d_output=ffn_output, activation=ffn_activation, n_layers=ffn_layers, dropout_p=ffn_dropout_p, dropout_at_input_no_act=ffn_dropout_at_input_no_act)

    def forward(self, pyg_batch: Batch) -> Union[torch.Tensor, Sequence[torch.Tensor]]:
        atom_features: torch.Tensor = pyg_batch['atom_features']
        f_ini_atoms_bonds: torch.Tensor = pyg_batch['f_ini_atoms_bonds']
        atom_to_incoming_bonds: torch.Tensor = pyg_batch['atom_to_incoming_bonds']
        mapping: torch.Tensor = pyg_batch['mapping']
        global_features: torch.Tensor = pyg_batch['global_features']
        molecules_unbatch_key: List = torch.diff(pyg_batch._slice_dict['atom_features']).tolist()
        encodings: torch.Tensor = self.encoder(atom_features, f_ini_atoms_bonds, atom_to_incoming_bonds, mapping, global_features, molecules_unbatch_key)
        output: torch.Tensor = self.ffn(encodings)
        final_output: Union[torch.Tensor, Sequence[torch.Tensor]]
        if self.mode == 'regression':
            final_output = output
        elif self.mode == 'classification':
            if self.n_tasks == 1:
                output = output.view(-1, self.n_classes)
                final_output = (nn.functional.softmax(output, dim=1), output)
            else:
                output = output.view(-1, self.n_tasks, self.n_classes)
                final_output = (nn.functional.softmax(output, dim=2), output)
        return final_output

mechanism.text:
Message-passing over a molecular graph: each layer computes new node embeddings by aggregating information from a node’s neighbors and combining it with the node’s previous embedding. The GNN module in GNNModular implements that abstraction as a configurable stack of graph-convolutional layers, with learnable embeddings for discrete node properties (node type, chirality), per-layer normalization and dropout, and an optional Jumping Knowledge-style readout that pools intermediate layer representations.

At the algorithmic core is the standard neighborhood-aggregation update:
h_v^{(k+1)} = Combine_k( h_v^{(k)}, Aggregate_k( { Messages_k(u->v) : u in N(v) } ) ).
The concrete Combine/Aggregate/Message operations are provided by the chosen convolutional backend (GIN, GCN, GraphSAGE, GAT), e.g.
- GIN: Aggregate = sum; Combine = MLP( (1+ε)·h_v + sum_{u∈N(v)} h_u ),
- GCN: Aggregate = normalized sum (D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2}) with linear transform,
- GraphSAGE: Aggregate = mean (or pool) then concatenation with h_v and linear transform,
- GAT: Aggregate = attention-weighted sum with learned edge attention coefficients.
The module exposes these conv layers as a ModuleList (gconvs) and mirrors them with per-layer batch_norms. Node-type and chirality embeddings are looked up and concatenated/added to initial atomic features. If jump/Jumping Knowledge is enabled, the module collects layer-wise h_v^{(k)} and performs a final aggregation (concatenation, max, or attention) over depths to produce the node embedding used downstream, reducing sensitivity to how many layers are stacked.

Key design decisions: (1) modular backend selection — one container can host multiple theoretical GNN variants so users trade off expressivity vs. stability; (2) per-layer batch-norm and dropout — stabilizes training and combats covariate shift across depths; (3) learnable categorical embeddings for node/chirality — encode discrete chemistry attributes compactly; (4) optional jump connections — mitigate over-smoothing and let the model select useful receptive field sizes.

Use this component when you need a flexible GNN backbone for molecular or general graph inputs and want to experiment with different convolutional semantics without reworking the surrounding code. Important constraints: expects categorical node-type/chirality inputs (or precomputed continuous node features), adjacency/edge-index in the graph batch format used by the chosen conv implementation, and limited scalability to very large graphs without batching or sampling. Choose specific conv backends depending on whether you need strong local injectivity (GIN), spectral normalization (GCN), inductive sampling (GraphSAGE), or edge-wise attention (GAT).
references: Representation Learning on Graphs with Jumping Knowledge Networks

mechanism.text:
Predicting a molecule’s total energy from its atoms and interatomic distances by learning many-body interactions. DTNN starts by embedding each atom type into a learnable vector, expands interatomic distances into a continuous radial basis, and then iteratively refines atomic feature vectors by passing distance‑modulated messages between atom pairs; per-atom energies are finally regressed and summed to produce a size‑extensive molecular energy.

Mathematical/core algorithm:
- Atom initialization: a_i(0) = A_Z(i), a learnable embedding for each atomic number Z.
- Distance expansion: r_ij is projected onto a set of Gaussian radial basis functions φ_k(r_ij) to produce a smooth, differentiable representation of pairwise geometry.
- Interaction/update (implements the DTNN equations): for t = 0..T−1,
  m_i(t) = Σ_j F(φ(r_ij)) · g(a_j(t))
  a_i(t+1) = a_i(t) + U(a_i(t), m_i(t))
  Here F is a learnable filter network mapping the distance basis to multiplicative filters, g maps neighbor features into message space, and U is a small update network (often additive residual). This factorized tensor structure approximates a full tensor product between atom features and distance filters (as in Eq.6–7 of the cited work) while keeping parameter counts manageable.
- Prediction: e_i = P(a_i(T)); E_total = Σ_i e_i (ensures extensivity).

Key design decisions and rationale:
- Continuous radial basis for r_ij: enforces smooth dependence on distances and allows gradient-based learning of geometry-sensitive interactions.
- Factorized tensor/filter layers: capture interaction between atomic features and distance-dependent effects without the cubic parameter blowup of an explicit full tensor.
- Iterative refinement (T steps): allows representation of many‑body effects beyond immediate neighbors by repeated message passing.
- Sum pooling of per-atom energies: ensures molecular-size scaling and permutation invariance.

When to use vs alternatives; constraints:
- Use DTNN for supervised prediction of quantum‑chemical properties (energies, per-atom contributions) when 3D geometry is available and you need physically motivated, size‑extensive models.
- Not ideal for very large systems: pairwise messages scale O(N^2) unless neighbor cutoffs or sparsity are imposed. Requires reliable geometries and consistent atomic labeling (nuclear charges). Compared with generic graph-based MPNNs, DTNN’s continuous filter and factorized tensor explicitly model distance-dependent physics, which can improve accuracy on small‑molecule QM tasks but may be less flexible for sparse graph inputs or heterogeneous long-range interactions unless extended.
references: Quantum-chemical insights from deep tensor neural networks

implementation:
class DTNN(nn.Module):

    def __init__(self, n_tasks: int, n_embedding: int=30, n_hidden: int=100, n_distance: int=100, distance_min: float=-1, distance_max: float=18, output_activation: bool=True, mode: str='regression', dropout: float=0.0, n_steps: int=2):
        super(DTNN, self).__init__()
        self.n_tasks = n_tasks
        self.n_embedding = n_embedding
        self.n_hidden = n_hidden
        self.n_distance = n_distance
        self.distance_min = distance_min
        self.distance_max = distance_max
        self.output_activation = output_activation
        self.mode = mode
        self.dropout = dropout
        self.n_steps = n_steps
        self.dtnn_embedding = layers.DTNNEmbedding(n_embedding=self.n_embedding)
        self.dtnn_step = nn.ModuleList()
        for i in range(self.n_steps):
            self.dtnn_step.append(layers.DTNNStep(n_embedding=self.n_embedding, n_distance=self.n_distance))
        self.dtnn_gather = layers.DTNNGather(n_embedding=self.n_embedding, layer_sizes=[self.n_hidden], n_outputs=self.n_tasks, output_activation=self.output_activation)
        self.linear = nn.LazyLinear(self.n_tasks)

    def forward(self, inputs: List[torch.Tensor]):
        dtnn_embedding = self.dtnn_embedding(inputs[0])
        for i in range(self.n_steps):
            dtnn_embedding = nn.Dropout(self.dropout)(dtnn_embedding)
            dtnn_embedding = self.dtnn_step[i]([dtnn_embedding, inputs[1], inputs[3], inputs[4]])
        dtnn_step = nn.Dropout(self.dropout)(dtnn_embedding)
        dtnn_gather = self.dtnn_gather([dtnn_step, inputs[2]])
        dtnn_gather = nn.Dropout(self.dropout)(dtnn_gather)
        output = self.linear(dtnn_gather)
        return output

mechanism.text:
Edge prediction training needs examples of both present and absent links; NegativeEdge supplies absent-link (negative) examples by sampling node pairs that are not edges in the input graph and attaching them to the graph data for use by losses or predictors.

Algorithmically it performs uniform random sampling over candidate node-pairs that are not present in the original graph (and typically excludes self-loops). Let E be the original set of edges and V the node set. The sampler constructs the set of allowable negatives N = {(u,v) | u,v in V, (u,v) not in E, u != v} and draws k = floor(|E|/2) samples from N without replacement (per graph in a batched BatchGraphData). Those sampled pairs are appended to the graph structure as “negative edges” so downstream code can treat them as absent-link targets (for example, label 0 vs existing edges label 1 in an edge-prediction loss).

Key design decisions and rationale
- Fixed sampling budget: adding half as many negatives as original edges balances positives and negatives moderately while keeping computation linear in |E|. It’s a pragmatic default that avoids overwhelming the positive class.
- Uniform random sampling: simple, unbiased baseline that requires no model signals or costly pre-computation; good as a general-purpose starter sampler.
- Per-graph sampling in batched data: prevents mixing nodes across graphs and preserves graph locality.
- No semantic heuristics or hard-negative mining: keeps implementation lightweight and deterministic in expectation.

When to use vs. alternatives; constraints
- Use NegativeEdge when you need a simple, computationally cheap negative set for training or evaluation, when no domain-specific notion of “hard negatives” exists, or as a baseline.
- If you need more informative negatives, prefer alternatives: degree-aware or distance-based sampling, structure-aware hard-negative mining, or learned negative samplers (which bias toward plausible but false links).
- Assumptions: sampling is within each graph (not between graphs), excludes existing edges and self-loops, and treats negatives as uniformly likely. For directed graphs or tasks where edge feasibility is constrained (e.g., chemical bonds), uniform negatives can be invalid or misleading and a constrained sampler should be used.
references: Strategies for Pre-training Graph Neural Networks

implementation:
def negative_edge_sampler(input_graph: BatchGraphData):
    data = copy.deepcopy(input_graph)
    num_nodes = data.num_nodes
    num_edges = data.num_edges
    edge_set = set([str(data.edge_index[0, i].cpu().item()) + ',' + str(data.edge_index[1, i].cpu().item()) for i in range(data.edge_index.shape[1])])
    redandunt_sample = torch.randint(0, num_nodes, (2, 5 * num_edges))
    sampled_ind = []
    sampled_edge_set = set([])
    for i in range(5 * num_edges):
        node1 = redandunt_sample[0, i].cpu().item()
        node2 = redandunt_sample[1, i].cpu().item()
        edge_str = str(node1) + ',' + str(node2)
        if edge_str not in edge_set and edge_str not in sampled_edge_set and (not node1 == node2):
            sampled_edge_set.add(edge_str)
            sampled_ind.append(i)
        if len(sampled_ind) == num_edges / 2:
            break
    data.negative_edge_index = redandunt_sample[:, sampled_ind]
    return data

mechanism.text:
Produces a length‑num integer sequence that is the natural indices 0..num-1 rotated left by shift (equivalently, a circular shift of the range). Concretely you get an index map where element i maps to (i+shift) mod num, implemented by creating a contiguous arange then overwriting the trailing slice with a fresh arange to wrap the overflow.

1) Algorithmic idea:
- Build the base sequence 0,1,...,num-1.
- Add shift to all entries so most indices become i+shift.
- Replace the last shift entries (which now exceed num-1) with 0,..,shift-1 to effect wraparound.
This is an in-place construction with O(num) time and O(num) memory for the result.

2) Domain knowledge:
- This is a standard technique for circular indexing, rotating buffers, or creating permutation indices for roll/rotate operations. Familiarity with modular arithmetic (index mod num) and with tensor indexing semantics (slices, negative indices) is useful. In PyTorch context, this returns a tensor of integer indices suitable for gather/permute operations.

3) Key constraints and assumptions:
- shift must be an integer in 0..num (semantically). The implementation as written misbehaves for shift==0 because arr[-0:] is the whole array; you must special-case shift==0 or use a modulo formulation. shift>num isn't handled; you should reduce shift %= num first.
- dtype/device: torch.arange defaults to CPU and default dtype (usually torch.int64); ensure consistency with the tensors you will index. These are integer operations and not differentiable — they don’t produce gradients.
- The code uses an in-place slice assignment; ensure no aliasing or gradient requirements would be violated.

4) When appropriate:
- When you need an explicit index mapping for circular shifts, rotating sequence data, or constructing permutation tensors for gather/advanced indexing. For robust code prefer the modular form (torch.arange(num).add(shift) % num) to avoid edge-case bugs and to be clearer about intent.

implementation:
def cycle_index(num, shift):
    arr = torch.arange(num) + shift
    arr[-shift:] = torch.arange(shift)
    return arr

Encapsulate a Grover pretraining pipeline: an embedding module with prediction heads that produce logits for atom- and bond-vocabulary tasks (from both atom and bond hidden states) and for functional-group (graph-level) prediction.
