mechanism.text:
Returns the discrete set of nonnegative frequency bin centers corresponding to an n-point real-input discrete Fourier transform (DFT), spaced by 1/(n·d) and including the Nyquist bin when n is even. Conceptually it computes the k·(1/(n d)) sequence for k = 0, 1, ..., floor(n/2) — the exact set of frequencies produced by a real-to-complex FFT (rfft) of length n sampled with interval d.

Algorithmically the routine is trivial and explicit: compute the frequency spacing val = 1/(n d), form an integer range 0..N−1 where N = n//2 + 1 (so floor(n/2)+1), and multiply the integer indices by the spacing to produce the frequency vector. No transforms, iteration-heavy math, or numerical approximations are used; complexity and memory are O(N) because it allocates the N-length array of indices and scales them.

Domain knowledge required includes understanding sampling theory and the mapping between discrete-time sampling and frequency: frequency units are cycles per unit of d (Hz when d is seconds); the highest representable nonnegative frequency is the Nyquist frequency (1/(2 d)) and appears as the last bin only for even n. Users must also know that rfft of real data produces only nonnegative-frequency bins with Hermitian redundancy omitted, so this frequency vector is appropriate to pair with rfft output.

Key constraints and assumptions: n must be an integer (and practically positive); d should be nonzero and typically positive; the routine assumes standard FFT length conventions (no normalization or windowing effects). It does not check for negative n or d; it returns integer-indexed bins tied to the specific DFT length n, so changing normalization conventions in other parts of a pipeline can affect interpretation.

Appropriate use cases: label or interpret frequency bins from an rfft, compute spectral axis values for plotting, or align frequency-dependent operations with rfft outputs. It is not appropriate for full complex FFTs (use symmetric frequency arrays) or when alternative frequency scaling or nonstandard FFT conventions are required.

mechanism.text:
Creates an array of a given shape whose every element equals a specified value by allocating uninitialized storage and then copying a scalar (or broadcastable array) into every element. Concretely, it first determines the output dtype (by converting the fill value to an array if dtype is not given), allocates an empty array of the requested shape and memory order, and then performs a bulk copy (multiarray.copyto) of the fill value into the whole buffer. Using empty+copy avoids per-element Python loops and leverages optimized memory-copy/broadcasting primitives.

Understanding how to use this requires basic array-programming concepts: shapes and broadcasting (the fill value must be scalar or broadcastable to the target shape), dtypes and casting rules (conversion can truncate or change representation), and memory layout (C vs Fortran order, contiguousness) because layout affects performance. If device semantics are present (for example GPU arrays), allocation and copy occur on the specified device, so knowledge of the device-backed array library matters.

Key constraints and assumptions:
- The allocated array is initially uninitialized; the code assumes the subsequent copy overwrites every location. If the copy fails partway (rare), some elements could remain uninitialized.
- When dtype is omitted, dtype inference is done by converting the fill value to an array; that can produce surprising dtypes for Python scalars (e.g., integers → int64).
- The copy uses unsafe casting: values will be coerced even if lossy (e.g., float→int truncation), so numeric fidelity is not guaranteed unless you choose an appropriate dtype.
- The fill value must be broadcast-compatible with the target shape.
- The implementation delegates to a “like” argument when provided, preserving array-like dispatch semantics.

Appropriate use cases include fast allocation of large constant-filled arrays (initializing buffers, setting sentinel values, creating masks), preallocating storage before computations where every element needs the same initial value, and moving simple constants to a specific device. Avoid it when you need elementwise computed values, when preserving exact dtype without casting risk, or when repeated scalar assignment with side effects is required.

mechanism.text:
Returns the indices that would sort an array along a given axis, delegating the actual computation to NumPy’s ndarray or MaskedArray argsort implementations and preserving masked-data semantics when present. Under the hood this is not a bespoke sorting routine: the code converts the input to an array-like object and then calls the array’s own argsort. For plain ndarrays that uses NumPy’s highly optimized quick/merge/heap sort implementations (average O(n log n) time, with an option for stable mergesort), while MaskedArray uses logic that treats masked entries specially (for example pushing them to the end or using a fill value) before returning ordering indices.

Using this correctly requires understanding masked arrays versus regular ndarrays, axis semantics, and the stability/behavior of different sorting algorithms. MaskedArray.argsort implements domain-specific choices: masked entries can be ordered last (or handled via a fill_value), and the function issues a compatibility deprecation for the default axis when dimensionality >1. You should also know how NaNs and masked elements interact with comparison-based sorts (they are not ordinary values and are often treated as “missing”).

Key constraints and assumptions:
- The heavy lifting is performed by NumPy’s array methods; this wrapper assumes those implementations for correctness and performance.
- The function preserves masked-array behavior and delegates parameters like endwith and fill_value only to MaskedArray paths.
- Defaults and warnings: axis selection has a deprecation path (None vs -1) and certain parameters (e.g., stable in this wrapper) may be forwarded or ignored depending on array type.
- Complexity is dominated by the chosen sort algorithm (typically O(n log n)) and memory/axis layout of the array.

Appropriate use cases include obtaining permutation indices for reordering data, preparing stable index-based sorts, and working with datasets that include missing values where mask-aware ordering is required.

mechanism.text:
Returns the input unchanged when it is already a masked-array that satisfies dtype and memory-layout requirements; otherwise it constructs (or wraps) a masked-array representation without forcing unnecessary copies. The implementation implements a fast-path check: if the object is an instance of the masked-array class and its dtype and layout flags already match the requested constraints, it returns the same object reference. If any requirement is unmet, it delegates to the masked-array constructor with options chosen to avoid copying and to preserve any existing mask.

Algorithmically this is a lightweight type-and-state guard plus conditional construction. The guard tests three invariants: type (already a masked-array), dtype compatibility, and memory-contiguity/order compatibility (C/F/A/K semantics mapped to the array’s flags). Passing the guard means no allocation, no data movement, and no change to mask or view identity. Falling through calls the masked-array constructor with parameters that favor rewrapping or minimal transformation rather than deep copying.

To use this correctly you need familiarity with NumPy-style masked arrays, the difference between views and copies, and how dtype and memory order affect operations and performance. Understanding the mask semantics (i.e., that masks can be preserved independently of underlying data) and array flags (c_contiguous, f_contiguous) is important for predicting whether the fast path will be taken and whether subsequent code will see aliasing.

Key constraints and assumptions: it assumes the caller’s notion of “compatible dtype” and “compatible order” is captured by simple equality and flag tests; it relies on MaskedArray’s flag attributes being accurate; and when returning the same object, callers must accept potential aliasing (in-place modifications will mutate the original). When appropriate: use this when you need to ensure an input is a masked-array type but want to avoid unnecessary copies and preserve masks—mirrors the philosophy of numpy.asanyarray but specialized for masked-array semantics.

print(mask_not_shrunk)  # array([False, False, False, False])

import numpy as np

# Using a flexible/structured dtype: each field is converted to a boolean field
m = [1, 0, 1, 1]
n = [0, 1, 0, 0]
arr = []
for man, mouse in zip(m, n):
    arr.append((man, mouse))

dtype = np.dtype({'names': ['man', 'mouse'], 'formats': [np.int64, np.int64]})
arr = np.array(arr, dtype=dtype)
print(arr)

mask_struct = np.ma.core.make_mask(arr, dtype=dtype)
print(mask_struct)
# array([( True, False), (False,  True), ( True, False), ( True, False)],
#       dtype=[('man', '|b1'), ('mouse', '|b1')])

mechanism.text:
Accepts a variety of inputs and returns a canonical mask representation suitable for NumPy's masked-array machinery: either the special nomask sentinel (meaning “no mask”) or an ndarray of mask values, possibly with a structured dtype that mirrors the original array's fields but uses the internal MaskType for each field.

Algorithmically, the routine normalizes several cases. If the input is already the nomask sentinel it propagates it. If given a structured ndarray (dtype with fields) and the requested mask dtype is a plain boolean, it creates a full-True boolean mask of the same shape — a conservative mask saying every element is masked. Otherwise it obtains a filled (non-masked) view of the input, forces it into an ndarray with the desired mask dtype (respecting sub-classing via subok), and optionally “shrinks” the result: if the mask has no structured fields and contains no True values, it collapses to the nomask sentinel. Auxiliary helpers detect and unwrap masked-array objects, handle dicts and other iterables, and map structured dtypes into corresponding mask dtypes.

Domain knowledge required: familiarity with masked arrays (the nomask sentinel vs explicit boolean masks), structured (record) dtypes, and the distinction between an unmasked array and an explicit mask array. Understanding how masks can be per-field for structured arrays (requiring structured mask dtype) versus a simple boolean mask for plain arrays clarifies why dtype translation and the special-case for structured inputs exist.

Key assumptions and constraints: filled(a) must produce an array-like shape-compatible object; structured arrays are treated specially; nomask is a singleton sentinel. Shrink-to-nomask only applies when there are no True entries and the mask dtype is not structured. Copy semantics are controlled but may be optimized away. The routine expects inputs that can sensibly be converted to ndarrays or already conform.

Use cases: canonicalizing user-provided masks, constructing masks from diverse inputs (scalars, lists, dicts, masked arrays), and producing mask arrays compatible with masked-array operations where you want consistent dtype handling and automatic nomask collapsing when nothing is masked.

s_param.name: a
s_param.description: Input array or masked array to be sorted.

s_param.name: stable

print('sorted mask:', sorted_x.mask)
print('sorted full:', sorted_x)

import numpy as np

# 2D masked array: sort along axis=0, place masked values at beginning (endwith=False)

mechanism.text:
Returns a sorted NumPy array (a copy) by converting the input to an ndarray and invoking NumPy’s in-place sort routine (or MaskedArray’s sort when given a masked array). The implementation first materializes a copy of the input as an ndarray (preserving subclassing via subok) and then either flattens it if axis is None or delegates to the array’s sort method with the requested axis and sorting algorithm family. For plain ndarrays this calls NumPy’s C-level sort implementation (typical complexity O(n log n) using quicksort/heapsort/mergesort variants; a stable option forces a stable algorithm), and for masked arrays it defers to MaskedArray.sort which additionally handles masked entries (often placing them at the end when requested and using a fill value during comparisons).

Conceptually, the routine is an in-place sort applied to a copied array. The copy at the start ensures the caller’s original object is not mutated; the subsequent sort modifies that copy and then returns it. Axis semantics determine which dimension is permuted; axis=None flattens to 1D first. For structured dtypes, sorting can operate on named fields (order) and obeys field-based comparisons.

You should know basic NumPy array semantics (ndarray vs MaskedArray), how axis and flattening affect element order, stable vs unstable sorts, and how NaNs or masked values interact with comparisons. Key constraints and assumptions: input is array-like and convertible to an ndarray; performance follows NumPy’s sort algorithms (memory use is roughly O(n) because of the initial copy, and time is typically O(n log n)); masked-array behavior (placement of masked values, use of fill_value) differs from plain ndarray sorting. Use this routine when you need a sorted copy of numeric or structured array data, want correct masked-value handling, and accept the cost of copying rather than in-place mutation of the original.

mechanism.text:
Converts any scalar-like input into a one-dimensional array while leaving already 1D-or-higher arrays unchanged, and returns a single array when given one input or a tuple of arrays when given several.

Algorithmically, each argument is first converted to an array-like object with asanyarray — this preserves ndarray subclasses (e.g., matrix, masked arrays) rather than forcing a plain ndarray. The implementation inspects ndim; if ndim == 0 (a zero-dimensional scalar array), it calls reshape(1) to produce a length-1 1D view or copy as needed. For a single argument the converted object is returned directly; for multiple arguments the results are collected and returned as a tuple, maintaining the original order.

Domain knowledge: familiarity with NumPy’s array model (ndarray dimensionality, zero-dimensional scalar arrays vs Python scalars, and the distinction between asarray and asanyarray) is important. Understanding how reshape can create views vs copies, and how dtype and subclass preservation matter, helps reason about memory and behavior. Also useful is knowledge of when functions expect at least 1D inputs (concatenation, elementwise operations that rely on iterability) and how broadcasting interacts with dimensionality.

Key constraints and assumptions: inputs must be acceptable to asanyarray. reshape(1) is only called for objects with ndim == 0; higher-dimensional objects are not changed. The function does not deep-inspect nested Python lists beyond what asanyarray does, and it preserves array subclasses. It returns a tuple when multiple inputs are provided (caller must handle that). No guarantees are made about contiguity or copies — whether reshape yields a view or copy depends on the underlying layout.

Appropriate use cases: normalizing inputs before operations that require at least one axis (stacking, concatenation, iteration), converting scalars to length-1 arrays for vectorized processing, and preserving array subclasses while ensuring minimum dimensionality. Avoid when you specifically need to preserve scalar types or when you require higher minimal dimensionality (use respective atleast_2d/3d).

mechanism.text:
Converts each input into an ndarray with at least two dimensions: scalars become 1×1, 1‑D arrays become row vectors (1×N), and higher‑dimensional arrays are returned unchanged. The implementation loops over all arguments, calls asanyarray to get an array view/instance, and then uses ndim checks: ndim == 0 → reshape(1,1); ndim == 1 → add a new leading axis (newaxis) to make shape (1, N); else → keep as is. Results are returned as a single array when one input was supplied or as a tuple when multiple inputs were given.

Algorithmically this is a straightforward type/shape normalization step: turn heterogeneous inputs (scalars, 1‑D lists, arrays) into a consistent 2‑D representation so later operations can assume at least two axes. The operations used (reshape and newaxis) typically produce views rather than copies when memory layout allows, so the cost is minimal unless a copy is forced by non‑contiguous data or subclass behavior.

Domain knowledge needed includes familiarity with NumPy array dimensionality (ndim), array creation/coercion semantics (asanyarray vs. array), and the distinction between views and copies. Understanding how row vs. column orientation affects linear-algebra and broadcasting rules is important: 1‑D → row (1×N) here, not column (N×1).

Key constraints and assumptions: inputs are convertible to arrays; subclasses are preserved by asanyarray; the function does not enforce contiguity or data type changes beyond what asanyarray does; it returns a tuple if multiple inputs are given. It does not convert 1‑D inputs to column vectors, nor does it add singleton trailing axes for vectors—orientation is intentional.

Appropriate uses include normalizing inputs before concatenation, stacking, matrix routines that expect 2‑D inputs, or APIs that require consistent dimensionality. Avoid it when you specifically need column vectors, when in-place memory layout matters, or when you require strict copying or dtype conversion guarantees.

mechanism.text:
Constructs a square array whose specified diagonal contains the elements of a 1‑D input and whose off‑diagonals are zero. Internally the routine flattens the input vector, computes the size n = len(v) + |k| of the output square matrix, allocates a zero matrix of shape (n,n) with the input's dtype, and writes the vector into the appropriate diagonal positions by calculating flat (1‑D) indices. The flat index arithmetic relies on row‑major layout: an element at row r, column c has index r*n + c, so entries on the k‑th diagonal satisfy a simple linear formula that is computed in vectorized form and used to assign the whole diagonal in one operation.

Relevant domain knowledge includes understanding row‑major (C‑order) linearization of 2‑D arrays and how diagonals translate to arithmetic progressions of flat indices, plus basic NumPy behaviors (raveling, dtype preservation, and flat indexing). Knowing how diagonal offset k shifts the alignment (positive k moves the diagonal to the right, negative to the left) is important for predicting output shape and placement.

Key constraints and assumptions: input is treated as a sequence that can be converted to an array and flattened; k is an integer offset; the output is always square with side length len(v)+|k|, so memory and time scale as O(n^2) for allocation (assignment of s elements is O(s)). The implementation uses platform integer index type (intp) for indexing; extremely large sizes may hit memory or index limits. Subclass handling is preserved via the converter/wrapper calls.

Appropriate use cases are creating a matrix with a specified diagonal (e.g., for constructing Toeplitz-like structures, initializing diagonal matrices in linear algebra, or tests), especially when a compact vector should be embedded exactly on one diagonal. It is not intended for sparse storage or huge dimensions where O(n^2) allocation would be prohibitive.

mechanism.text:
Stacks one-dimensional inputs as columns and concatenates multi-dimensional inputs horizontally to produce a 2‑D array. Conceptually the routine walks the input sequence, normalises each item to an array-like object, promotes any 1‑D sequence into a column vector (by forcing at least two dimensions and transposing), collects these 2‑D blocks, then performs a single horizontal concatenation (axis=1) to produce the final array.

Algorithmically this is simple: for each element do a light-weight conversion (asanyarray) to preserve array subclasses when possible; if the array has ndim < 2 create an ndmin=2 array and transpose it so its shape becomes (N, 1) instead of (1, N); append to a list; finally call a single concatenate across the column axis. That single concatenate is where the actual memory allocation and element copy typically occurs, so most cost is in the final merge rather than the per-item checks.

Domain knowledge needed: familiarity with array dimensionality (1‑D vs 2‑D), row/column orientation, dtypes and dtype promotion rules, and how concatenation requires matching sizes along the non-concatenation axes. Understanding that a 1‑D input is treated as a column vector (shape (N,1)) is key to avoid surprising transposes.

Key constraints and assumptions: all inputs must have the same length along the first axis after normalization (same number of rows); ragged or unequal lengths will raise an error. Dtype promotion can occur, and subclasses may be converted during the ndmin/transpose step. Performance costs come from the final concatenate (allocation + copying). Inputs that are already 2‑D are taken as-is; 0‑D scalars are promoted to (1,1).

Appropriate uses: assembling a matrix from several column vectors or mixing column-oriented 2‑D blocks into a single dataset, e.g., building design matrices, feature matrices, or combining multiple columnar outputs. For large collections where you can preallocate storage, constructing the destination array directly may be more efficient than concatenating many pieces.

mechanism.text:
Ensures each input array has at least three dimensions by inserting singleton axes where needed so subsequent code can rely on ndim >= 3 for broadcasting or shape-based indexing.

Algorithmically, it loops over all provided inputs, converts each to an array-like object, inspects its current rank (ndim), and applies the minimal transformation to raise its rank to three: a 0-D scalar is reshaped to (1,1,1); a 1-D vector becomes (1, N, 1) by adding leading and trailing singleton axes; a 2-D matrix becomes (M, N, 1) by adding a trailing singleton axis; anything already with three or more dimensions is left unchanged. The transformed arrays are collected and returned as either a single array (when one input was given) or a tuple of arrays (when multiple inputs were given).

Domain knowledge required: familiarity with array rank (dimensions), singleton axes, broadcasting rules, and the idea that inserting axes (via reshape or newaxis) does not duplicate data but changes the view/shape. Understanding how broadcasting aligns dimensions of different length and how singleton dimensions can be used to enable elementwise operations across intended axes is central.

Key constraints and assumptions: inputs must be convertible to array-like objects; singleton axes are inserted at specific positions (beginning/end as shown), so the relative order of existing axes is preserved. The operation typically produces views (no data copy) when possible, but reshape semantics and subclass behavior (e.g., matrix or masked arrays) depend on the conversion function used. It does not attempt to reorder axes or insert singletons in arbitrary positions.

Appropriate use cases: preparing heterogeneous inputs for elementwise broadcasting, aligning shapes before concatenation along a non-singleton axis, or normalizing scalar/vector/matrix inputs to a consistent 3-D tensor form (for example, batch×height×width image pipelines). Not suitable when you need different insertion positions or when you must enforce exactly three dimensions (it leaves higher-rank arrays unchanged).

mechanism.text:
Works by partitioning the input ndarray along its “horizontal” axis: for a 2D-or-higher array that is the second axis (axis=1, i.e., columns), and for 1D arrays it uses the single available axis (axis=0). The implementation is a thin wrapper that chooses which axis to split and then defers the actual partitioning to a generic split routine; the split routine computes cut indices (either from an integer count or an explicit index list) and returns subarrays that reference the original memory when possible.

Algorithmically, the core work is index arithmetic: compute boundaries, check they lie inside the axis length, and create views (slices) or copies for the requested segments. If an integer number of sections is requested, the routine either divides the axis length evenly or raises when it cannot (depending on split’s behavior). If explicit indices are provided, they define exact cut points. Complexity is linear in the number of resulting pieces plus the work to create views; copying cost only occurs if the slicing cannot be represented as views or if further operations force copies.

Domain knowledge required includes understanding ndarray dimensionality and axis semantics (rows vs columns), the difference between views and copies, and how slicing affects memory layout/strides. Users must know how 0-D, 1-D, and N-D arrays behave differently — notably that there is no sensible “horizontal” axis for scalars, so a scalar input is rejected.

Key constraints and assumptions: input must be at least 1-D; indices_or_sections must be a valid integer or sequence that yields valid cuts; for integer sections an exact division of length may be required; returned parts may be views sharing memory with the original (so in-place modification can affect all pieces). For higher-dimensional arrays the split is always along axis 1.

Appropriate use cases: when you want to partition columns of a matrix, chunk a 1-D vector into segments, or prepare column-wise blocks for separate processing. Avoid using it for scalars or when you need axis semantics different from the default horizontal interpretation (use a general split with an explicit axis instead).

mechanism.text:
Stacks input arrays along a new third axis after promoting any 0–2D inputs to three dimensions, yielding a depth-wise concatenation (axis index 2). Concretely, scalars become shape (1,1,1), 1‑D vectors become (1, N, 1), 2‑D matrices become (M, N, 1), and existing 3+‑D arrays are left unchanged; the promoted arrays are then concatenated along the third axis to produce a single array whose third-dimension indexes the stacked inputs.

Algorithmic approach:
- Normalize all inputs to ndarray-like objects (via asanyarray) and map each to a 3D view using newaxis/reshape rules. These promotions are cheap views whenever possible (no data copy if memory layout allows).
- Collect the promoted arrays and call a standard concatenate routine along axis=2. Concatenate handles dtype promotion and allocates the output buffer when shapes match on the non-concatenation axes.

Domain knowledge required:
- Familiarity with array dimensionality (ndim), axes indexing, and how newaxis adds singleton dimensions.
- Understanding that concatenation requires equal sizes on all axes except the one being concatenated.
- Awareness of dtype promotion rules and difference between views and copies in NumPy, and how subclasses (e.g., masked arrays) interact with asanyarray.

Key constraints and assumptions:
- All inputs must be shape-compatible in the first two dimensions after promotion; otherwise concatenate raises an error.
- Promotion preserves data ordering but may create copies during concatenate; memory cost grows with the number and size of inputs.
- Inputs that are already >3D are not modified and contribute their full higher-dimensional shape; mixing such arrays with lower-dimension ones can produce unintuitive shapes.
- Masked-array behavior depends on asanyarray and subclass handling.

When appropriate to use:
- Combining several 1‑D or 2‑D arrays into a single “stacked” 3‑D array (e.g., stacking image channels, a sequence of 2‑D slices, or feature columns as depth).
- Preparing inputs for routines that expect a third axis as the “stack” or sample index.
- Not suitable when automatic broadcasting across mismatched spatial shapes is desired; explicit resizing or broadcasting must be done beforehand.

# result will have shape (2, 3, 3)
result = np.ma.extras.hstack((a, b), casting='safe')
print(result.shape)  # -> (2, 3, 3)
print(result.dtype)  # -> int32

mechanism.text:
Concatenates a sequence of array-like objects along their column direction for 2D-or-higher arrays, and for 1D inputs simply joins them end-to-end into a longer 1D array. The implementation first normalizes inputs with atleast_1d (using asanyarray so subclasses like masked arrays stay their type) so every element has at least one dimension. It then treats a single 1D array specially: if the first element is 1D, all inputs are concatenated along axis 0 (the 1D case), otherwise concatenation happens along axis 1 (the column axis for stacks of 2D+ arrays). dtype and casting arguments are forwarded to the underlying concatenate operation.

Algorithmically this is a thin wrapper around a general concatenation routine: normalize shapes, pick the axis based on input dimensionality, and call concatenate. No complex reshaping or broadcasting logic is applied beyond turning scalars into 1D arrays; there is no automatic promotion of lower-rank arrays to match higher ranks except by the check for zero-dimensional values (they become 1D).

Domain knowledge required: basic array shape and axis semantics (row vs. column orientation), the difference between 1D and 2D in concatenation, and awareness of dtype/casting rules. Familiarity with array subclasses (masked arrays, matrix-like classes) helps because asanyarray preserves subclasses rather than forcing ndarray.

Key constraints and assumptions: inputs must be convertible to arrays and have compatible shapes along the non-concatenation axes (e.g., for 2D arrays, matching number of rows). Empty input sequences will not produce a meaningful array and will typically error. Scalars are promoted to 1D length-1 arrays. The operation may allocate a new array (copies) and perform dtype casting if required.

Use cases: horizontally combining columns of 2D datasets (assembling feature matrices), concatenating multiple 1D signals into a single long vector, and merging arrays when column-wise alignment is intended. Avoid when you need implicit broadcasting or when inputs have mismatched ranks that should be expanded automatically; in such cases reshape or use stack/column_stack with explicit reshaping first.

import numpy as np

arrays = [rng.normal(size=(3, 4)) for _ in range(10)]

# Stack them along a new first axis using numpy.ma.extras.stack
result = np.ma.extras.stack(arrays, axis=0)
print(result.shape)  # (10, 3, 4)

import numpy as np

# Create a random number generator and a list of 5 (2,3) arrays
rng = np.random.default_rng()

mechanism.text:
Creates a single higher‑rank array by inserting a new axis into each input array at a common position and then concatenating those expanded views along that axis. Conceptually the algorithm does two simple steps: (1) verify all inputs share the same shape and convert them to array-like objects, (2) for each array create a view with an extra dimension (using indexing with newaxis) and then perform a single concatenation along that new axis. The concatenation preserves the relative ordering of the input sequence, producing an output whose ndim = input_ndim + 1.

Understanding how NumPy represents arrays (shape, ndim), how slicing with newaxis creates a view that increases dimensionality, and how concatenation assembles blocks along an axis is enough to reason about correctness and performance. You should also know about axis normalization (negative indices) and how dtype/casting affect promotion or copying.

Key constraints and assumptions:
- All inputs must have identical shapes (elementwise alignment across the non-inserted axes).
- At least one array is required.
- Axis index is interpreted in the result space (which has one more dimension).
- Memory cost is O(total number of elements) — concatenation generally allocates a new array unless inputs can be coerced without copying.
- Uses asanyarray, so array subclasses are preserved but may be coerced during concatenation subject to dtype/casting rules.

Appropriate uses:
- Building a new leading/batch/time/channel dimension from a list of same‑shaped samples (e.g., stacking images into a batch).
- Combining sequence elements into a single tensor when element order matters.
Avoid using it when input shapes differ (use padding, broadcasting, or structured containers) or when you only want to join along an existing axis (use concatenate, hstack/vstack/column_stack for convenience).

mechanism.text:
Implements NumPy-style slicing semantics for sequences of characters (string/array-of-strings) by normalizing start/stop/step into explicit integer arrays and delegating to a lower-level _slice routine that does the actual extraction.

At a high level the algorithm converts the high-level slice shorthand into concrete integer indices: absent start/stop are mapped to extreme indices that represent “beginning” or “end” depending on direction (positive or negative step), step is validated and broadcast to integer form, and zero-valued steps are rejected. This normalization lets the core _slice routine operate on well-defined numeric ranges and handle vectorized (array) broadcasting across inputs. Using np.where with step < 0 ensures symmetric handling of reversed slices by choosing maxima/minima of platform-sized integer type so that subsequent index arithmetic can compute effective positions consistently.

Domain knowledge needed: familiarity with Python/NumPy slicing conventions (negative steps imply reversed traversal; omitted start/stop default to start/end depending on step direction), broadcasting rules for array inputs, and integer-index semantics (including platform-dependent maximum/minimum integer values). Also useful is an understanding of vectorized operations: this code accepts scalars or arrays for start/stop/step and prepares them for elementwise application.

Key constraints and assumptions:
- step must be an integer type (or convertible); non-integer steps raise TypeError.
- step cannot be zero (ValueError).
- start/stop semantics rely on sentinel extremes (np.iinfo(np.intp).max/min) rather than explicit sequence lengths — the lower-level implementation must interpret these sentinels correctly relative to actual string lengths.
- Behavior for out-of-bounds indices, negative starts/stops, and broadcasting follow NumPy conventions and are resolved downstream by _slice.
- The function assumes _slice exists and understands the normalized representations.

Appropriate use cases: vectorized extraction of substrings from NumPy string arrays where users want NumPy-like slice semantics across many elements at once (including reversed slices). Avoid when you need Python-level slicing on individual Python strings or when you require explicit length-based indexing—use this when working in the NumPy string-processing pipeline or when performing bulk slice operations that benefit from broadcasting and C/compiled backing in _slice.

mechanism.text:
Allocates an uninitialized array with the requested shape and then fills every element with the scalar value 1. The implementation uses a two-step approach: first allocate storage via an empty-like constructor (so memory layout, shape, dtype and device are determined), then broadcast a scalar 1 into that storage using a vectorized copy routine. That copy routine handles broadcasting, dtype casting, and device-aware transfer (so it can write on CPU or other supported devices), and it typically maps to an efficient bulk fill (for simple numeric dtypes this can be implemented as an optimized memset or vectorized store).

Understanding and using this correctly requires basic array/memory model knowledge: what dtype and memory order mean, how broadcasting works, and how array subclasses or alternative devices (GPU) interact with allocation and copy semantics. Because allocation and filling are distinct steps, any behavior that depends on uninitialized data is irrelevant—every element is overwritten by the scalar copy—but performance characteristics depend on the allocation cost plus the cost of the bulk fill.

Key constraints and assumptions:
- The scalar 1 must be representable (or castable) to the target dtype; the copy uses an "unsafe" casting mode so truncation/precision loss can occur without error if the dtype differs.
- Memory layout requested at allocation (C/F/strided) is respected; some layouts may require extra work to fill efficiently.
- The routine delegates to device-aware primitives, so correct device/context must be available for non-CPU targets.
- Array subclasses are respected via the "like" dispatch path, so subclass semantics may alter allocation/fill.

Appropriate use cases are simple initialization of arrays filled with ones where allocation and a bulk set are sufficient—common for masks, biases, and tiled constants. For elementwise patterns or non-scalar initialization, other construction methods are preferable.

mechanism.text:
Controls global formatting state used when converting NumPy arrays (and related scalars) to text, by delegating the real work to an internal implementation that updates library-wide settings rather than performing numeric computation.

Algorithmically it is a thin wrapper: it collects formatting preferences and forwards them to a lower-level routine (_set_printoptions) which stores those choices in a global configuration object. The internal implementation then influences how array __repr__/__str__ paths and print routines build strings (for example by selecting number-formatters, truncation thresholds, edge-item counts). There is no per-call numeric processing—only registration of formatting rules that subsequent array-to-text conversions consult.

Effective use requires basic domain knowledge of NumPy’s representation model: arrays have their textual rendering produced by central routines that look up global print settings; formatting choices affect rounding, truncation of large arrays, handling of special values (NaN/Inf), and whether scientific notation is used. Understand that these settings are about presentation, not computation: they do not change stored values or numeric accuracy.

Key constraints and assumptions: the settings are global and persistent across the process, so changes affect all code that prints arrays. They are not inherently thread-local or atomic—concurrent code that prints arrays may observe different states. Some options interact (e.g., width + edgeitems determine line breaks and truncation), and backends or custom formatters can override defaults. The wrapper assumes the lower-level routine enforces validation and compatibility of options.

Appropriate use cases include improving readability in interactive sessions, generating human-oriented logs, or creating consistent prints for examples and debugging. Avoid relying on global printoptions for program logic, deterministic machine-readable output, or in library internals that other code might depend on; prefer local context managers or explicit formatting when isolation or reproducibility is required.

examples.code:
from pandas.api.types import is_hashable

# Simple built-in immutable object: should be hashable
result = is_hashable(42)
print(result)  # True

from pandas.api.types import is_hashable

# Tuple containing a mutable list: collections.abc.Hashable may claim True, but hashing fails
a = ([],)
print(is_hashable(a))  # False

from pandas.api.types import is_hashable

# Slice behavior: by default slices are considered hashable; disallow them with allow_slice=False
s = slice(None)
print(is_hashable(s))                # True (default allow_slice=True)
print(is_hashable(s, allow_slice=False))  # False

mechanism.text:
Returns True iff the object can be passed to Python’s built-in hash() without raising TypeError, with an optional special-case that treats slice objects (and tuples containing slices) as unhashable when allow_slice is False. The implementation uses a try/except around hash(obj): the call either produces a hash value (success) or raises TypeError (failure). Before that it optionally inspects tuple and slice types to implement the slice policy.

1. Algorithmic approach
- A small, constant-time check: optionally inspect the object’s type for slices, then attempt hash(obj) in a try/except. The try/except pattern is the idiomatic way in Python to test runtime capabilities (EAFP: “easier to ask forgiveness than permission”). Complexity is O(1) for typical objects; the cost is dominated by Python’s built-in hash implementation for the object’s type.

2. Domain knowledge required
- Understanding Python’s hash protocol: an object is considered hashable if it implements __hash__ and hash(obj) returns an integer (and typically if __eq__ is compatible). Knowledge that hashability is commonly used for dict/set keys, grouping, and internal indexing in libraries like pandas. Recognize that static typing is aided by the TypeGuard[Hashable] return annotation: callers can narrow types for type checkers.

3. Key constraints and assumptions
- Hashability does not guarantee immutability or stable identity over time; mutable objects may implement __hash__ (though uncommon) and still produce surprising behavior if mutated after being used as keys. The check relies on runtime behavior of hash(); types with unusual __hash__ semantics or side-effects may affect results. The optional slice policy is a library-level convention (pandas-specific) rather than a language rule.

4. Appropriate use cases
- Pre-flight checks before using an object as a dictionary/set key, or before inserting into data structures that require hashability (indexing/groupby operations). Avoid relying on this check to guarantee semantic immutability or long-term safety as a key for persisted structures. The slice-special-casing is useful when slices should be treated as non-hashable for higher-level logic even though Python’s hash may accept them.

s_param.name: name
s_param.description: Namespace that will be accessed under, e.g. ``df.foo``; the attribute name to register on the pandas object.

s_param.name: accessor
s_param.description: Class implementing the accessor methods. Its __init__ should accept a single argument (the pandas object: Series, DataFrame, or Index) and typically stores it (e.g. self._obj).

examples.code:
import pandas as pd
from pandas.core.accessor import Accessor

# Define a DataFrame accessor class; __init__ takes the DataFrame instance
class SummaryAccessor:
    def __init__(self, df: pd.DataFrame):
        self._df = df

    def column_counts(self):
        # return a Series with non-null counts per column
        return self._df.count()

# Register the accessor on DataFrame under the attribute name 'summary'
setattr(pd.DataFrame, "summary", Accessor("summary", SummaryAccessor))

# Example usage
df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, None, 3], "b": [4, 5, None]})
counts = df.summary.column_counts()
print(counts)

import pandas as pd
from pandas.core.accessor import Accessor

# Define a Series accessor class; __init__ takes the Series instance
class NegPosAccessor:
    def __init__(self, s: pd.Series):
        self._s = s

    def counts(self):
        # count negative, zero, positive values
        neg = (self._s < 0).sum()
        zero = (self._s == 0).sum()
        pos = (self._s > 0).sum()
        return pd.Series({"neg": int(neg), "zero": int(zero), "pos": int(pos)})

# Register the accessor on Series under the attribute name 'np'
setattr(pd.Series, "np", Accessor("np", NegPosAccessor))

# Example usage
s = pd.Series([-1, 0, 1, 2, -3])
print(s.np.counts())

mechanism.text: Provide a descriptor that creates a property-like accessor bound to a specific namespace on pandas-like objects (Series, DataFrame, Index). Instances manage the link between the host object and an auxiliary class implementing extension methods; when the attribute is accessed, the descriptor returns an accessor instance constructed with the host object. Typical use: attach grouped or domain-specific methods under df.foo, created at class definition time and invoked at runtime via attribute access.

df2 = df.assign(name_titlecase=pd.col("name").str.title())

import pandas as pd

# Example 2: use pd.col in loc for filtering
df = pd.DataFrame({"name": ["beluga", "narwhal"], "speed": [100, 110]})
# select rows where the deferred 'speed' column is greater than 105

mechanism.text:
Returns a lazily-evaluated column accessor: it builds an Expression object wrapping a closure that, when applied to a DataFrame, looks up and returns the Series for the given column name or raises a descriptive error if the name is absent. The closure first enforces that the provided name is hashable (so it can be used as a dictionary-like key), then at evaluation time checks membership in df.columns and uses df[col_name] to extract the Series.

Underlying algorithmic approach: a small factory pattern + closure. The outer call performs cheap static validation (hashability) and constructs a callable that captures the column name. The callable performs a constant-time membership test against the DataFrame’s column index (typically O(1) for hashed indices) and then delegates to the DataFrame’s item access. Error reporting is enhanced by constructing a truncated, human-readable list of available columns so users can spot typos quickly.

Domain knowledge required: familiarity with tabular dataframes (pandas-style APIs), the distinction between column labels and positions, and that DataFrame.columns is an iterable/index object. Understanding Series as a column vector and hashability as the requirement for keys in Python mappings is helpful. Also useful is the concept of lazy/evaluated expressions vs immediate data access, since the returned Expression defers DataFrame interaction until it’s called.

Key constraints and assumptions: assumes a pandas-like DataFrame with .columns and __getitem__ semantics; col_name must be hashable and correspond exactly to a label in df.columns; the membership check relies on the columns object supporting "in" semantics; error messages truncate long column lists to 90 characters. It does not handle multi-index column disambiguation, positional indexing, or automatic fuzzy matching beyond listing options.

Appropriate usage: when building composable, reusable expressions that reference a named column by label and should be evaluated later against concrete DataFrames, and when clear, developer-friendly errors for missing columns are desired.

examples.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# Example 1: use a plain NumPy ndarray with default keep='first'
values = np.array([1, 2, 2, 3, 1])
result = pd.core.algorithms.duplicated(values)
print(result)  # [False False  True False  True]

import pandas as pd

# Example 2: use a pandas ExtensionArray (nullable integer Int64) and keep='last'
ext_arr = pd.array([1, 1, 2, 2, 3], dtype="Int64")
result = pd.core.algorithms.duplicated(ext_arr, keep='last')
print(result)  # boolean ndarray, True for duplicates except for the last occurrence

import pandas as pd

# Example 3: supply a boolean mask to exclude elements from duplicate checking
values = np.array(['a', 'b', 'a', 'c', 'b'])
mask = np.array([False, True, False, False, False])  # exclude index 1 ('b') from checking
result = pd.core.algorithms.duplicated(values, keep=False, mask=mask)
print(result)  # True for all duplicates among the checked positions

mechanism.text:
Detects duplicate entries by first normalizing heterogeneous input into a compact, hash-friendly numpy representation and then using a hash-table duplicate detection routine (htable.duplicated) to mark which positions repeat according to the chosen “keep” policy.

At a high level the approach has two stages. Stage one (_ensure_data) coerces many pandas/NumPy-backed types to simple numpy arrays with predictable dtypes so the deduplication step can be efficient and type-stable: categorical becomes integer codes, booleans become uint8, many datetime-like and timedelta-like types are viewed as i8, masked/nullable arrays are either unwrapped to their underlying data or preserved if they contain NA, object arrays are canonicalized, and certain small/odd float widths are promoted. Stage two hands that normalized array to a hash-table implementation (htable.duplicated) that scans values and records duplicates with O(n) expected time and O(n) extra memory for the table (unless specialized views are possible).

Domain knowledge: familiarity with NumPy dtypes, pandas’ nullable/masked and categorical abstractions, and how missing values (NA/NaN) are represented is important. Understanding that some types are handled via integer views (e.g., timestamps -> int64) and that categorical uses codes helps predict behavior and performance.

Key constraints and assumptions: input is array-like (Series, ndarray, Index, MultiIndex) and must be reducible to a one-dimensional numpy representation. The algorithm assumes values become hashable/compareable after normalization and that NA handling is encoded in the normalized form. Memory and performance depend on making copies vs views (some branches return views, others copy/convert), and htable uses extra memory proportional to unique values. Edge cases include complex nested python objects (object dtype) where equality or hashing cost dominates, and masked arrays where NA semantics are preserved only when necessary.

Appropriate uses: fast duplicate detection for Series- or column-like data before drop_duplicates, grouping, or filtering; deduplicating homogeneous typed columns (numerical, datetime, categorical) where the normalization makes comparisons cheap. Avoid relying on this for multi-field record deduplication (use DataFrame methods) or for highly heterogeneous/very large object-dtype arrays where hashing and Python-level comparisons become expensive.

s_param.description: Input array-like to map over. Accepts numpy arrays, pandas Index, Series, ExtensionArray, or other array-like objects.

s_param.name: mapper
s_param.description: Mapping correspondence. Can be a function to apply to each element, a dict for lookup, or a Series whose index provides keys and values provide mapped outputs. Dictionary subclasses with __missing__ are converted to a lookup function; plain dicts are converted to a Series for efficient mapping.

s_param.name: na_action
s_param.description: If 'ignore', propagate NA values without passing them to the mapper. If None, NA values are passed to the mapper. Must be either 'ignore' or None.

examples.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# Example 1: map with a function on a NumPy array
arr = np.array([1, 2, 3])
mapper = lambda x: x * 10
result = pd.core.algorithms.map_array(arr, mapper)
print(result)  # expected: array([10, 20, 30])

import pandas as pd

# Example 2: map with a dict on a pandas Index
idx = pd.Index(["a", "b", "c", "a"])
mapper = {"a": 1, "b": 2}
result = pd.core.algorithms.map_array(idx, mapper)
print(result)  # expected: array([1, 2, nan, 1], dtype=object) or similar, unmapped -> NA

import pandas as pd

# Example 3: map with a Series as mapper and propagate NA when na_action='ignore'

mapper = pd.Series({1: "one", 2: "two"})
result = pd.core.algorithms.map_array(arr, mapper, na_action="ignore")
print(result)  # expected: array(['one', <NA>, 'two'], dtype=object or ExtensionArray)

mechanism.text:
Performs element-wise mapping of array-like values to replacement values using a mapping object (dict-like, Series) or a callable, with special handling for missing values and optimized code paths for Series-backed mappings.

1. Algorithmic approach
- If the mapper is dict-like it is converted into a pandas Series so mapping can be performed by index-alignment lookup. For a Series mapper, get_indexer is used to translate each input value to an integer index into the mapper's values; take_nd then gathers mapped values in a vectorized (C-level) operation.  
- For non-Series mappers (callables or other objects), the array is cast to object dtype and a C-level loop (lib.map_infer) applies the mapper to each element. If na_action == 'ignore', a precomputed mask of NA positions is used so NA inputs are left untouched (lib.map_infer_mask), avoiding calling the mapper on NA entries.  
- Special case: dicts with a __missing__ method are wrapped so that missing-key behavior is preserved. Empty mappers become Series to keep a consistent lookup path.

2. Required domain knowledge
- Familiarity with pandas/Numpy NA semantics (np.nan vs pandas NA) and how isna() identifies missing values.  
- Understanding of Index/Series alignment semantics (get_indexer) — mapping by value membership in the mapper’s index, not by positional correspondence.  
- Awareness of object dtype consequences: using object arrays falls back to Python-level objects which affects performance and dtype preservation.

3. Key constraints and assumptions
- Input is treated as 1-D array-like; multi-dimensional inputs aren’t handled.  
- Mapping by Series requires that input values match the mapper’s index value-equality semantics (hashable/comparable). Unmatched values produce missing/lookups determined by get_indexer semantics.  
- NA handling assumes isna() accurately detects missing entries; na_action='ignore' preserves NAs rather than sending them to the mapper.  
- Performance: Series-backed lookup and C-level take_nd are fast for large arrays; callable mapping on object arrays is slower.

4. When to use
- Use when you need an element-wise replacement or translation of values (e.g., category relabeling, label encoding) and you have a mapping dict/Series or a callable. Prefer a Series mapper for large, many-to-one mappings (vectorized lookup). Use na_action='ignore' when you must preserve NAs and avoid mapping them. Avoid this path for multi-dimensional data or when you require preservation of original input dtypes beyond what pandas/NumPy will return.

mechanism.text:
Attempts to import an optional dependency and, if present, verify it meets a minimum-version requirement; on failure it either raises, warns, or silently returns None. Conceptually this is an import-then-validate pattern: try a standard dynamic import, map package name to an install-friendly name when needed, extract the top-level package for version checks, read the package version attribute, compare semantic versions, and handle errors according to a chosen policy.

Algorithmically it is straightforward: run importlib.import_module(name); if that fails, propagate or suppress the ImportError based on policy. If import succeeds, determine which module object should be queried for version metadata (the imported submodule or its top-level parent), obtain a textual version via __version__ (with small, package-specific normalization rules), parse versions into comparable objects, and compare to the minimum required version. If the installed version is older, either warn, raise, or return None.

Domain knowledge needed includes Python packaging and import mechanics (difference between top-level package and submodules, presence and reliability of __version__), semantic-versioning concepts (how versions are compared), and practical packaging quirks (some projects embed extra tokens in __version__ requiring normalization). Familiarity with importlib, sys.modules, and typical error-handling idioms in libraries (raise vs. warn vs. silent fallback) is also important.

Key constraints and assumptions: __version__ must exist and be parseable; package-specific special-casing (e.g., psycopg2) may be required; version parsing relies on a Version comparator (PEP 440 semantics assumed); mapping from internal name to install name must be maintained externally; behavior is synchronous and imports code during runtime (side effects possible). 

Appropriate when a library has optional, non-critical dependencies: use to gate features on external packages while providing clear diagnostics or graceful degradation depending on desired user experience.

s_param.name: codes
s_param.description: An array of category codes (integer codes) to be converted to correspond to new_categories.

s_param.name: old_categories
s_param.description: The Index of existing categories corresponding to the input codes.

s_param.name: new_categories
s_param.description: The Index of target categories to which codes should be recoded.

s_param.name: copy
s_param.description: Whether to copy the codes array if the codes are unchanged.

s_param.name: warn
s_param.description: Whether to warn on silent-NA mapping (map to -1 for unmapped categories).

examples.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# Example from the docstring: simple recode where one category becomes unmapped
old_cat = pd.Index(["b", "a", "c"])  # old categories
new_cat = pd.Index(["a", "b"])        # new target categories
codes = np.array([0, 1, 1, 2], dtype=np.int8)  # integer codes referencing old_cat

# Call the function exactly as named
new_codes = pd.core.arrays.categorical.recode_for_categories(codes, old_cat, new_cat, copy=True)
print(new_codes)  # expected: array([ 1,  0,  0, -1], dtype=int8)

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# Recode where categories are reordered; preserve the same array object when possible
old_cat = pd.Index(["x", "y", "z"]) 
new_cat = pd.Index(["z", "y", "x"]) 
codes = np.array([0, 2, 1, 0], dtype=np.int64)

# Request no copy when unchanged mappings would allow in-place reuse
new_codes = pd.core.arrays.categorical.recode_for_categories(codes, old_cat, new_cat, copy=False)
print(new_codes)  # integer array of new codes corresponding to new_cat

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# Demonstrate warn=True: unmapped categories become -1; warn controls whether a warning is emitted
old_cat = pd.Index(["red", "green", "blue"]) 
new_cat = pd.Index(["green"]) 
codes = np.array([0, 1, 2, 1], dtype=np.int32)

# With warn=True, unmapped (red, blue) map to -1; function still returns the integer codes array
new_codes = pd.core.arrays.categorical.recode_for_categories(codes, old_cat, new_cat, copy=True, warn=True)
print(new_codes)  # contains -1 for unmapped entries

mechanism.text:
Re-maps integer category codes produced for one category set to the corresponding integer codes for a different category set, producing a new integer array where entries that no longer map get a sentinel (−1). The core idea is to build an indexer that tells, for each old category, the position of that category in the new category list; then that indexer is used to translate the entire codes array by simple array indexing (vectorized take), which yields O(n) cost in the number of coded values plus the cost to build the indexer.

Conceptually this is about categorical encoding: categorical values are represented internally by small integers that index a category palette. When the palette changes (reorder, subset, superset, replacement), you must translate the integer codes so they refer to the new palette rather than re-scanning string/object values. get_indexer_for computes the mapping from old palette entries to new palette positions; a value not present in the new palette is represented by −1 and typically stands for “missing/NA.” coerce_indexer_dtype ensures the indexer has a compatible integer dtype for the subsequent vectorized take_nd operation.

Required domain knowledge: understanding of categorical encodings (integer codes + category palette), sentinel values for missingness, and the semantics of indexer operations (how -1 is treated by take_nd). Familiarity with vectorized array operations and the need to preserve dtype/shape is helpful.

Key constraints and assumptions: codes must already be integer indices for old_categories and fit the indexing semantics; old_categories/new_categories must supply an indexer API (get_indexer_for, equals); −1 is used as the missing sentinel and must be handled downstream; empty category lists and identical category lists are short-circuited; correct behavior assumes consistent integer dtype for efficient take operations. A warning path signals deprecated cases where old category values aren’t in the new palette.

Appropriate use: when you need to efficiently remap stored category codes after changing or aligning category palettes (reordering, merging, subsetting) without materializing the full object-valued array — e.g., in categorical data pipelines, merging datasets with different category sets, or performing dtype-preserving transformations.

s_param.name: value
s_param.description: Value to validate; the argument that will be checked for being an acceptable NA indicator or sentinel.

s_param.name: name
s_param.description: Name of the argument (used in error messages) — identifies which argument failed validation.

examples.code:
import pandas as pd
from pandas.core.arrays.string_arrow import validate_na_arg

# Example 2: pandas.NA is an accepted NA sentinel; should not raise
validate_na_arg(pd.NA, name='na')
print('pd.NA accepted as NA')

mechanism.text:
Accepts only values representing "missing" (pd.NA, np.nan, None, a library sentinel) or booleans; any other input triggers an error. The code implements a short-circuit validation: it checks a small set of predicates that characterize acceptable sentinel/missing values and returns immediately when one matches; if none match, it raises a ValueError. The checks combine identity tests (e.g., comparing to a sentinel object), type checks (isinstance for bool), and a numeric NaN-detection path (an auxiliary float-test plus np.isnan) to avoid calling isnan() on non-floats.

Understanding how pandas/NumPy represent missing data is essential. pd.NA is a scalar “missing” object that should be compared by identity or equality depending on context; np.nan is a floating-point IEEE NaN that requires isnan-style detection; None is Python’s null singleton; some libraries expose a distinct sentinel (lib.no_default) to mean “no argument supplied.” Also important: bool is a subclass of int in Python, so explicitly testing isinstance(value, bool) prevents booleans from being misidentified as numeric and incorrectly passed to the isnan path.

Key constraints and assumptions:
- The helper names (lib.no_default, lib.is_float, NA) must be defined and behave as expected; identity comparisons assume NA is a unique sentinel.
- The float-path first ensures the value is a float-like (lib.is_float) before calling np.isnan to prevent TypeErrors.
- Booleans are intentionally allowed; other numeric types (ints) are not treated as missing and will raise.
- The code treats np.nan only when lib.is_float recognizes the value; unusual types implementing isnan may be excluded.

Appropriate use cases include validating function arguments that are intended to accept only missing-value sentinels or explicit boolean flags (e.g., optional parameters accepting None/NA/NaN or True/False). It is not appropriate when other legitimate values (strings, integers, or custom sentinel objects) should be permitted or when a different notion of “missing” is required.

s_param.name: obj
s_param.description: Pandas object (DataFrame or Series). The function checks whether this object is a local variable in the caller's frame to help detect chained assignment; if it is local in the caller's frame it should not be treated as chained assignment.

examples.code:
import pandas as pd

# Example 1: object is a local variable in the caller frame -> typically True
def check_local_df():

    # The caller frame of is_local_in_caller_frame is this function's frame,
    # and `df` is a local variable here.

check_local_df()

import pandas as pd

# Example 2: object defined at module (global) scope -> typically False
df_global = pd.DataFrame({"x": [10, 20]})
# The caller frame is the module frame where df_global is a global, not a local variable.

import pandas as pd

    s = pd.Series([0.1, 0.2, 0.3])
    # `s` is local to this function, so the check should reflect that
    print("is_local_in_caller_frame (local Series):", pd.core.common.is_local_in_caller_frame(s))

check_local_series()

mechanism.text:
Checks whether a given object exists among the local variables of a stack frame two levels up, using object identity comparisons. Concretely, it obtains a frame object via sys._getframe(2), iterates through that frame's f_locals values and returns True if any value is the exact same object (v is obj); otherwise it returns False.

Algorithmically this is simple stack-frame inspection plus a linear scan: obtaining a FrameType is O(1) (subject to interpreter implementation), then iterating over f_locals.values() is O(n) in the number of local variables in that frame. The identity check ("is") is constant time per element. No hashing or deep comparisons are performed.

Domain knowledge required: familiarity with Python's runtime stack and frame objects (sys._getframe, FrameType, f_locals), and the difference between identity (is) and equality (__eq__). Also understanding that f_locals exposes the function's local namespace as a mapping view provided by the interpreter; it is an introspection/metaprogramming tool rather than a language-level variable access.

Key constraints and assumptions:
- sys._getframe is CPython-specific and may not be available or behave identically in alternative Python implementations or restricted environments.
- f_locals can be a snapshot or a mapping synchronized lazily with the interpreter's fast locals; contents and timing may be implementation dependent.
- Using frames can keep objects reachable longer (risk of reference cycles) and is relatively expensive compared to ordinary code paths.
- The check uses identity, so distinct objects that compare equal will not be matched.
- The hard-coded depth 2 assumes a fixed call-stack layout (fragile if wrappers or different call patterns are introduced).

Appropriate use cases: debugging, assertion/enforcement helpers, or metaprogramming utilities that need to know whether a specific object is one of another frame's locals. It is inappropriate for core program logic, security checks, or performance-sensitive code because it is implementation-sensitive, brittle, and not guaranteed across interpreters.

s_param.name: use_numexpr
s_param.description: Whether to attempt to use the numexpr engine for accelerated evaluation; falls back to standard Python evaluation when not possible.

examples.code:

# Series - Series

mechanism.text:
Evaluates a binary operation by dispatching between a fast expression engine (when available) and a standard Python/Pandas call. The code first resolves an operation string from a mapping; if a string exists and the caller opts into the accelerated path (use_numexpr=True), it attempts to use a specialized evaluator (_evaluate) that typically delegates to a vectorized expression engine (e.g., numexpr) for elementwise computation. If that path is not taken or not available, it falls back to a direct call of the operator callable (op(left, right)) via _evaluate_standard. A tiny test-mode hook records a sentinel value before executing the standard path to allow deterministic test checks.

Underlying algorithm and computational approach
- Dispatch-based evaluation: choose between a high-performance vectorized evaluator and a standard Python-level call depending on availability and flags.
- Vectorized expression engines (like numexpr) evaluate operations by compiling expressions and applying them in chunks, reducing Python overhead and improving memory/cache usage for large arrays/Series. The fallback simply invokes the operator on the operands, relying on their built-in broadcasting and implementation (Pandas/NumPy).

Domain knowledge required
- Familiarity with NumPy/Pandas broadcasting semantics and elementwise operations, since both paths rely on operand behavior.
- Understanding of vectorized engines (numexpr) trade-offs: memory chunking, supported operations, and when they outperform plain NumPy.
- Awareness of how operator callables are represented (e.g., operator.add or a Pandas override) and how mapping to string tokens enables expression evaluations.

Key constraints and assumptions
- The mapping must correctly translate operator objects to expression strings; None means no accelerated path.
- The accelerated evaluator must support the specific operation and operand types; otherwise correctness or performance can degrade.
- The code assumes op(left, right) is a valid way to compute the result for the fallback.
- _TEST_MODE affects only the standard path and requires the test infra to interpret stored results.

When appropriate to use
- Use this dispatch when you want opportunistic performance: enable vectorized engines for large, homogeneous arrays where they are known to help, while retaining correctness via the fallback for unsupported cases or mixed/custom types. Avoid forcing the accelerated path for small arrays or when operands implement nonstandard operator semantics that the engine cannot reproduce.

import pandas as pd

# Example 1: Basic conversion from ISO-8601 strings

mechanism.text:
Converts an object-typed ndarray of date/time-like values into a NumPy datetime64 array (and optionally extracts a timezone), using a parsing-and-coercion pipeline that distinguishes successfully parsed uniform datetimes, timezone-aware values, and uncoercible mixed or heterogenous inputs.

Algorithmically, the routine first normalizes input to an object ndarray and delegates heavy lifting to a lower-level parser (tslib.array_to_datetime). That parser attempts elementwise interpretation of strings, Python datetimes, and numeric epoch values into a common NumPy datetime64 representation, optionally normalizing to UTC and snapping to a requested unit (via a unit-abbreviation → NumPy unit conversion). The parser also returns any detected timezone information. Post-parsing logic inspects three outcomes: a datetime64-typed array (success), a non-datetime object array (mixed or uncoercible), or a timezone tag separate from the dtype. The wrapper enforces error policy (raise vs coerce) and rejects ambiguous mixed-timezone results unless explicitly allowed to return the raw object array.

Domain knowledge required includes understanding of NumPy datetime64 semantics (fixed-resolution integer-based timestamps), Python tzinfo vs timezone-naive datetimes, and the implications of coercing heterogeneous inputs (string parsing ambiguity, day-first/year-first ordering). Familiarity with precision/unit differences (seconds vs milliseconds vs nanoseconds) matters because converting to a coarser unit can lose information; converting between timezones requires normalization rules (e.g., convert vs preserve local time).

Key constraints and assumptions: input is an object array of parseable items; tslib.array_to_datetime can parse the given formats; timezone detection is unambiguous or else the function rejects the result; unit rounding may occur. It is appropriate to use when you need a homogeneous NumPy datetime64 array from mixed object representations and when you want explicit control over UTC normalization and error/coercion behavior. Avoid using it when preserving per-item timezone diversity is required unless you accept object-typed output.

s_param.name: cond
s_param.description: Boolean condition array that selects elements from left_op where True and from right_op where False.

s_param.name: left_op
s_param.description: Values returned where cond is True (array-like or scalar). Caller is responsible for extracting ndarray if necessary.

s_param.name: right_op
s_param.description: Values returned where cond is False (array-like or scalar). Caller is responsible for extracting ndarray if necessary.

s_param.name: use_numexpr
s_param.description: Whether to try to use numexpr for accelerated evaluation when available and appropriate (defaults to True).

examples.code:
import numpy as np
from pandas.core.computation.expressions import where

# Example 1: scalar left and right
cond = np.array([True, False, True, False], dtype=bool)
left = 10  # scalar returned where cond is True
right = 0  # scalar returned where cond is False
result = where(cond, left, right)
print(result)  # expected: array([10, 0, 10, 0])

import numpy as np
from pandas.core.computation.expressions import where

# Example 2: array-like left and right of the same shape as cond
cond = np.array([True, False, True], dtype=bool)
left = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
right = np.array([9.0, 8.0, 7.0])
result = where(cond, left, right)
print(result)  # expected: array([1.0, 8.0, 3.0])

from pandas.core.computation.expressions import where

# Example 3: mixed scalar and array, explicitly disabling numexpr

left = np.array([100, 200, 300])
right = -1  # scalar used where cond is False

mechanism.text:
Chooses elements from left_op or right_op for every position according to the boolean mask cond, producing an array where each output element is left_op[i] if cond[i] is True and right_op[i] otherwise. Conceptually this is a vectorized ternary (if-then-else) operation implemented either by NumPy’s elementwise selection (np.where) or by an alternative backend (_where) that can be a numexpr-based evaluator for faster, chunked, multithreaded evaluation.

Underlying algorithmic approach
- NumPy route: np.where iterates (in C) over aligned memory buffers and builds a result array, applying broadcasting rules and performing any dtype promotion required to represent both choices.
- Numexpr route: expressions are compiled and evaluated in blocks, using multiple threads and a small working set in cache to reduce peak memory and improve throughput for large numeric arrays. Both are pure elementwise computations with no side effects.

Domain knowledge required
- Understanding of vectorized array semantics: broadcasting, elementwise operations, and how boolean masks control selection.
- Familiarity with dtype promotion rules: mixing ints/floats/objects can change result type.
- Awareness of index alignment when using pandas Series/DataFrame: operations are usually on raw values; index mismatches need handling before selection.
- Performance trade-offs between direct NumPy and numexpr: numexpr helps for large numeric arrays but has restrictions.

Key constraints and assumptions
- cond must be a boolean mask (or convertible to boolean) matching or broadcastable to the shapes of left_op and right_op.
- _where must be assigned; the code asserts its presence.
- numexpr (if used) typically supports numeric dtypes only and limited Python constructs; it won’t handle arbitrary Python objects reliably.
- Resulting dtype follows promotion rules; missing values (NaN/NA) and object dtypes can behave differently across backends.

When appropriate to use
- Best for elementwise conditional selection on arrays or Series where you need a full vectorized result (avoid Python loops).
- Use the numexpr/backed path when working with large numeric arrays and memory/CPU throughput matter; use the standard NumPy path for small arrays, non-numeric/object dtypes, or when backend limitations matter.

mechanism.text:
Emits a run‑time deprecation warning when callers pass more positional arguments than a small, permitted set, while also exposing a modified function signature that shows most parameters as keyword-only. The decorator inspects the original signature, computes which parameters will remain allowed as positional, builds a new signature where remaining parameters are marked KEYWORD_ONLY (so help(), IDEs, and introspection show the intended future API), and wraps the original callable with a thin wrapper that warns if excessive positional arguments are actually used at call time. The wrapper itself forwards all arguments unchanged to preserve current behavior.

Domain knowledge required: familiarity with Python introspection (inspect.signature and Parameter kinds), PEP conventions around keyword-only parameters, the warnings module and how to raise deprecation-style notices (including stacklevel), and library versioning/deprecation policies so messages and allowed grace periods are meaningful. Understanding how __signature__ affects tooling and how functools.wraps preserves metadata is helpful.

Key constraints and assumptions: the decorator does not change runtime calling semantics — it only warns and updates the visible signature; callers are not prevented from using disallowed positional forms. It assumes pure-Python functions (setting __signature__ may not affect C-builtins), that parameter defaults and kinds are stable, and that allowed positional arguments are correctly identified (e.g., 'self' handling). Correct stacklevel calculation is needed to point warnings at the user code. The algorithm relies on introspection, so dynamic or generated callables with unusual signatures may be mishandled.

Appropriate use cases: staged API migrations where you want to move from positional to keyword-only parameters without immediate breaking changes. Useful in public libraries to notify users of forthcoming changes, improve introspection for tooling, and provide a clear upgrade path. Avoid for internal APIs or when you need to enforce behavior immediately (use signature validation or change the API instead).

mechanism.text:
Combines a collection of pandas Index objects into a single canonical Index by folding either a set-union or set-intersection operation over them, with careful handling of empty inputs, type preservation, and optional sorting.

Algorithmically, the code first de-duplicates identical Index objects to avoid redundant work, then treats three base cases: zero inputs → return an empty default Index; one input → return it unchanged; multiple inputs → either iteratively intersect (left-fold of intersection) or compute a union via a specialized union_indexes routine. The union path hands off to utilities that preserve Index subclass/type information and then normalizes the result with ensure_index. Sorting is applied in two places: union_indexes can accept a sort hint, and after construction a final conditional safe_sort_index enforces a stable, dtype-aware ordering when sorting was explicitly requested. A special sentinel (lib.no_default) distinguishes “no explicit sort preference” from an explicit False/True, influencing whether union_indexes receives a sort hint.

Domain knowledge required: familiarity with pandas Index semantics (Index subclasses, dtype and name maintenance, monotonicity, and uniqueness), set-like operations on index objects, and the consequences of sorting vs. preserving original ordering. Understanding how alignments and reindexing depend on Index values is important: unions expand the key space, intersections restrict it.

Key constraints and assumptions: inputs are Index-like and comparable; some Index types (e.g., MultiIndex, IntervalIndex, DatetimeIndex) have specialized union/intersection behavior that must be respected; iterative intersection is order-dependent only in cost (not result), while union uses a dedicated implementation for efficiency and type preservation. Sorting behavior uses a sentinel to avoid changing existing order unless explicitly requested.

Appropriate uses include axis/label consolidation when concatenating, aligning, or merging multiple DataFrame/Series objects, or computing the shared or combined label set for subsequent reindexing or broadcasting. Avoid when you need custom merge semantics (e.g., weighted merges) or when very large collections require more optimized streaming algorithms.
