mechanism.text:
Represents a lightweight adapter around a pandas.DataFrame that exposes the frame and its columns through a dataframe-exchange style interface. Each instance owns a reference to a DataFrame and a flag controlling whether column data may be copied; during construction it normalizes column names to str and may replace individual column objects with "rechunked" views to satisfy internal layout expectations. The adapter does not duplicate the whole DataFrame unless rechunking or allow_copy semantics force per-column replacements.

Lifecycle: created from an existing pandas.DataFrame, used to query metadata (pandas index), number of rows/columns, iterate or extract column objects (PandasColumn wrappers), select subsets by index or name, and produce chunked views. get_chunks either yields the same adapter (logical single-chunk view) or yields new adapter instances each wrapping a row-slice of the original DataFrame. There is no explicit resource management API — no close/dispose is required; the adapter holds only Python references and relies on normal garbage collection. Note that construction can mutate the wrapped DataFrame by calling isetitem on columns when rechunking occurs.

Key invariants and role in the library:
- Column names are stored as strings and the adapter exposes them as an Index.
- Metadata includes the original pandas index under the key 'pandas.index'.
- The adapter treats the DataFrame as a single logical chunk (num_chunks == 1) unless users request chunked iterators, which create new adapters for each slice.
- Column access always returns PandasColumn wrappers created with the adapter's allow_copy policy.
- It is an adapter/coordinator in the data-exchange layer: bridging pandas internals and higher-level consumers that expect a stable column/metadata API, providing selection, slicing, and per-column layout normalization without managing external resources.

mechanism.text:
Operates by detecting whether a pandas Series backed by a pyarrow ChunkedArray has more than one physical chunk, and—if permitted—merging those chunks into a single contiguous Arrow array so downstream code can assume a single-buffer layout. Conceptually this is a small data-layout normalization step: many Arrow-based producers produce chunked arrays (a logical array split across multiple physical buffers); some consumers (or APIs) expect or perform better with one contiguous chunk. The routine inspects the Series’ ArrowDtype, reads the underlying pa.ChunkedArray, and either leaves it alone (already single chunk) or calls Arrow’s combine_chunks() to produce a new single-chunk pa.Array, then constructs a new pandas Series that preserves the logical metadata (dtype, name, index).

Relevant domain knowledge includes understanding pyarrow’s chunked vs. single arrays, zero-copy semantics, and how pandas represents Arrow-backed Series (ArrowDtype and the .array._pa_array bridge). combine_chunks may allocate and copy buffers: this changes memory identity and can be expensive for large arrays. Consumers relying on zero-copy views into original buffers or on exact memory addresses must account for that.

Key constraints and assumptions: input must be an Arrow-backed Series (ArrowDtype); chunk count is available via pa.ChunkedArray.chunks; combining produces a new array that may copy data; the routine preserves Series index/name but produces a new Series object when rechunking. It also refuses to copy when caller disallows it (raising an error).

mechanism.text:
Converts a DataFrame into plain Python-native containers (mappings, lists) using a small set of deterministic strategies that preserve column/row layout and attempt to "box" complex pandas/NumPy values into simple Python objects when necessary. The core approach selects one of several orientations (e.g., columns-as-keys, rows-as-records, split/tight structures) and then emits values by iterating rows or columns using efficient iterators (itertuples and to_numpy) to minimize per-element overhead. For purely object-dtype columns it applies a boxing function to ensure any pandas-specific or extension-array items become plain Python values; for non-object dtypes it prefers raw numpy scalars/arrays to retain numeric types and performance.

Understanding this requires basic pandas/NumPy domain knowledge: differences between object dtype, NumPy dtypes, and ExtensionDtype; how pandas represents missing data (masked/NA vs. numpy.nan); and the cost trade-offs between row-wise (itertuples) and column-wise (to_numpy) iteration. The implementation uses optimized paths—column conversion to numpy for homogeneous numeric columns, row tuples for mixed/object columns—and treats masked dtypes specially so missing values are represented consistently.

Key constraints and assumptions:
- Column labels may be non-unique (a warning is issued and some columns may be dropped in certain orientations).
- orient='index' requires a unique index; index inclusion/exclusion is only supported for certain orientations.
- Object/extension dtypes trigger boxing, which can change representations (e.g., pandas Timestamp → Python datetime).
- The result is intended to be Python-native, not preserving pandas metadata beyond index/column names when using “tight”/“split”.

Appropriate usage: producing JSON-serializable or mapping/list representations of a DataFrame for export, interop, or testing, especially when you need one of the standard layouts (records, index, split/tight, columns-as-dicts). Avoid when you need to preserve full pandas types, extension-array semantics, or extremely large datasets where copying via to_numpy/itertuples would be too costly.

mechanism.text:
Produces a boolean mask marking array locations equal to a given replacement value while handling masked/Arrow-backed arrays and NA/NaN semantics. Conceptually it implements value-equality detection with care for three tricky regimes: floating-point NaN behavior, explicit “missing”/masked arrays, and mixed dtype compatibility (numeric vs boolean vs object vs Arrow).

1. Algorithmic approach
- Short-circuits when the input array uses a masked/Arrow dtype and the requested value is a floating NaN: it uses the underlying storage (raw NumPy buffer or PyArrow compute) plus the array’s own isna information to identify true NaNs but not already-missing entries.
- If the value is considered NA (via isna), it delegates to the array’s NA test, returning locations that are NA.
- For object-dtype arrays, it first excludes NA positions then tests equality (arr == value) only on non-missing entries to avoid NA propagation.
- For other dtypes it computes arr == value, converting Arrow/extension-array results into a boolean NumPy array if needed.
- There are deliberate no-op branches (pass) to avoid misleading equality tests when mixing numeric/boolean/string types where comparisons are semantically inappropriate.

2. Domain knowledge required
- Understanding of missing-data semantics: difference between NaN and library-defined NA, and that equality comparisons with NaN are false by IEEE rules.
- Familiarity with extension arrays (pandas BaseMaskedDtype, ArrowDtype), that may pack validity masks separately from storage.
- Awareness of dtype categories (numeric, boolean, object) and that equality behavior differs across them and across backends (NumPy vs PyArrow).

3. Key constraints and assumptions
- Assumes helper functions/is-tests (isna, is_numeric_dtype, is_bool_dtype, infer_dtype_from, is_nan_na) are available and accurate.
- Expects Arrow/extension arrays expose raw buffers or conversion APIs (._data, ._pa_array, to_numpy).
- Relies on arr == value returning an array-like truth mask or convertible result; non-NumPy truthy objects are coerced with to_numpy.
- Intentionally avoids attempting cross-type equality in certain mixed-type cases; callers should not expect matching semantics for such mixes.

4. When appropriate to use
- Use when you need a reliable boolean mask of positions equal to a sentinel value while respecting library-specific missing-value semantics and extension-array backends.
- Not intended for general-purpose elementwise comparison when types are mismatched or when you want raw IEEE equality semantics for NaNs without consulting higher-level NA markers.

mechanism.text:
Produces integer label arrays for two input key arrays that encode equal-value groups and then uses those labels to compute indexer pairs for non-unique relational joins (inner, left, right, full outer). Conceptually it factorizes values into compact integer codes (one code per unique key, with a reserved code for nulls), optionally sorts the unique key order, and then dispatches a join implementation that uses those labels to emit matching index positions. For some numeric cases an optimized hash-based path can short-circuit and directly produce indexers without needing separate label arrays.

Understanding this requires familiarity with relational join semantics (inner/left/right/full-outer), the idea of factorization / dictionary-encoding (mapping unique values to small integer labels), and how nulls/NA are treated as a distinct key that may be assigned a special label. It also relies on knowledge of dtype-specific representations (datetimes with timezones, categoricals, Arrow-backed arrays, masked/nullable arrays) because correct equality and missing-value handling must be preserved when converting to integer codes.

Key constraints and assumptions:
- Equality semantics of the original arrays must be preserved during conversion (special handling for timezone-aware datetimes, categoricals, Arrow/string types).
- A reserved label is used for missing values; count reflects the number of distinct non-null keys (and is incremented if nulls are present).
- The optimized hash join is only used for certain inner-joins on plain numeric-like types and when no sorting is requested; otherwise label-based compare/joining is used.
- Memory/CPU tradeoffs: factorization and potentially copying (e.g., Arrow dictionary encoding, conversion to i8) can be expensive for large inputs.
- Stable/expected output ordering depends on the sort flag and chosen join algorithm.

Appropriate use cases:
- Generating indexer pairs for merging or aligning two sequences with possibly repeated keys (the typical backend step in DataFrame.merge/Join).
- Any situation needing efficient matching of non-unique keys while preserving dtype-aware equality and null semantics. It is not a general-purpose high-level API; it’s intended as an internal building block for join algorithms where low-level control of labels, ordering, and NA handling matters.

Normalizes an optional mapping of JIT-related flags into a small, predictable dictionary of boolean options so calling code always receives the same three keys with concrete truth values. Conceptually it implements a simple defaults-and-override pattern: if the caller omits the whole mapping, a new empty one is used; for each expected flag the mapping is queried and a fallback default is supplied. The result is a pure, side-effect-free value that can be passed directly to a JIT engine or used to decide compilation behavior.

Understanding how to use this correctly requires basic domain knowledge about ahead-of-time or just-in-time compilation flags (for example, what "nopython", "nogil", and "parallel" mean in a JIT toolchain). Those flags control low-level behaviors (whether to compile to native code without Python object handling, whether to release the global interpreter lock, whether to enable multi-threaded parallel loops), so users must know the performance and compatibility implications of enabling them.

Key constraints and assumptions: inputs are expected to be a mapping from string keys to booleans or None; no type coercion or validation beyond dictionary lookup is performed, so non-boolean values will be propagated as-is. It assumes callers will pass only the known keys or rely on sensible defaults. The function is deterministic and stateless—calling it with the same input always yields the same output—and cheap to run.

Appropriate use cases include any code path that needs a canonical set of JIT configuration flags derived from user-supplied options: normalizing user configuration before invoking a compiler, storing a stable configuration for caching, or comparing requested compilation modes. It is not a replacement for validating semantics or for translating higher-level policy into safe flag combinations.

Looks up a set of option keys that match a pattern, builds human-readable descriptions for each, and either prints the combined text or returns it as a single string. The implementation is a simple pipeline: select, map, join, and output. Selection is delegated to _select_options(pat) which yields zero or more keys; each key is transformed by _build_option_description(k) into a one-line or multi-line description; the descriptions are concatenated with newline separators; if no keys were found an OptionError is raised; if printing is requested the concatenated text is printed and the function returns None, otherwise the text is returned.

Algorithmically this is linear in the number of matched keys plus the cost of building each description. Complexity is O(n * cost_build) where n is the number of keys; memory use is proportional to the total length of all descriptions because they are materialized into one string before printing/returning.

Correct use requires domain knowledge of what the “options” represent in the surrounding system (configuration keys, CLI flags, feature flags, etc.), how patterns are interpreted by _select_options, and what information _build_option_description emits (default values, types, documentation). Calling code must also understand the dual I/O behavior: the function either prints for side-effect or returns a string for further processing; these two modes are mutually exclusive in the design.

Key constraints and assumptions: _select_options must return an iterable of keys and should raise no exceptions itself (other than being allowed to return an empty list); _build_option_description must return text for any key provided. The function enforces that an empty result is exceptional (raises OptionError). Side effects (printing) mean the function is not purely functional; consumers that need programmatic use should request a return value, not rely on printed output. Thread-safety and reentrancy depend entirely on the underlying helper functions and any shared option registry.

Appropriate usage patterns: interactive help or debugging (print mode), or generation of documentation/snippets for further processing (return mode). Avoid for high-performance tight loops when many keys are matched repeatedly unless description-building is cheap or cached.

mechanism.text:
Provides and maintains the mutable state needed to compute exponential weighted moving averages (EWMA) incrementally over an existing DataFrame/Series. Instances encapsulate the running summary (through an EWMMeanState), configuration for weighting behavior (decay form, adjustment, NA handling, minimum periods), and the selected JIT engine hookup used to execute an online EWMA kernel efficiently.

Lifecycle and use:
- Construction wires together the input object metadata and creates an EWMMeanState that holds the internal last EWMA values and any per-column bookkeeping. At construction the object validates unsupported modes (e.g., time-based windows) and requires the supported JIT engine (numba).
- Typical use is calling mean() to compute EWMA for the current buffer. mean() either computes from scratch for the stored selection or performs an incremental update when passed a new chunk (update). For incremental updates the instance appends the new samples to the last EWMA state and runs the online kernel; the first call that provides update must be preceded by an initial call (update=None) to establish last_ewm.
- The instance exposes reset() to clear the saved running state so subsequent computations start fresh. There is no external resource that must be closed—no file/connection handles—so no formal disposal is required.

Invariants and architectural role:
- The class enforces that time-based windows are unsupported and that only a specific engine (numba) is used, ensuring predictable execution semantics.
- It maintains shape and index/column alignment between stored state and incoming updates: last_ewm must match the selection dimensionality, and result construction preserves original index/columns.
- last_ewm presence is required for update-mode calls; min_periods, adjust, and ignore_na semantics are held consistently in the EWMMeanState and respected by the JIT kernel.
- Architecturally it is a coordinator/adaptor: it does not implement statistical kernels itself but manages state, prepares arrays, selects a generated JIT EWMA function, and delegates numeric computation to that engine while providing an incremental, streaming EWMA API to the surrounding library.

mechanism.text:
Retrieves a configuration value by resolving a pattern into a canonical key, finding the associated container (root) for that key, and returning the value stored at that key in the container.

Algorithm / computational approach:
- The code follows a three-step resolution pipeline: normalize/validate the input pattern to a single lookup key (_get_single_key), determine the container that holds that key plus the actual lookup token (_get_root), then perform a direct mapping lookup (root[k]) to return the stored value. Conceptually this is a path-resolution followed by an associative-array access. Cost is dominated by the helper work: key normalization and root discovery typically walk the pattern (O(depth) or O(length)), while the final lookup is an average O(1) dictionary/mapping access.

Domain knowledge required:
- Familiarity with hierarchical configuration or option stores, where keys may be expressed as patterns (e.g., dotted paths, globs, or aliases) that must be resolved to a concrete storage key and container. Knowledge of Python mapping semantics (KeyError on missing keys) and mutability/aliasing behavior of containers is also important.

Key constraints and assumptions:
- _get_single_key and _get_root are relied upon to perform validation, disambiguation, and to return a valid (root, k) pair. There is no built-in default or fallback: missing keys will raise exceptions. Concurrency/side-effects: concurrent mutation of root between root discovery and lookup may change the result or raise. The code assumes root supports __getitem__ with k and that k is hashable where applicable.

When appropriate to use:
- Use when you need a direct, synchronous retrieval from a structured options store where patterns must be resolved first and where absence should be treated as an error. Not ideal for bulk lookups, tolerant lookups (needs defaults), or highly concurrent contexts without additional locking.

implementation:
def get_option(pat: str) -> Any:
    key = _get_single_key(pat)
    root, k = _get_root(key)
    return root[k]

mechanism.text:
If a selector is given as a callable, it is applied to each column name and the function returns the set of indices of names for which the callable returns a truthy value; otherwise, the input is returned unchanged. The computational approach is a simple single-pass filter with enumeration: iterate once over the sequence of names, call the predicate on each name, and collect the zero-based positions where the predicate holds. This is O(n) in time and O(k) in auxiliary space, where n is number of names and k is the count of selected names. No sorting or additional scans are performed.

Domain knowledge: the pattern is common in data-frame or table APIs where columns can be selected either by index-like sequences or by predicate functions that accept a column identifier (often a string) and answer whether it should be included. Understanding how callables are expected to behave (pure predicate returning truthy/falsey values and not mutating state) is important. Familiarity with zero-based indexing and how selection sets of indices are consumed downstream (order sensitivity, duplication handling) is also needed.

Key constraints and assumptions: the names iterable is enumeratable in a stable, predictable order (it must support a single pass). The callable must accept each name value and be side-effect free or at least safe when invoked multiple times. Returned indices correspond to the original enumeration order and are unique (a set is used). If the provided usecols is not callable, it is assumed already to be the desired sequence or set (no validation or conversion is done). No type coercion or error handling for bad callables or non-hashable names occurs beyond what Python raises.

Appropriate usage: use this when an API allows flexible column selection via either explicit index/sequence or a predicate over names, and you need a canonical set of integer positions for downstream processing. Avoid if selection needs to preserve duplicate positions, depend on order of selection beyond natural order, or if the names iterable is huge and the callable is expensive — in those cases consider lazy evaluation or more explicit validation.

mechanism.text:
Returns a deduplicated set of column identifiers (as elements drawn from the provided columns sequence) that should be treated as date columns, while validating that any string names actually exist and raising a clear error if they do not.

Algorithm / computational approach
- The routine first short-circuits non-list inputs (commonly boolean flags) by returning an empty set — it only processes a list form of the option.
- It scans each entry in the provided list and classifies it: if the entry is a string it is treated as a column name and checked for membership in the columns sequence; otherwise the code attempts to resolve it to a column via membership or by indexing into the columns sequence.
- Two sets are built: one for missing string names (to collect errors) and one for unique resolved column identifiers (to eliminate duplicates).
- If any string names were missing, it reports them together as a ValueError; otherwise it returns the resolved set.

Domain knowledge required
- Familiarity with tabular data where columns can be referenced by name or by positional index and where a caller might request certain columns be parsed as dates.
- Understanding of Python sequence membership/indexing semantics and the distinction between a column’s name/value versus its numeric position in the sequence.

Key constraints and assumptions
- The columns parameter is a sequence of hashable identifiers and supports both membership checks and integer indexing (e.g., list of names).
- Non-list parse_dates values are treated as “no explicit columns to validate”; callers expecting boolean semantics must pass something other than a list to get that behavior.
- Ambiguity exists if a non-string entry is equal to a column value — the code prefers membership over positional interpretation, which may surprise callers who intended numeric indexing.
- Duplicate entries are collapsed by the set; ordering is not preserved.

When to use it
- Use this validation step when accepting a user-provided list of columns to be parsed as dates, to produce a canonical, unique set of columns and to surface missing-name errors early before performing parsing. It is suitable for preprocessing options in CSV/table readers or similar ETL steps.

mechanism.text:
Aggregates a DataFrame into a multi-dimensional table by grouping on one or more index and column keys and applying one or more aggregation functions, returning a pivot-style result. The implementation delegates the heavy lifting to an internal pivot routine and handles the multi-aggregation case by computing separate tables for each aggregation, then concatenating those tables along the column axis to produce a single DataFrame whose top-level columns label the aggregation applied.

Algorithmically, the approach is: for a single aggfunc, compute grouped summaries directly (via __internal_pivot_table), preserving options like margins, observed categories, sorting, and fill values. For multiple aggfuncs, iterate over the functions, build an intermediate table for each, collect them, and call concat with keys so the final DataFrame has a hierarchical column index (aggregation name → original column labels). The concat helper resolves object shapes and alignment (union vs intersection of axes), decides whether to sort non-concatenation axes, sanitizes mixed-dimensional inputs, and constructs the final block/axis-aligned result while warning about deprecated default behaviors.

Practical domain knowledge: understanding group-by semantics, aggregation idempotence, and how categorical/DatetimeIndex ordering and observed categories affect grouping and result shape. Familiarity with MultiIndex layouts helps interpret multi-aggregation outputs. Awareness of memory/layout implications (concatenation may reindex/align, potentially copying data) and copy-on-write behavior is useful for performance-sensitive workflows.

Key constraints and assumptions: inputs are pandas Series/DataFrame objects with compatible axes; aggfuncs must be callable or name-resolvable; when multiple aggfuncs are provided, each aggregation is computed independently and then aligned by concat (so differing shapes can result in NaNs). concat assumes only 'inner' or 'outer' join semantics for the other axis and enforces keys if ignore_index is false. Default sorting behavior can change across versions and may cause warnings for DatetimeIndex concatenations.

Appropriate use cases: summarizing tabular data into cross-tabulated reports, computing multiple summary metrics simultaneously (e.g., mean and sum) and producing a readable MultiIndex column result, or generating contingency-like tables with marginal totals. Avoid when per-group custom multi-column aggregations that require nontrivial alignment logic are needed; in such cases, compute aggregations in a single grouped operation to avoid an extra concat and reindexing.

mechanism.text:
Selects the appropriate representation of "missing" values for a given column by choosing between per-column and global specifications and falling back to a configured default set when requested. At its core the code implements a simple conditional dispatch: if the caller supplied a mapping of per-column NA definitions, look up the column; if present, return the pair of NA-token set and NA-fillers for that column; if absent, either return a global default set of NA tokens (when keep_default_na is true) or empty sets (when false). If no per-column mapping was provided at all, the provided global NA specifications are returned unchanged.

Algorithmically this is constant-time branching and dictionary lookup (O(1) average for the lookup). The function is pure in that it makes no mutations and simply returns a tuple describing how to treat values as missing for downstream parsing/cleaning.

Domain knowledge: missing-value semantics in tabular data parsing (CSV/TSV/etc.). Practitioners should know the distinction between tokens that denote missingness (strings like "NA", "null", empty strings) and the values or transformations used to fill/flag missing entries. Also useful is familiarity with per-column overrides versus global defaults: some columns may use domain-specific NA tokens that differ from general dataset-wide conventions.

Key constraints and assumptions: na_values may be either a dict mapping column identifiers to token-sets or a global token-set; na_fvalues is assumed to be the corresponding per-column or global filler structure and, when na_values is a dict, must contain the same keys; STR_NA_VALUES (a module constant) must be defined as the canonical default token set; types returned are expected by callers (typically sets or similar iterables). The function assumes column identifiers used for lookup match those in the input mapping.

Appropriate usage: when determining which tokens to treat as missing for a specific column prior to parsing, cleaning, or imputing—especially in systems that support both per-column NA overrides and dataset-wide defaults.

mechanism.text:
Resets one or more registered options to their default values according to a pattern-matching selection and then applies the same assignment machinery used for explicit option setting.

Algorithm / computational approach
- Pattern selection: an initial helper (_select_options) expands the given pattern into a set of option keys. That set must be non-empty; otherwise an error is raised.
- Safety restriction: when the pattern yields multiple keys, a minimum specificity check prevents accidental mass resets (pattern must be at least 4 characters unless the special keyword "all" is used).
- Iterative reset through existing set-option machinery: for each selected key, the implementation calls the set-option path (set_option) with the option key and its registered default value. This reuses the same validation, storage, and callback semantics as ordinary assignment.
- The set-option path enforces an even number of args, accepts dict-style bulk updates, runs optional validators on new values, writes into the option storage root, and triggers any registered callbacks.

Domain knowledge required
- Understanding of a central option registry: options are registered elsewhere with metadata (default value, validator function, storage root, and callback).
- Familiarity with pattern-to-key semantics provided by _select_options (wildcards, prefixes, or literal keys) and the special "all" keyword.
- Awareness of validators and side-effectful callbacks that run on assignment.

Key constraints and assumptions
- _select_options must deterministically map patterns to existing keys.
- _registered_options contains defval, validator, storage root mapping, and cb fields for each key.
- Validators raise on invalid input; callbacks can have side effects and must be safe to call during resets.
- The minimum-characters rule guards against accidental broad matches but is heuristic, not foolproof.

When appropriate to use
- Use when you need to restore one or a controlled group of configuration options to their canonical defaults, while preserving validation and notification semantics. Avoid using it for arbitrary state reset if callbacks or validators have side effects you cannot tolerate. For wholesale resets use the explicit "all" keyword after understanding its implications.

mechanism.text:
Accepts paired keys and values (or a single dict) and applies them atomically into a shared options/storage model: each key is normalized, validated if a validator is registered, then written into the underlying storage, and a post-write callback is invoked when present.

1. Algorithmic approach
- Flattening/normalization: input can be a mapping or a sequence of alternating keys and values. A small preprocessing stage converts a single dict into a flat sequence so the rest of the routine can operate on a uniform alternating list.
- Pairwise iteration: the routine iterates over key/value pairs in lockstep (using a strict zip-like mechanism), ensuring every key has an associated value; an odd-length input is rejected early.
- Per-key processing pipeline: for each key the algorithm performs three main operations in order — key normalization/resolution, optional validation, and storage assignment — followed by an optional callback. This is effectively a map of (normalize → validate → assign → notify) applied to each pair.
- Fail-fast semantics: validation and other checks run before modification so invalid inputs trigger exceptions rather than producing partial or inconsistent state.

2. Domain knowledge required
- Familiarity with the system’s option-naming scheme and normalization rules (what _get_single_key returns).
- Awareness of registered options and their validators/callbacks: what constraints validators enforce and what side effects callbacks produce.
- Understanding of the backing storage model (what _get_root returns) so callers know where/when updates are visible.

3. Key constraints and assumptions
- Inputs must be either a single mapping or an even-length sequence of alternating keys and values.
- Validators are expected to raise on invalid values; the code assumes validators are synchronous and exception-based.
- Callbacks are synchronous and can safely run immediately after assignment.
- No transactional rollback: if one key fails after prior keys succeeded, earlier assignments remain.

4. When to use
- Appropriate for bulk-updating configuration/options where normalization, validation, and notification are required per key.
- Not suitable when transactional all-or-nothing semantics are needed, or when asynchronous validation/callbacks are required.

mechanism.text:
Converts arbitrary scalar or list-like inputs into pandas datetime-like objects using a type-dispatched, vectorized parsing pipeline with optional caching and timezone handling. The implementation first normalizes the time origin (e.g., non-unix epoch shifts), then selects a conversion path based on the input’s type (Timestamp, Series, Index, DataFrame/dict of units, generic list-like, or single scalar). Heavy lifting is delegated to a vectorized converter for "listlike" data; for Series/Index and generic arrays the code attempts to reuse a precomputed cache of parsed values to avoid re-parsing repeated strings. Timezone-aware handling is done by localizing or converting Timestamps when utc is requested.

Required domain knowledge
- Basics of datetime representations: epoch/origin, units (seconds, milliseconds, etc.), naive vs timezone-aware timestamps.
- Parsing caveats: ambiguous date orders (dayfirst/yearfirst), and performance trade‑offs between a fixed format parse and general multi-format parsing.
- Pandas data model: distinctions among scalar Timestamp, DatetimeIndex/Series, Index/ExtensionArray, and how vectorized operations differ from per-element mapping.

Key constraints and assumptions
- Certain combinations are invalid: e.g., providing an "exact" parsing flag with mixed/ISO8601 formats is rejected.
- Origin adjustments occur before parsing and assume the provided unit is consistent with origin.
- Cache is only used when beneficial; empty-cache branches fall back to full vectorized parsing.
- Error handling follows the chosen policy (raise/coerce/ignore) and OutOfBounds datetime errors may be propagated or suppressed depending on that policy.
- Behavior differs for single scalars vs collections (returns scalar Timestamp/NaT vs Index/Series).

When to use
- Converting heterogeneous input (strings, integers, arrays, Series, dicts-of-units) into pandas datetime types in a robust, vectorized way.
- When you need timezone localization/normalization or epoch-based origin adjustment.
- Not ideal when you need ultra-strict per-element custom parsing beyond available format controls, or when you require streaming/one-pass parsing with minimal memory (this is optimized for in-memory, vectorized workloads).

mechanism.text:
Maps discrete-sampled data indices to the corresponding angular-frequency (well: linear frequency) bins used by the discrete Fourier transform, returning the sequence 0, 1, ..., floor((n-1)/2), negative frequencies ..., -1 scaled by 1/(n·d). The implementation itself is a thin dispatcher: if the provided array module (xp) exposes an FFT module and is not the numpy package, it calls that backend's fftfreq (allowing GPU-backed libs like CuPy to produce device arrays); otherwise it falls back to numpy.fft.fftfreq and rejects a device argument for plain NumPy.

Algorithmically, fftfreq computes the standard DFT frequency grid: for n samples spaced by interval d, frequencies are k/(n·d) for k = 0..n-1, then reinterpreted modulo n to give a sequence with positive low frequencies in ascending order and the negative (high) frequencies at the end. For even n the Nyquist term appears at n/2 as +1/(2d); for odd n the split is asymmetric. Complexity is O(n) to fill the array.

Correct use requires domain knowledge of discrete-time sampling and DFT conventions: how FFT bin indices map to physical frequency (units are 1/d), the Nyquist limit (1/(2d)), and that bin ordering matches the unshifted FFT output (i.e., zero frequency at index 0, positive frequencies up to Nyquist, then negative frequencies). Understand aliasing and that the DFT assumes periodic extension of the finite sequence.

Key constraints and assumptions: xp must be an array-like backend with a compatible fftfreq when non-NumPy; device only supported for those backends; semantics are inherited from the backend implementation. Use this when you need a frequency axis aligned with an FFT result for spectral analysis, filtering design, or plotting; do not use it as a substitute for frequency-shifted representations (use fftshift for centered plots).

mechanism.text:
Produces the frequency-bin centers associated with the real-input discrete Fourier transform (RFFT), dispatching to either NumPy or a compatible array library’s FFT implementation. Conceptually, the RFFT of an n-sample real signal yields n//2+1 nonredundant complex frequency bins spanning 0 up to the Nyquist frequency (1/(2d)). The computed array returns those bin center frequencies with uniform spacing 1/(n·d), so the k-th entry is k/(n·d) for k = 0..floor(n/2).

Algorithmically this is a trivial arithmetic construction rather than a transform: it computes an evenly spaced sequence based on n and the sample spacing d. The function is a thin dispatcher: if the provided array-library “xp” exposes an FFT module and is not the NumPy module object (checked via xp.__name__ != 'numpy'), it calls xp.fft.rfftfreq (allowing libraries like CuPy to run on accelerator devices). Otherwise it falls back to numpy.fft.rfftfreq and rejects a device argument when using NumPy.

Domain knowledge needed: understanding Nyquist frequency, sample spacing (or sampling rate as 1/d), and the relationship between discrete Fourier transform bin indices and physical frequency. Use this to interpret spectral plots, scale power spectral densities correctly, and align frequency arrays with RFFT outputs (which have length floor(n/2)+1).

Key constraints and assumptions: n and d define a uniform grid; the routine assumes evenly sampled, real-valued input. The wrapper assumes xp.fft.rfftfreq exists and that xp.__name__ reliably distinguishes non-NumPy libraries (a brittle check). The device parameter is only meaningful for non-NumPy backends; passing device with NumPy raises an error. Edge cases (n ≤ 0, nonstandard xp objects) defer to underlying implementations.

Appropriate use: constructing frequency axes for spectra computed by real-input FFT routines, ensuring correct physical-frequency labeling for plots or conversions (e.g., to Hz). For full-complex FFTs or nonuniform sampling, use other utilities or derive bins differently.

mechanism.text:
Represents a node in a hierarchical (agglomerative) clustering tree: either a leaf that corresponds to an original observation or an internal node that records a merge of two child clusters. Each instance holds immutable structural state (id, left and right child references), a non‑negative linkage distance at which the merge occurred, and a count of original observations contained below that node.

Construction enforces key invariants: the numeric id and distance must be non‑negative; a node must be either a leaf (no children) or a proper binary internal node (both left and right present); and count is at least one. For internal nodes the count is derived from the counts of its two children, guaranteeing that count always equals the total number of observations in the subtree. These checks prevent malformed trees (e.g., unary nodes) and ensure aggregation semantics remain consistent.

Usage pattern is straightforward: instances are constructed (normally by a clustering algorithm as it merges clusters), linked into a binary tree, and then read by consumers—distance-based comparisons, subtree size queries, and traversals. Comparison operators (<, >, ==) compare nodes by their merge distance, making nodes suitable for ordering in heaps or for determining merge priorities during algorithm execution. The provided pre_order method performs an explicit, iterative preorder traversal producing a list of values obtained by applying a function to each visited node; it uses stack-like storage plus visited sets to avoid recursion and to visit children in left-then-right order.

Nodes do not manage external resources and have no disposal/close requirement—garbage collection suffices once references are dropped. In the library architecture, ClusterNode acts as the elemental data structure for representing the dendrogram produced by clustering routines, enabling traversal, inspection, and distance‑based ordering of cluster merges.

mechanism.text:
Rescaling each column so its values have unit standard deviation while leaving column means unchanged. The routine computes the standard deviation per column (axis=0) and divides each column by that value. Columns whose computed standard deviation equals zero are treated specially: their divisor is set to 1 to avoid division-by-zero, the values remain numerically unchanged, and a runtime warning may be emitted. The implementation also respects an array-backend abstraction (xp) and handles “lazy” array types by optionally checking for finite values before computing statistics.

Conceptually this is a form of feature scaling or normalization (often called standardization when centering is included). It enforces equal scale across features so that algorithms sensitive to input magnitudes (gradient-based optimizers, distance metrics, regularized linear models, k-nearest neighbors, clustering) do not bias behavior toward larger-variance features. It is not whitening in the linear-algebra sense (no decorrelation or sphering): covariances between columns remain unchanged.

Key assumptions and constraints:
- Works column-wise (axis=0) and assumes numeric, finite data; NaNs/Infs can break std computation unless checked/handled.
- Uses population standard deviation (typical numpy/xp default, ddof=0), not the unbiased sample estimator; downstream expectations about variance must match.
- Zero-variance columns are left unchanged to preserve stability; downstream algorithms that require non-constant inputs may still fail.
- Outliers strongly influence the standard deviation, so robust scaling may be preferable when heavy tails exist.
- Does not remove means; if zero-centered data is required, subtract the mean first.
- When using lazy array backends, finite checks may be deferred to avoid materializing data.

Appropriate use cases:
- Preprocessing features prior to methods sensitive to scale (SVMs, k-means, many ML pipelines).
- A lightweight, fast scaling step when correlation structure should be preserved.
- Not appropriate when full whitening (decorrelation/sphering), mean-centering, or outlier-robust scaling are needed.

mechanism.text:
Estimates the first derivative by forming finite-difference stencils at multiple step sizes and adaptively refining them until a convergence criterion based on absolute and relative tolerances is met. The implementation builds central and one‑sided stencils, computes the corresponding finite‑difference weights by solving Vandermonde systems, evaluates f at the shifted sample points, combines those samples into derivative estimates, and monitors the change in successive estimates to separate truncation and round‑off error. If the estimate does not improve when the step is reduced, or if non‑finite values appear, the procedure flags an error for that point. The algorithm uses repeated halving (or a user-specified factor) of the step and Richardson-type extrapolation behaviour (through combining different geometric sequences of h) to accelerate convergence.

Relevant domain knowledge
- Numerical differentiation theory: truncation error scales with some power of h (depends on stencil/order) while round‑off error grows as h→0; optimal h balances these effects.
- Construction of finite‑difference weights via polynomial interpolation (solving a Vandermonde linear system).
- Behavior of floating‑point arithmetic (machine epsilon, smallest normal) and how tolerances should be chosen relative to data scale and desired accuracy.
- Smoothness of f: higher‑order stencils assume the function is sufficiently differentiable over the stencil interval.

Key constraints and assumptions
- f must be callable and well‑behaved (smooth) on the evaluation neighborhood; noisy or discontinuous functions will give poor or unstable results.
- Tolerances and step parameters must be nonnegative scalars; initial step > 0; maxiter and order are positive integers.
- The method exploits vectorized array backends (NumPy-like array namespace) and expects broadcasting-compatible x and step parameters.
- The algorithm is expensive in function evaluations and sensitive to the chosen order and step factor; extremely high order or tiny steps can cause ill-conditioning in the Vandermonde solve and numerical instability.
- It only computes first derivatives and returns NaN/flags for points that fail convergence or produce non‑finite results.

Appropriate use cases
- When analytic derivatives or automatic differentiation are unavailable and a moderate-accuracy numerical derivative is required on smooth functions.
- For vectorized evaluation over arrays where many derivative points can be computed in parallel.
Avoid using this when f is noisy, non-smooth, or when exact derivatives via AD or symbolic methods are available; also avoid unnecessarily high orders or tiny steps because of numerical conditioning and cost.

implementation:
@xp_capabilities(skip_backends=[('array_api_strict', _array_api_strict_skip_reason), ('dask.array', _dask_reason)], jax_jit=False)
def derivative(f, x, *, args=(), tolerances=None, maxiter=10, order=8, initial_step=0.5, step_factor=2.0, step_direction=0, preserve_shape=False, callback=None):
    res = _derivative_iv(f, x, args, tolerances, maxiter, order, initial_step, step_factor, step_direction, preserve_shape, callback)
    func, x, args, atol, rtol, maxiter, order, h0, fac, hdir, preserve_shape, callback = res
    temp = eim._initialize(func, (x,), args, preserve_shape=preserve_shape)
    func, xs, fs, args, shape, dtype, xp = temp
    finfo = xp.finfo(dtype)
    atol = finfo.smallest_normal if atol is None else atol
    rtol = finfo.eps ** 0.5 if rtol is None else rtol
    x, f = (xs[0], fs[0])
    df = xp.full_like(f, xp.nan)
    hdir = xp.broadcast_to(hdir, shape)
    hdir = xp.reshape(hdir, (-1,))
    hdir = xp.astype(xp.sign(hdir), dtype)
    h0 = xp.broadcast_to(h0, shape)
    h0 = xp.reshape(h0, (-1,))
    h0 = xp.astype(h0, dtype)
    h0 = xpx.at(h0)[h0 <= 0].set(xp.nan)
    status = xp.full_like(x, eim._EINPROGRESS, dtype=xp.int32)
    nit, nfev = (0, 1)
    il = hdir < 0
    ic = hdir == 0
    ir = hdir > 0
    io = il | ir
    work = _RichResult(x=x, df=df, fs=f[:, xp.newaxis], error=xp.nan, h=h0, df_last=xp.nan, error_last=xp.nan, fac=fac, atol=atol, rtol=rtol, nit=nit, nfev=nfev, status=status, dtype=dtype, terms=(order + 1) // 2, hdir=hdir, il=il, ic=ic, ir=ir, io=io, diff_state=_RichResult(central=[], right=[], fac=None))
    res_work_pairs = [('status', 'status'), ('df', 'df'), ('error', 'error'), ('nit', 'nit'), ('nfev', 'nfev'), ('x', 'x')]

    def pre_func_eval(work):
        n = work.terms
        h = work.h[:, xp.newaxis]
        c = work.fac
        d = c ** 0.5
        if work.nit == 0:
            hc = h / c ** xp.arange(n, dtype=work.dtype)
            hc = xp.concat((-xp.flip(hc, axis=-1), hc), axis=-1)
        else:
            hc = xp.concat((-h, h), axis=-1) / c ** (n - 1)
        if work.nit == 0:
            hr = h / d ** xp.arange(2 * n, dtype=work.dtype)
        else:
            hr = xp.concat((h, h / d), axis=-1) / c ** (n - 1)
        n_new = 2 * n if work.nit == 0 else 2
        x_eval = xp.zeros((work.hdir.shape[0], n_new), dtype=work.dtype)
        il, ic, ir = (work.il, work.ic, work.ir)
        x_eval = xpx.at(x_eval)[ir].set(work.x[ir][:, xp.newaxis] + hr[ir])
        x_eval = xpx.at(x_eval)[ic].set(work.x[ic][:, xp.newaxis] + hc[ic])
        x_eval = xpx.at(x_eval)[il].set(work.x[il][:, xp.newaxis] - hr[il])
        return x_eval

    def post_func_eval(x, f, work):
        n = work.terms
        n_new = n if work.nit == 0 else 1
        il, ic, io = (work.il, work.ic, work.io)
        work_fc = (f[ic][:, :n_new], work.fs[ic], f[ic][:, -n_new:])
        work_fc = xp.concat(work_fc, axis=-1)
        if work.nit == 0:
            fc = work_fc
        else:
            fc = (work_fc[:, :n], work_fc[:, n:n + 1], work_fc[:, -n:])
            fc = xp.concat(fc, axis=-1)
        work_fo = xp.concat((work.fs[io], f[io]), axis=-1)
        if work.nit == 0:
            fo = work_fo
        else:
            fo = xp.concat((work_fo[:, 0:1], work_fo[:, -2 * n:]), axis=-1)
        work.fs = xp.zeros((ic.shape[0], work.fs.shape[-1] + 2 * n_new), dtype=work.dtype)
        work.fs = xpx.at(work.fs)[ic].set(work_fc)
        work.fs = xpx.at(work.fs)[io].set(work_fo)
        wc, wo = _derivative_weights(work, n, xp)
        work.df_last = xp.asarray(work.df, copy=True)
        work.df = xpx.at(work.df)[ic].set(fc @ wc / work.h[ic])
        work.df = xpx.at(work.df)[io].set(fo @ wo / work.h[io])
        work.df = xpx.at(work.df)[il].multiply(-1)
        work.h /= work.fac
        work.error_last = work.error
        work.error = xp.abs(work.df - work.df_last)

    def check_termination(work):
        stop = xp.astype(xp.zeros_like(work.df), xp.bool)
        i = work.error < work.atol + work.rtol * abs(work.df)
        work.status = xpx.at(work.status)[i].set(eim._ECONVERGED)
        stop = xpx.at(stop)[i].set(True)
        if work.nit > 0:
            i = ~(xp.isfinite(work.x) & xp.isfinite(work.df) | stop)
            work.df = xpx.at(work.df)[i].set(xp.nan)
            work.status = xpx.at(work.status)[i].set(eim._EVALUEERR)
            stop = xpx.at(stop)[i].set(True)
        i = (work.error > work.error_last * 10) & ~stop
        work.status = xpx.at(work.status)[i].set(_EERRORINCREASE)
        stop = xpx.at(stop)[i].set(True)
        return stop

    def post_termination_check(work):
        return

    def customize_result(res, shape):
        return shape
    return eim._loop(work, callback, shape, maxiter, func, args, dtype, pre_func_eval, post_func_eval, check_termination, post_termination_check, customize_result, res_work_pairs, xp, preserve_shape)

# --- helper: scipy.differentiate._differentiate._derivative_iv ---
def _derivative_iv(f, x, args, tolerances, maxiter, order, initial_step, step_factor, step_direction, preserve_shape, callback):
    xp = array_namespace(x)
    if not callable(f):
        raise ValueError('`f` must be callable.')
    if not np.iterable(args):
        args = (args,)
    tolerances = {} if tolerances is None else tolerances
    atol = tolerances.get('atol', None)
    rtol = tolerances.get('rtol', None)
    message = 'Tolerances and step parameters must be non-negative scalars.'
    tols = np.asarray([atol if atol is not None else 1, rtol if rtol is not None else 1, step_factor])
    if not np.issubdtype(tols.dtype, np.number) or np.any(tols < 0) or np.any(np.isnan(tols)) or (tols.shape != (3,)):
        raise ValueError(message)
    step_factor = float(tols[2])
    maxiter_int = int(maxiter)
    if maxiter != maxiter_int or maxiter <= 0:
        raise ValueError('`maxiter` must be a positive integer.')
    order_int = int(order)
    if order_int != order or order <= 0:
        raise ValueError('`order` must be a positive integer.')
    step_direction = xp.asarray(step_direction)
    initial_step = xp.asarray(initial_step)
    temp = xp.broadcast_arrays(x, step_direction, initial_step)
    x, step_direction, initial_step = temp
    message = '`preserve_shape` must be True or False.'
    if preserve_shape not in {True, False}:
        raise ValueError(message)
    if callback is not None and (not callable(callback)):
        raise ValueError('`callback` must be callable.')
    return (f, x, args, atol, rtol, maxiter_int, order_int, initial_step, step_factor, step_direction, preserve_shape, callback)

# --- helper: scipy.differentiate._differentiate._derivative_weights ---
def _derivative_weights(work, n, xp):
    fac = float(work.fac)
    diff_state = work.diff_state
    if fac != diff_state.fac:
        diff_state.central = []
        diff_state.right = []
        diff_state.fac = fac
    if len(diff_state.central) != 2 * n + 1:
        i = np.arange(-n, n + 1)
        p = np.abs(i) - 1.0
        s = np.sign(i)
        h = s / fac ** p
        A = np.vander(h, increasing=True).T
        b = np.zeros(2 * n + 1)
        b[1] = 1
        weights = np.linalg.solve(A, b)
        weights[n] = 0
        for i in range(n):
            weights[-i - 1] = -weights[i]
        diff_state.central = weights
        i = np.arange(2 * n + 1)
        p = i - 1.0
        s = np.sign(i)
        h = s / np.sqrt(fac) ** p
        A = np.vander(h, increasing=True).T
        b = np.zeros(2 * n + 1)
        b[1] = 1
        weights = np.linalg.solve(A, b)
        diff_state.right = weights
    return (xp.asarray(diff_state.central, dtype=work.dtype), xp.asarray(diff_state.right, dtype=work.dtype))

mechanism.text:
Implements a linear, shift‑invariant filter by convolving the input 1‑D signal with a precomputed kernel whose samples are proportional to cosh(a k)/cosh(b k). The implementation builds a reusable convolution operator (likely FFT/circulant-based) for the given signal length and kernel shape, caches it per thread to avoid recomputing, and applies it to the real and imaginary parts separately for complex inputs. If a physical period is supplied the a and b parameters are scaled into angular units first.

Underlying algorithm and computational approach
- The core operation is convolution: output = x * ω, where ω is the kernel sampled at integer lags k. Instead of forming ω and doing direct O(n^2) convolution, the code initializes an optimized convolution kernel object (convolve.init_convolution_kernel) that typically uses FFT or another fast convolution engine to perform the operation in near O(n log n) time. Caching avoids repeated kernel construction across repeated calls with the same (n,a,b). For complex inputs the filter is linear so the real/imag parts are filtered separately and recombined.

Domain knowledge required
- Basic signal processing: convolution, frequency response, and the meaning of sampling period vs. angular frequency. Understanding of circular (periodic) convolution vs. linear convolution and how FFT-based convolution assumes periodicity is important. Familiarity with numerical stability of functions like cosh for large arguments is useful.

Key constraints and assumptions
- Input is a uniformly sampled 1‑D array; irregular sampling invalidates the mathematical meaning. FFT/circulant convolution implies implicit periodic extension unless the convolution engine handles zero‑padding. Parameters a and b must be chosen to keep cosh(a k)/cosh(b k) numerically well‑behaved (large arguments produce huge values and division may under/overflow). Cache size is bounded (evicted when >20 entries). Thread-local caching semantics are relied upon.

When it’s appropriate to use
- When you need a fixed, linear, shift‑invariant filter whose kernel follows cosh(a k)/cosh(b k) and you will reuse the same (n,a,b) many times (benefits from caching and fast FFT convolution). Not appropriate for irregularly sampled data, nonlinear filtering, or when extreme parameter values cause numerical instability. Use the period argument when working with physical units so a and b express frequencies correctly.

mechanism.text:
Computes a numerically estimated Jacobian by finite-difference sampling of f at small coordinate perturbations and adaptively refining step sizes with error estimates. The routine builds a batched evaluator that perturbs each component of the input vector independently, evaluates f at symmetric (central) or one-sided offsets, and forms difference quotients. Multiple orders and a hierarchical sequence of step sizes (controlled by a reduction factor) produce Richardson-like extrapolation: successive refinements combine into improved derivative estimates and an error estimate used to decide convergence. The implementation is vectorized so many per-coordinate function evaluations are arranged in blocks and managed together for efficiency.

Understanding numerical differentiation and floating-point behavior is essential: truncation error shrinks with step size up to round-off noise, so an optimal step balances both. The method assumes f is sufficiently smooth (locally differentiable) and that function evaluations are deterministic and inexpensive enough that many calls (per component, per iteration) are feasible. Familiarity with central versus forward/backward differences, Richardson extrapolation, and stability/conditioning of the Jacobian problem helps interpret returned error/status flags.

Key constraints and assumptions:
- Input x must be at least 1-D and treated as a finite-dimensional vector; the code perturbs the first axis.
- f must accept the batched input layout produced by the wrapper and return consistent shaped outputs (no side effects).
- Relying on floating-point behavior: tolerances default to machine-scale values; extremely small or large scales can break accuracy.
- Cost scales roughly with m (dimension) times the number of probe points and iterations, so high-dimensional problems or very expensive f evaluations are costly.
- Non-smooth, noisy, or discontinuous functions produce unreliable derivative estimates and may trigger error flags.

Appropriate use cases:
- When analytic derivatives or automatic differentiation are unavailable or infeasible.
- Low-to-moderate dimensional problems where f is smooth and evaluable many times.
- Situations requiring a quick approximate Jacobian or diagnostic error estimates. Avoid for very high-dimensional, noisy, or discontinuous problems, or when exact/automatic gradients are available and affordable.

@xp_capabilities(skip_backends=[('array_api_strict', _array_api_strict_skip_reason), ('dask.array', _dask_reason)], jax_jit=False)
def jacobian(f, x, *, tolerances=None, maxiter=10, order=8, initial_step=0.5, step_factor=2.0, step_direction=0):
    xp = array_namespace(x)
    x0 = xp_promote(x, force_floating=True, xp=xp)
    if x0.ndim < 1:
        message = 'Argument `x` must be at least 1-D.'
        raise ValueError(message)
    m = x0.shape[0]
    i = xp.arange(m)

    def wrapped(x):
        p = () if x.ndim == x0.ndim else (x.shape[-1],)
        new_shape = (m, m) + x0.shape[1:] + p
        xph = xp.expand_dims(x0, axis=1)
        if x.ndim != x0.ndim:
            xph = xp.expand_dims(xph, axis=-1)
        xph = xp_copy(xp.broadcast_to(xph, new_shape), xp=xp)
        xph = xpx.at(xph)[i, i].set(x)
        return f(xph)
    res = derivative(wrapped, x, tolerances=tolerances, maxiter=maxiter, order=order, initial_step=initial_step, step_factor=step_factor, preserve_shape=True, step_direction=step_direction)
    del res.x
    return res

# --- helper: scipy.differentiate._differentiate.derivative ---
@xp_capabilities(skip_backends=[('array_api_strict', _array_api_strict_skip_reason), ('dask.array', _dask_reason)], jax_jit=False)
def derivative(f, x, *, args=(), tolerances=None, maxiter=10, order=8, initial_step=0.5, step_factor=2.0, step_direction=0, preserve_shape=False, callback=None):
    res = _derivative_iv(f, x, args, tolerances, maxiter, order, initial_step, step_factor, step_direction, preserve_shape, callback)
    func, x, args, atol, rtol, maxiter, order, h0, fac, hdir, preserve_shape, callback = res
    temp = eim._initialize(func, (x,), args, preserve_shape=preserve_shape)
    func, xs, fs, args, shape, dtype, xp = temp
    finfo = xp.finfo(dtype)
    atol = finfo.smallest_normal if atol is None else atol
    rtol = finfo.eps ** 0.5 if rtol is None else rtol
    x, f = (xs[0], fs[0])
    df = xp.full_like(f, xp.nan)
    hdir = xp.broadcast_to(hdir, shape)
    hdir = xp.reshape(hdir, (-1,))
    hdir = xp.astype(xp.sign(hdir), dtype)
    h0 = xp.broadcast_to(h0, shape)
    h0 = xp.reshape(h0, (-1,))
    h0 = xp.astype(h0, dtype)
    h0 = xpx.at(h0)[h0 <= 0].set(xp.nan)
    status = xp.full_like(x, eim._EINPROGRESS, dtype=xp.int32)
    nit, nfev = (0, 1)
    il = hdir < 0
    ic = hdir == 0
    ir = hdir > 0
    io = il | ir
    work = _RichResult(x=x, df=df, fs=f[:, xp.newaxis], error=xp.nan, h=h0, df_last=xp.nan, error_last=xp.nan, fac=fac, atol=atol, rtol=rtol, nit=nit, nfev=nfev, status=status, dtype=dtype, terms=(order + 1) // 2, hdir=hdir, il=il, ic=ic, ir=ir, io=io, diff_state=_RichResult(central=[], right=[], fac=None))
    res_work_pairs = [('status', 'status'), ('df', 'df'), ('error', 'error'), ('nit', 'nit'), ('nfev', 'nfev'), ('x', 'x')]

    def pre_func_eval(work):
        n = work.terms
        h = work.h[:, xp.newaxis]
        c = work.fac
        d = c ** 0.5
        if work.nit == 0:
            hc = h / c ** xp.arange(n, dtype=work.dtype)
            hc = xp.concat((-xp.flip(hc, axis=-1), hc), axis=-1)
        else:
            hc = xp.concat((-h, h), axis=-1) / c ** (n - 1)
        if work.nit == 0:
            hr = h / d ** xp.arange(2 * n, dtype=work.dtype)
        else:
            hr = xp.concat((h, h / d), axis=-1) / c ** (n - 1)
        n_new = 2 * n if work.nit == 0 else 2
        x_eval = xp.zeros((work.hdir.shape[0], n_new), dtype=work.dtype)
        il, ic, ir = (work.il, work.ic, work.ir)
        x_eval = xpx.at(x_eval)[ir].set(work.x[ir][:, xp.newaxis] + hr[ir])
        x_eval = xpx.at(x_eval)[ic].set(work.x[ic][:, xp.newaxis] + hc[ic])
        x_eval = xpx.at(x_eval)[il].set(work.x[il][:, xp.newaxis] - hr[il])
        return x_eval

    def post_func_eval(x, f, work):
        n = work.terms
        n_new = n if work.nit == 0 else 1
        il, ic, io = (work.il, work.ic, work.io)
        work_fc = (f[ic][:, :n_new], work.fs[ic], f[ic][:, -n_new:])
        work_fc = xp.concat(work_fc, axis=-1)
        if work.nit == 0:
            fc = work_fc
        else:
            fc = (work_fc[:, :n], work_fc[:, n:n + 1], work_fc[:, -n:])
            fc = xp.concat(fc, axis=-1)
        work_fo = xp.concat((work.fs[io], f[io]), axis=-1)
        if work.nit == 0:
            fo = work_fo
        else:
            fo = xp.concat((work_fo[:, 0:1], work_fo[:, -2 * n:]), axis=-1)
        work.fs = xp.zeros((ic.shape[0], work.fs.shape[-1] + 2 * n_new), dtype=work.dtype)
        work.fs = xpx.at(work.fs)[ic].set(work_fc)
        work.fs = xpx.at(work.fs)[io].set(work_fo)
        wc, wo = _derivative_weights(work, n, xp)
        work.df_last = xp.asarray(work.df, copy=True)
        work.df = xpx.at(work.df)[ic].set(fc @ wc / work.h[ic])
        work.df = xpx.at(work.df)[io].set(fo @ wo / work.h[io])
        work.df = xpx.at(work.df)[il].multiply(-1)
        work.h /= work.fac
        work.error_last = work.error
        work.error = xp.abs(work.df - work.df_last)

    def check_termination(work):
        stop = xp.astype(xp.zeros_like(work.df), xp.bool)
        i = work.error < work.atol + work.rtol * abs(work.df)
        work.status = xpx.at(work.status)[i].set(eim._ECONVERGED)
        stop = xpx.at(stop)[i].set(True)
        if work.nit > 0:
            i = ~(xp.isfinite(work.x) & xp.isfinite(work.df) | stop)
            work.df = xpx.at(work.df)[i].set(xp.nan)
            work.status = xpx.at(work.status)[i].set(eim._EVALUEERR)
            stop = xpx.at(stop)[i].set(True)
        i = (work.error > work.error_last * 10) & ~stop
        work.status = xpx.at(work.status)[i].set(_EERRORINCREASE)
        stop = xpx.at(stop)[i].set(True)
        return stop

    def post_termination_check(work):
        return

    def customize_result(res, shape):
        return shape
    return eim._loop(work, callback, shape, maxiter, func, args, dtype, pre_func_eval, post_func_eval, check_termination, post_termination_check, customize_result, res_work_pairs, xp, preserve_shape)

mechanism.text:
Computes a second derivative (Hessian) by applying numerical finite-difference differentiation twice: first building a Jacobian by perturbing each input coordinate, then differentiating that Jacobian to obtain the matrix of second partials. The implementation is essentially a nested finite-difference scheme that treats the Jacobian as a vector-valued function of the input and uses an adaptive multi-step finite-difference/step-refinement routine (varying step sizes, orders, and iteration limits) to reduce truncation error while monitoring round‑off limits from floating‑point precision.

Understanding and using this correctly requires basic numerical-analysis knowledge: how finite differences trade truncation error (too-large step) against roundoff error (too-small step), how higher-order difference formulas and step refinement (Richardson-like strategies) can reduce truncation error, and that differentiability (smoothness) of the underlying function is essential. Familiarity with machine epsilon and conditioning is important because the code enforces a minimum relative tolerance related to floating-point epsilon to avoid unreliable error estimates.

Key constraints and assumptions:
- The input must be at least 1-D and representable as floating-point; integer inputs are promoted to floats.
- The target function must be sufficiently smooth around the evaluation point; nonsmooth or noisy functions yield poor Hessian estimates.
- Computational cost grows quickly: forming the full Hessian via componentwise perturbations is O(n^2) function-evaluation work and memory for an n-dimensional input.
- Error control is heuristic and limited by machine precision; extremely small tolerances below an epsilon-derived threshold are warned and bumped.
- The routine relies on an array-backend abstraction for broadcasting and stacking, so backend compatibility matters.

Appropriate use cases: obtaining approximate Hessians when analytic derivatives are unavailable or too difficult to derive, for low-to-moderate dimensional problems (tens, not thousands), and for well-behaved smooth functions where moderate accuracy suffices. Avoid for high-dimensional models, highly noisy or nondifferentiable objectives, or when exact/automatic-differentiation Hessians are attainable and affordable.

@xp_capabilities(skip_backends=[('array_api_strict', _array_api_strict_skip_reason), ('dask.array', _dask_reason)], jax_jit=False)
def hessian(f, x, *, tolerances=None, maxiter=10, order=8, initial_step=0.5, step_factor=2.0):
    kwargs = dict(maxiter=maxiter, order=order, initial_step=initial_step, step_factor=step_factor)
    tolerances = {} if tolerances is None else tolerances
    atol = tolerances.get('atol', None)
    rtol = tolerances.get('rtol', None)
    xp = array_namespace(x)
    x0 = xp_promote(x, force_floating=True, xp=xp)
    finfo = xp.finfo(x0.dtype)
    rtol = finfo.eps ** 0.5 if rtol is None else rtol
    rtol_min = finfo.eps * 100
    message = f'The specified `rtol={rtol!r}`, but error estimates are likely to be unreliable when `rtol < {rtol_min}`.'
    if 0 < rtol < rtol_min:
        warnings.warn(message, RuntimeWarning, stacklevel=2)
        rtol = rtol_min

    def df(x):
        tolerances = dict(rtol=rtol / 100, atol=atol)
        temp = jacobian(f, x, tolerances=tolerances, **kwargs)
        nfev.append(temp.nfev if len(nfev) == 0 else temp.nfev.sum(axis=-1))
        return temp.df
    nfev = []
    res = jacobian(df, x, tolerances=tolerances, **kwargs)
    nfev = xp.cumulative_sum(xp.stack(nfev), axis=0)
    res_nit = xp.astype(res.nit[xp.newaxis, ...], xp.int64)
    res.nfev = xp.take_along_axis(nfev, res_nit, axis=0)[0]
    res.ddf = res.df
    del res.df
    del res.nit
    return res

    xp = array_namespace(x)

    if x0.ndim < 1:
        message = 'Argument `x` must be at least 1-D.'

    m = x0.shape[0]

    def wrapped(x):
        p = () if x.ndim == x0.ndim else (x.shape[-1],)
        new_shape = (m, m) + x0.shape[1:] + p
        xph = xp.expand_dims(x0, axis=1)
        if x.ndim != x0.ndim:
            xph = xp.expand_dims(xph, axis=-1)
        xph = xp_copy(xp.broadcast_to(xph, new_shape), xp=xp)
        xph = xpx.at(xph)[i, i].set(x)

mechanism.text:
A 1‑D discrete Hilbert transform is implemented by convolving the input sequence with the discrete kernel that corresponds to a ±90° phase shift in the frequency domain. Concretely, the routine builds (and caches) a discrete convolution kernel whose frequency response is sign(k): positive frequency bins get +1, negative bins −1, and the DC bin 0. Applying that kernel to a real sequence produces the Hilbert transform; for complex inputs the transform is applied separately to the real and imaginary parts and recombined. The heavy lifting is done by a convolution routine that likely uses FFT-based convolution to realize the frequency‑domain multiplication efficiently for arbitrary lengths.

Required domain knowledge: basic digital signal processing (Fourier duality, convolution vs. frequency multiplication), the definition of the Hilbert transform as a 90° phase shifter (or equivalently as multiplication by −j·sign(ω) in the continuous Fourier domain), and implications of discrete sampling (aliasing, Nyquist bin). Understanding analytic signals (x + j·H[x]) and why the DC and potentially the Nyquist component are handled explicitly is helpful.

Key constraints and assumptions:
- Input is a regularly sampled 1‑D sequence. Nonuniform sampling invalidates the frequency interpretation.
- The transform is defined for finite discrete sequences; implementation choices imply circular/convolution boundary behavior and possible edge artifacts unless padding is used externally.
- DC (k=0) is mapped to zero; for even-length signals the Nyquist bin is ambiguous and may be zeroed by this kernel, which is standard but important to know.
- The code caches kernels by length and uses thread‑local storage; cache eviction occurs when many sizes accumulate.

Appropriate use cases: creating analytic signals for instantaneous amplitude/phase estimation, envelope detection, quadrature demodulation, and any offline batch processing that needs a 90° phase shift. Not suitable for nonuniform or streaming real‑time causal filtering without additional buffering/padding and attention to edge effects.

The implementation hides the Fourier transforms behind convolution initialization and a convolve call, and takes care to zero the mean mode (k=0) so constants differentiate to zero.

Key constraints and assumptions: evenly spaced samples; input length determines discrete mode set; order should be a non‑negative integer; the k=0 mode is forced to zero; high derivative orders amplify noise and aliasing; nonperiodic discontinuities produce ringing. import numpy as np
import scipy.integrate

# Scalar-valued integrand on a 2D domain: f(x,y) = sin(x)*cos(y)
# Integrate over x in [0, pi], y in [0, pi/2]
def f(x):
    # x has shape (npoints, ndim)
    return np.sin(x[:, 0]) * np.cos(x[:, 1])

a = np.array([0.0, 0.0])
b = np.array([np.pi, np.pi / 2])

result = scipy.integrate.cubature(f, a, b)
print("estimate:", result)

import numpy as np
import scipy.integrate

# Vector-valued integrand returning two components per point:
# g0(x,y) = x^2, g1(x,y) = y^3 over the unit square [0,1]^2
# The exact integrals are [1/3, 1/4].
def f(x):
    # x shape: (npoints, ndim)
    x0 = x[:, 0]
    x1 = x[:, 1]
    # return shape (npoints, 2)
    return np.vstack((x0 ** 2, x1 ** 3)).T

a = np.array([0.0, 0.0])
b = np.array([1.0, 1.0])

result = scipy.integrate.cubature(f, a, b)
print("estimate (g0, g1):", result)

import numpy as np
import scipy.integrate

# Integrate a radially symmetric Gaussian over R^2: f(x,y) = exp(- (x^2 + y^2) )
# The integral over R^2 is pi.
def f(x):
    r2 = x[:, 0] ** 2 + x[:, 1] ** 2
    return np.exp(-r2)

# Use infinite limits for both dimensions
a = np.array([-np.inf, -np.inf])
b = np.array([np.inf, np.inf])

result = scipy.integrate.cubature(f, a, b, rtol=1e-6)
print("estimate:", result)

mechanism.text:
Adaptive cubature over a hyper-rectangular region approximates the vector-valued definite integral by repeatedly applying a fixed one-shot quadrature rule on subregions, estimating local error from paired rules, and refining the partition where error is largest until prescribed tolerances are met. The SciPy function exposes a generic adaptive integration abstraction: given a callable f(x) and arrays a, b defining the hypercube corners, it repeatedly evaluates f at the chosen rule nodes (possibly for multiple points at once because f may return arrays) and combines results to produce an overall integral estimate and an error bound.

Algorithmically, the core is an adaptive subdivision loop built around two kinds of base quadrature backends. One backend uses Gauss–Kronrod rules by forming tensor-product or product-based evaluations so that a high-order rule and a nested lower-order rule produce a difference-based error estimate (this is the Quadpack/Gauss–Kronrod idea). Another backend implements the Genz–Malik multidimensional rule family that uses a predefined node/weight pattern tailored for N-dimensional rectangular regions. In all cases the algorithm: (1) evaluates the high- and low-accuracy estimates on a subregion; (2) computes an error estimate from their difference (combined with absolute/relative tolerances and component-wise handling for array outputs); (3) selects the subregion with largest estimated error; and (4) bisects it (typically along the longest edge) and repeats. Work is prioritized by estimated contribution to the global error.

Key design decisions: use of paired rules (higher- and lower-order) gives cheap local error estimates without extra analytic derivatives; adaptive bisection concentrates effort where integrand structure (peaks, oscillation, singular behavior) causes larger errors; supporting array-valued f avoids repeated separate integrations; and exposing multiple backends lets users trade dimensional efficiency (Genz–Malik is designed for moderate N) versus simplicity and nesting properties (Gauss–Kronrod products are robust but scale poorly with dimension). Practical controls (absolute/relative tolerances, max evaluations) prevent runaway work.

When to use it: good for low-to-moderate dimensional integrals (say up to 4–6 dims) of reasonably smooth functions where deterministic error estimates are useful and vector-valued outputs are needed. Avoid for very high dimensions, discontinuous or strongly singular integrands, or when only statistical estimates are acceptable—in those cases Monte Carlo, quasi-Monte Carlo, or specialized singular-integration techniques are preferable. Convergence is not guaranteed for all integrands, and cost grows rapidly with dimension because tensor-product node counts or multidimensional rule complexity explode.
references: Quadpack: A Subroutine Package for Automatic Integration (files: dqk21.f, dqk15.f)
Remarks on algorithm 006: An adaptive algorithm for numerical integration over an N-dimensional rectangular region (A. C. Genz, A. A. Malik, Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics, 1980)
