mechanism.text:
It ensures that identical write targets shared across multiple save plans are performed only once, assigning each distinct write item (identified by an index) to exactly one plan and removing it from the others. The assignment is done greedily: for each distinct write item it picks a single plan to host the write either by (a) choosing the lowest-ranked plan index (if save_to_lowest_rank is true) or (b) choosing the plan with the currently smallest accumulated assigned size (a simple online load-balancing heuristic). The chosen plan’s accumulated size is incremented by the write item’s storage size (falling back to 1 if unknown), and other plans that referenced that write item have it removed. The function then produces new plan objects whose item lists contain only the write items kept for that plan.

Domain knowledge
- This is intended for systems that create multiple overlapping "save plans" (for example, distributed checkpoints, replicated serialization lists, or per-shard save schedules) where several plans may reference the same logical data item.  
- Understanding that write items are identified by stable, canonical indices and that their storage size is a meaningful proxy for I/O/work is important for correct balancing.

Key constraints and assumptions
- Items are considered identical when their index matches; no deeper equality checks are done.  
- Size estimates (tensor_storage_size) may be missing; the code uses 1 as a default, which affects balance quality.  
- It is a greedy, deterministic assignment (ties broken by min or by current load); it is not globally optimal and can produce suboptimal load balance in adversarial inputs.  
- No concurrency control; caller must manage thread/process safety if plans are shared.

When appropriate to use
- When you need to eliminate duplicate writes across several planned write lists to avoid duplicated I/O or work, and a simple, fast heuristic assignment is sufficient.  
- When deterministic, reproducible choices (lowest index or greedily smallest load) are required and when items have reasonably accurate size estimates. Avoid if you need provably optimal balancing or if items cannot be uniquely identified by a stable index.

mechanism.text:
Orchestrates planning for saving a PyTorch state dictionary across processes: a DefaultSavePlanner instance holds the prepared state_dict (optionally flattened), per-key planner mappings, caching keys/state for plan deduplication, and flags that control flattening and plan caching behavior. It is neither the actual writer nor the coordinator; instead it builds local SavePlan objects, merges them into a global plan, validates and optionally deduplicates overlapping tensor chunks, and resolves individual write items back into serialisable objects for the writer.

Lifecycle: constructed with configuration flags that influence how input state is transformed and whether plan caching is active. set_up_planner prepares internal state (flattening the dictionary and sharded tensors as needed) and marks whether this instance is running on a coordinator process. create_local_plan synthesises a local SavePlan for the current process; create_global_plan consumes all local plans and returns either a full global plan or a delta when caching is enabled. finish_plan selects the effective plan for execution and resolve_data/lookup_object/transform_object are used during the actual write to map plan entries to serialisable payloads. The planner does not hold external resources (files, sockets) and therefore does not require explicit disposal; its lifetime is tied to the higher-level checkpoint operation that uses it.

Invariants and role: the planner ensures its internal state_dict and planner mappings remain consistent (flattening and mapping metadata are kept together so index hints remain valid), and that global plans validate against metadata (no out-of-bounds or overlapping chunks, chunk volumes matching tensor volumes). When caching is enabled it preserves previously computed local/global plans and produces deltas to avoid unnecessary work. Architecturally, it is the policy/coordination layer between raw model state and the concrete write stage: responsible for decomposition of tensors into write items, deduplication across ranks, assembling global write plans, and providing the lookup/serialization hooks required by the writer.

mechanism.text:
Pauses all distributed processes at a synchronization point while opening an interactive debugger on one designated rank, letting that rank inspect and step through code while peers wait. Conceptually it implements a coordinated breakpoint for multi-process PyTorch: one process enters an interactive pdb session (with stdin redirected to the controlling terminal), and all processes synchronize on a distributed barrier so they stop at the same program point until the debugger session completes and the barrier is released.

Mechanisms: it updates per-process process-group timeouts (via internal torch.distributed APIs) so the distributed barrier won’t time out prematurely, temporarily disables the Torch dispatch path that routes meta/override behavior (to avoid side effects during the breakpoint), and uses a pdb subclass that rebinds sys.stdin to /dev/stdin to ensure interactive input works in typical Unix-run worker processes. A small skip counter mechanism hashes the current traceback text to avoid repeatedly stopping on the same call-site across repeated exceptions/calls.

Domain knowledge required: familiarity with PyTorch’s distributed concepts (ranks, process groups, barriers), how multi-process training synchronizes, and the implications of interacting with one process while others are suspended. Understanding of Python pdb, stdin handling in worker processes (terminals vs redirected IO), and private/internal torch APIs (meta-dispatch and c10d internals) helps interpret the side-effecting calls.

Key constraints and assumptions: torch.distributed must be initialized; /dev/stdin must be accessible (Unix assumption); use of private/internal APIs may change across PyTorch versions; the skip logic is local and relies on traceback text hashing; only one rank receives an interactive prompt while others block—so long-running UI or mistakes can stall the whole job. Use this when debugging distributed behavior at a deterministic synchronization point and you need an interactive inspection on one worker while keeping others paused. Avoid in production or where automated job schedulers will kill stalled processes.

Conforming types expose a small staging interface: a stage_data(state_dict) method that returns a training-safe snapshot for parallel serialization, a synchronize_staging() method to complete any outstanding transfers, and a should_synchronize_after_execute boolean indicating whether the saver should wait immediately. Typical concrete implementations include CPU-memory stagers that copy tensors to host RAM, pinned-memory or CUDA-to-CPU transferers, and async uploaders/queues that stream staged data to disk or remote object storage.

mechanism.text:
Starts a central debug coordinator on rank 0 and registers per-worker endpoints so a lightweight networked debugger can collect periodic dumps (stacks, trace fragments) and route debug requests to worker-local servers. Conceptually the routine sets up two cooperating components: a small HTTP/TCP worker server on every process and a single separate process on the chief (rank 0) that acts as the debug frontend. Each worker publishes its reachable address into a shared TCP-backed key-value store so the frontend can discover and contact workers across hosts.

Algorithmically the approach is straightforward: create a worker listener (ephemeral port), write its address to a distributed store under a rank-specific key, and — only on rank 0 — spawn a separate OS-level process to run the debug frontend. Spawning uses Python’s multiprocessing contexts optionally chosen (fork, spawn, forkserver) to control how the subprocess is created and how the interpreter state is replicated. The frontend process is daemonized so it won’t block program exit.

Domain knowledge required: distributed PyTorch concepts (process ranks, rendezvous/tcpstore), basic networking (hostnames and reachable ports), and Python multiprocessing semantics (differences and safety of fork vs spawn, especially on macOS/Windows). Also useful is an understanding of debug data—what “dumps” are, file permissions and storage layout for dump_dir, and how handlers process incoming debug requests.

Key constraints and assumptions: only one debug frontend can be started (global guard), rank 0 is assumed to be the coordinator, worker addresses must be addressable from the frontend, and multiprocessing start method affects safety and available resources. The frontend runs as a separate process (daemon), so lifetime and cleanup are tied to the parent process. Not intended for high-security or high-throughput production telemetry; suited for interactive debugging of distributed workloads where collecting occasional dumps and routing inspector traffic are required.

import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.distributed.checkpoint import state_dict

# Simple model and single optimizer example
model = nn.Linear(10, 1)
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)

# Do one forward/backward/step to initialize optimizer state
x = torch.randn(4, 10)
target = torch.randn(4, 1)
loss = nn.functional.mse_loss(model(x), target)
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()
optimizer.zero_grad()

# Obtain optimizer state dict (the type accepted by set_optimizer_state_dict)
optim_state = state_dict.get_optimizer_state_dict(model, optimizer)

# Create a fresh optimizer instance and load the saved state into it
new_optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)
# set_optimizer_state_dict must be called either before backward() or after step()
state_dict.set_optimizer_state_dict(model, new_optimizer, optim_state)

# new_optimizer now has the same state as optimizer
print('Loaded optimizer state size:', len(new_optimizer.state))

import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.distributed.checkpoint import state_dict

# Model with two submodules and two optimizers operating on disjoint parameter sets
class TwoLayerModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.a = nn.Linear(8, 4)
        self.b = nn.Linear(4, 1)
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.b(torch.relu(self.a(x)))

model = TwoLayerModel()
opt_a = torch.optim.Adam(model.a.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
opt_b = torch.optim.Adam(model.b.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

# Run one training step to populate optimizer states
x = torch.randn(2, 8)
target = torch.randn(2, 1)
loss = nn.functional.mse_loss(model(x), target)
loss.backward()
opt_a.step()
opt_b.step()
opt_a.zero_grad()
opt_b.zero_grad()

# Get optimizer state for both optimizers
optim_state = state_dict.get_optimizer_state_dict(model, [opt_a, opt_b])

# Create fresh optimizers and load the saved state
new_opt_a = torch.optim.Adam(model.a.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
new_opt_b = torch.optim.Adam(model.b.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
state_dict.set_optimizer_state_dict(model, [new_opt_a, new_opt_b], optim_state)

print('opt a state entries:', len(new_opt_a.state))
print('opt b state entries:', len(new_opt_b.state))

mechanism.text:
Loads optimizer state into one or more PyTorch optimizers while reconciling sharded/full checkpoints, FSDP-wrapped parameters, device placement, and possible CPU offload or broadcast semantics. The code first gathers and validates mapping between model parameter FQNs (fully-qualified names) and actual tensors, then prepares a context (disabling GC briefly for memory pressure) and conditional FSDP state translation. For FSDP sharded checkpoints it rewrites optimizer parameter keys to match compiler-added prefixes, optionally calls FSDP utility to convert a saved optimizer state into the per-rank form to load, and otherwise builds a local “target” optimizer state by either unflattening a saved dictionary or merging a full state with local parameter mappings. When a full-state checkpoint is available, it flattens both saved and local optimizer states, moves tensor shards to a common device (and optionally broadcasts from rank 0), distributes or broadcasts entries so each rank gets the pieces it needs, then unflattens back into the optimizer’s expected nested dict before calling the optimizer’s load_state_dict.

Domain knowledge required: familiarity with PyTorch optimizer internals (state dict layout with "state" and "param_groups"), distributed training concepts (model sharding, FullyShardedDataParallel/FSDP), how parameter FQNs map across compiler/graph transformations, and device semantics (CPU/GPU tensors and offload). Understanding rank-based checkpointing and flattening/unflattening of nested state dicts is important.

Key constraints and assumptions: model parameter FQNs must be mappable and stable; shared parameters and compiler-added prefixes are handled but expect predictable one-to-one mappings; full-state merging assumes consistent tensor devices per rank; FSDP modules must expose the expected fsdp_state. The code errors if required state is missing or inconsistent (e.g., empty optimizer state when one is required, device mismatches).

Use this when restoring optimizer state in distributed/sharded training scenarios where checkpoints may be full or sharded, especially with FSDP or CPU-offload options — i.e., whenever saved optimizer state must be reconciled with local parameter layouts across ranks before loading into torch.optim.

mechanism.text:
Acts as the transport/coordinator for exchanging serialized model checkpoints between ranks over a torch.distributed ProcessGroup. An instance encapsulates the communication logic and low-level invariants needed to take a Python state dict (with tensors, DTensor, and ShardedTensor leaves), turn it into a sequence of raw byte tensors plus a small metadata blob, and reliably deliver and rehydrate that state on a remote rank.

Construction binds together three resources: a ProcessGroup used to perform sends/receives, a target device where raw byte buffers live during transfer, and an optional local state_dict factory used to allow in-place receives. After construction you call send_checkpoint to push a prepared state to one or more destination ranks, or recv_checkpoint to pull and rebuild a state from a source rank. Calls are synchronous at the API level: send_checkpoint and recv_checkpoint issue non-blocking sends/receives as Work objects and then wait as needed to ensure correct ordering and memory safety. There is no separate close/dispose API — the underlying ProcessGroup lifecycle governs resource cleanup.

Key invariants and responsibilities:
- Message ordering and tags: a metadata length (tag=1), metadata bytes (tag=2), then tensor payloads (tag>=3) are sent in a defined sequence to allow a receiver to allocate buffers correctly.
- Byte-level fidelity: tensors are transmitted as uint8 byte-storage; receivers reconstruct tensors via recorded shape, dtype, stride, storage_offset and must preserve storage nbytes. If an in-place tensor exists, its storage size must match the incoming data.
- Special handling for DTensor and ShardedTensor leaves: local pieces are sent/received, with sharded metadata updated to reflect local placement on the receiving rank.
- Zero-copy and device placement: where possible the code reuses existing storage (casting with _cast_tensor) or performs transfers on the configured device to minimize extra copies.

Role in the library: a focused transport abstraction that isolates checkpoint serialization, device-aware buffer management, and ProcessGroup communication patterns so higher-level checkpoint logic can rely on robust, ordered, and size-consistent transfers across distributed ranks.

Stops the running debug server and terminates its associated frontend debug server process, releasing network ports and related resources. On success it typically completes without returning a value (void) in synchronous APIs or resolves a completion/promise in asynchronous APIs; errors are reported by thrown exceptions or rejected promises. Call it when a debugging session ends — before application exit, when restarting the server, or to ensure no orphaned debug process continues using resources.

def stop_debug_server() -> None:
    global _WORKER_SERVER, _DEBUG_SERVER_PROC
    assert _DEBUG_SERVER_PROC is not None
    assert _WORKER_SERVER is not None
    logger.info('Stopping debug server')
    _DEBUG_SERVER_PROC.terminate()
    _WORKER_SERVER.shutdown()
    _DEBUG_SERVER_PROC.join()
    _WORKER_SERVER = None
    _DEBUG_SERVER_PROC = None

mechanism.text:
Maps a torch device type (for example 'cpu', 'cuda', 'xpu', or 'mps') to a canonical distributed backend name and enforces that a mapping exists. The lookup algorithm is simple and deterministic: normalize the input to a torch.device.type string, consult a dictionary (default_device_backend_map) to find the backend name, and raise an error if no mapping is registered. Complementary registration logic lets callers add new backend names and associate them with devices and capabilities; registration appends the backend to lists, sets up a plugin entry (creator function and API flag), records capability/device support, and marks the backend type as CUSTOM.

Required domain knowledge
- Familiarity with PyTorch distributed concepts: backends (NCCL, GLOO, MPI, etc.), ProcessGroup types, and that some backends are device-specific (e.g., NCCL for GPU).
- Understanding of torch.device and its .type attribute vs. string device specifications.
- Awareness that some device availability checks (e.g., torch.xpu.is_available()) affect default assumptions when registering backends.

Key constraints and assumptions
- Device keys are the normalized device.type strings; passing nonstandard device strings will be normalized via torch.device(...) but may still fail if type isn't recognized.
- The mapping must exist at call time; otherwise a ValueError is raised — no fallback or discovery is attempted.
- Registration mutates global class-level state (backend_list, default_device_backend_map, backend_capability, backend_type_map, _plugins); these updates are not synchronized and can conflict in concurrent contexts.
- If devices are omitted during registration, a heuristic capability list is assigned and a warning is emitted; this assumes common device availability patterns.
- Backend names are normalized to lowercase for storage, and Backend.__new__ maps unknown names to their lowercase value.

When appropriate to use
- Use this lookup to decide which distributed backend to instantiate when you know the device type but want the library’s configured default backend choice.
- Use the registration machinery when integrating a new custom backend plugin and you need to declare which devices it supports and provide a creator function.

mechanism.text:
Returns a process-local device index by first consulting the LOCAL_RANK environment variable and using an optional fallback value if that variable is absent; if neither is available it raises an error. Conceptually the routine implements a simple precedence rule: environment-specified local rank takes priority, otherwise a caller-supplied fallback is used, otherwise fail fast.

Algorithmically it is trivial: look up a well-known environment key, parse its string value as an integer, and return it; if the key is missing, convert and return the provided fallback; if neither exists, raise a RuntimeError. There is no iteration, I/O, or communication with other processes — it is purely local and deterministic.

Domain knowledge required: familiarity with distributed execution models (multi-process, multi-node GPU/accelerator training). “Local rank” commonly means the index of a process among the processes running on the same physical node (e.g., which GPU to bind to). Many job launchers (torchrun, torch.distributed.launch, SLURM, etc.) set LOCAL_RANK so that libraries and user code can pick the correct device. Understanding the difference between local rank, global/world rank, and device IDs is important.

Key constraints and assumptions:
- Assumes LOCAL_RANK, if present, is a string representing an integer; invalid strings will raise a ValueError on int conversion.
- Assumes that an environment variable is the authoritative source of local rank in multi-process runs.
- The fallback is intended only for non-distributed or single-process local runs; using it in true multi-device contexts can produce incorrect device assignment.
- No validation against available devices is performed; returned index might be out of range for the hardware.

Appropriate use cases: small scripts or training loops that need a quick way to determine which device a process should use when run under common distributed launchers, or for local debugging when you can supply a safe fallback. Avoid relying on it where dynamic discovery or inter-process coordination is required.

mechanism.text:
Serializes Python objects to raw bytes, packs those bytes into a contiguous uint8 tensor on the chosen device, broadcasts the per-object sizes first, then broadcasts a single concatenated byte tensor from the source to all group members, and finally reconstructs the original objects on receivers by slicing and unpickling the received bytes. The two-stage protocol (sizes then payload) ensures each receiver can allocate the exact buffer and correctly demarcate objects in the concatenated stream without extra round trips.

Conceptually this is a general-purpose object-distribution primitive built on top of collective broadcast. It reduces many small broadcasts into two collective calls (one for sizes, one for payload) by concatenating per-object byte tensors at the root. The implementation leverages pickling for arbitrary Python objects, torch ByteTensors/LongTensors for transport, and the ProcessGroup broadcast operation which may use different backends (Gloo, NCCL, etc.) depending on device and configuration.

Important domain knowledge: distributed-process groups and rank canonicalization (local group ranks vs global ranks), device placement (CPU vs GPU backends), pickling semantics and security, and collective synchronization semantics (broadcast is a coordinated, usually blocking, collective unless async is used). Backend-specific behaviors (e.g., NCCL requiring GPU tensors and sometimes exposing different debugging/hash behavior) matter for performance and correctness.

Key constraints and assumptions: only group members participate; the root must serialize and produce the concatenated tensor; receivers must trust and unpickle incoming bytes (security risk if data is untrusted); object sizes must fit memory on target device; all ranks must agree on ordering and number of objects; non-root ranks allocate buffers based on the broadcast sizes. The implementation is optimized for sending moderate-sized arbitrary objects, not for high-throughput transfer of large binary blobs—large payloads on GPU may be better handled with dedicated tensor collectives.

Appropriate usage: distributing Python metadata, small models/configurations, or arbitrary picklable objects to all processes in a group when a simple broadcast semantics is required. Avoid for untrusted data, extremely large objects, or where zero-copy, high-performance tensor streaming is needed.

mechanism.text:
Implements a serialized-object scatter across a distributed process group by converting Python objects to byte tensors on the source, equalizing buffer sizes, broadcasting that size, scattering bytes, and reconstructing the object on each receiver.

Conceptually, the algorithm reduces the arbitrary-memory problem of Python objects to a fixed-size numeric communication primitive. The source rank pickles each object to bytes, packs those bytes into torch.ByteTensors and records their lengths. All objects are padded to the same maximum length (so a single contiguous tensor size can be scattered), and that maximum length is broadcast to every rank. The byte buffers are then scattered (one chunk per destination) and each destination uses the accompanying original-size metadata (also scattered) to slice the received byte array and unpickle the object. Communication operations rely on the ProcessGroup implementation (backend-specific collective primitives), so actual data movement is performed by the group.scatter and broadcast primitives.

Domain knowledge needed: basic distributed programming concepts (ranks, process groups, source/root semantics), PyTorch collective operations and device semantics (CPU vs CUDA tensors), and Python object serialization (pickle). Awareness of backend differences (e.g., NCCL limitations and device support) is important because object scatter uses byte tensors and may require CPU buffers depending on group/device support.

Key constraints and assumptions: the source must supply a list of objects; all processes must participate in the collective, even if non-source ranks provide only an output placeholder; objects are serialized with pickle (so picklability and security considerations apply); buffers are padded to a common max size, which can increase memory use and communication cost; device chosen for object buffers depends on the ProcessGroup device support; nonparticipating ranks outside the group are warned and return without action.

Appropriate usage: when you need to distribute arbitrary Python objects (not raw tensors) from one rank to many in a PyTorch-distributed job and are willing to pay the cost of pickling, padding, and byte-level communication. Not suitable for very large objects, latency-sensitive paths, or unpicklable objects—use tensor-based collectives instead for numeric data.

mechanism.text:
Reads an environment variable that names a UNIX-domain socket and, if set, constructs a short-lived worker server object bound to that socket for the duration of a with-block, guaranteeing shutdown when the block exits. Conceptually this is a lightweight resource-management wrapper: an outer contextmanager uses an ExitStack to conditionally enter an inner contextmanager that constructs a C++-backed _WorkerServer; control is yielded to the caller while the server runs, and the finally clause calls server.shutdown() to tear it down deterministically.

Algorithmically this is simple RAII-style lifecycle management implemented in Python: check configuration (env var), instantiate the server only when needed, and ensure cleanup even if the caller raises. The use of ExitStack lets additional conditional context managers be composed easily without nested try/finally clutter. The @contextmanager decorator turns a generator into a context manager; @record (presumably a tracing/telemetry decorator) records invocation metadata but does not change the resource semantics.

Domain knowledge: familiarity with distributed training orchestration (PyTorch Elastic), inter-process control-plane mechanics, and UNIX-domain sockets is required. Users should understand that a local control server coordinates worker processes (e.g., heartbeats, state transitions) rather than performing tensor computation. The server implementation lives in a C++ extension (_distributed_c10d._WorkerServer), so its behavior, performance, and failure modes follow that native component.

Key constraints and assumptions: the server is only started when the environment variable TORCH_WORKER_SERVER_SOCKET is defined and points to a valid socket path; shutdown is performed synchronously in the finally block; no automatic retry or error propagation beyond normal exception flow is provided. The code assumes the C++ server constructor succeeds and that server.shutdown() is sufficient to release resources. It is intended for process-local control-plane usage and not for general-purpose network services.

Appropriate uses: temporarily providing a worker control-plane endpoint inside worker processes during orchestration phases (tests, per-worker setup/teardown, or elastic job lifecycles) where deterministic startup/shutdown and minimal boilerplate are desired. Avoid using it as a long-running production daemon manager or when more sophisticated failure handling is required.

mechanism.text:
Determines whether to launch worker processes as OS-managed subprocesses or as Python multiprocessing children, constructs a corresponding process context, starts all workers, and guarantees cleanup if startup fails. The core algorithm is simple: validate that per-rank argument and environment dictionaries form a complete rank set, choose between two runtime strategies based on the type of entrypoint (string → external subprocess, callable → Python multiprocessing), instantiate the appropriate context object capturing logging, NUMA and duplication/filtering behavior, call its start method, and on any exception call close to release resources and re-raise.

Understanding when and how to use this requires domain knowledge of process lifecycles and multiprocessing semantics. You should know the difference between spawning independent OS processes that execute an external binary (subprocess model) versus launching Python interpreter children that import and call a provided callable (multiprocess model). Platform-specific start methods (e.g., fork vs spawn on Unix) affect memory sharing, pickling requirements, and safety with threads or CUDA contexts. NUMA placement influences memory/CPU affinity for high-performance workloads. Logging capture, duplication, and line-prefixing are important for multi-rank diagnostics.

Key constraints and assumptions: the args/envs mappings must form a contiguous, full rank set (typically 0..n-1); callable entrypoints must be picklable if multiprocessing spawn/forkserver is used; external entrypoints require executables accessible in the launched environment; logging and duplication filters assume line-oriented stdout/stderr. The implementation assumes context.start will perform all heavy lifting (process creation, piping, affinities) and that context.close safely undoes partially completed startup. Resource limits, kernel process table, and file-descriptor usage are external constraints.

Appropriate uses include launching multi-rank parallel jobs (distributed training, parameter-server setups, or multi-process workers) where per-rank environments/arguments and coordinated startup are required. Avoid it for lightweight threading tasks or when in-process execution is sufficient.

    nprocs = len(args)
    _validate_full_rank(args, nprocs, 'args')
    _validate_full_rank(envs, nprocs, 'envs')
    context: PContext
    if isinstance(entrypoint, str):
        context = SubprocessContext(name=name, entrypoint=entrypoint, args=args, envs=envs, duplicate_stdout_filters=duplicate_stdout_filters, duplicate_stderr_filters=duplicate_stderr_filters, logs_specs=logs_specs, log_line_prefixes=log_line_prefixes, numa_options=numa_options)
    else:
        context = MultiprocessContext(name=name, entrypoint=entrypoint, args=args, envs=envs, duplicate_stdout_filters=duplicate_stdout_filters, duplicate_stderr_filters=duplicate_stderr_filters, log_line_prefixes=log_line_prefixes, start_method=start_method, logs_specs=logs_specs, numa_options=numa_options)
    try:
        context.start()
        return context
    except Exception:
        context.close()
        raise

mechanism.text:
Each participant writes its payload into a shared key-value store and then reads everyone else’s entries; a lightweight barrier mechanism ensures everyone has finished writing before the caller proceeds. Conceptually this is a rendezvous pattern built on a distributed store: deterministic keys (prefix+rank) are used so each actor can publish and later retrieve a fixed array of values. A nonblocking barrier key is created and one rank (rank 0) waits for that key to indicate completion, which serializes the final “all-set” synchronization point.

Understanding and using this correctly requires distributed-systems intuition: how a consensus-like store (etcd, Redis, GCS-backed file store, etc.) behaves under partial failure, network partitions, and client timeouts. You must know that the store provides basic primitives—set, multi_get, and a wait mechanism—and what guarantees they provide (atomicity, eventual consistency, visibility delays). Familiarity with common distributed-training rendezvous semantics (per-rank publishing of metadata, deterministic key naming, and barriers) is also necessary.

Key constraints and assumptions: all ranks must invoke the rendezvous; world_size is accurate and stable; keys are unique and deterministic; stored payloads are small enough for the store’s value-size limits; the store’s timeout semantics are respected (the context manager temporarily changes store timeout). The approach assumes no node permanently fails mid-protocol—a crashed participant can cause wait/timeout or deadlock—and that multi_get returns values in index order (possibly with Nones for missing entries).

Appropriate uses are small-scale metadata or configuration exchange and rendezvous for initializing distributed jobs (sharing seeds, port numbers, small state). It is not suited for bulk tensor exchange, low-latency frequent synchronization, or scenarios requiring strong fault-tolerance and automatic recovery; for those, use higher-bandwidth collective communication (NCCL/P2P) or a dedicated coordination service with explicit failure handling.

def synchronize(store, data: bytes, rank: int, world_size: int, key_prefix: str, timeout: float=300) -> list[bytes]:
    with store_timeout(store, timeout):
        store.set(f'{key_prefix}{rank}', data)
        agent_data = get_all(store, rank, key_prefix, world_size)
        return agent_data

# --- helper: torch.distributed.elastic.utils.store.get_all ---
def get_all(store, rank: int, prefix: str, world_size: int):
    data_arr = store.multi_get([f'{prefix}{idx}' for idx in range(world_size)])
    barrier_key = _barrier_nonblocking(store=store, world_size=world_size, key_prefix=f'{prefix}/finished')
    if rank == 0:
        store.wait([barrier_key])
    return data_arr

# --- helper: torch.distributed.elastic.utils.store.store_timeout ---
@contextmanager
def store_timeout(store, timeout: float):
    old_timeout = store.timeout
    store.set_timeout(timedelta(seconds=timeout))
    yield
    store.set_timeout(old_timeout)

class JobConfig:

    def __init__(self: 'JobConfig'):
        self.parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description='PyTorch Flight recorder analyzing script.')
        self.parser.add_argument('trace_dir', nargs='?', help='Directory containing one trace file per rank, named with <prefix>_<rank>.')
        self.parser.add_argument('--selected-ranks', default=None, nargs='+', type=int, help='List of ranks we want to show traces for.')
        self.parser.add_argument('--allow-incomplete-ranks', action='store_true', help='FR trace require all ranks to have dumps for analysis. This flag allows best-effort partial analysis of results and printing of collected data.')
        self.parser.add_argument('--pg-filters', default=None, nargs='+', type=str, help='List of filter strings, it could be pg name or pg desc. If specified, only show traces for the given pg.')
        self.parser.add_argument('-o', '--output', default=None)
        self.parser.add_argument('-p', '--prefix', help='Common filename prefix to strip such that rank can be extracted. If not specified, will attempt to infer a common prefix.', default=None)
        self.parser.add_argument('-j', '--just_print_entries', action='store_true')
        self.parser.add_argument('-v', '--verbose', action='store_true')
        self.parser.add_argument('--print_stack_trace', action='store_true')
        self.parser.add_argument('--mismatch_cap', type=int, default=10, help='Maximum number of mismatches we print (from earliest).')

mechanism.text:
All processes coordinate via a shared key/value store to implement a barrier: each process atomically increments a “member count” key and the last arriving process writes a sentinel key that everyone waits on. The core idea is a non‑blocking rendezvous (atomic add returns an index); when the returned index equals the declared world size, that process sets the “last member” key. Others block on that last-member key until it appears or a timeout triggers. On timeout, an optional tracing protocol attempts to discover which ranks never checked in by having ranks write per-rank trace keys and a designated rank (0) scan for missing trace keys and publish a gating key so waiters can collect diagnostic info instead of only receiving a generic timeout.

Domain knowledge required:
- Basics of distributed process synchronization and barriers.
- Familiarity with consistency/atomicity semantics of a shared store: atomic increment (add), set, and wait primitives with timeout behavior.
- Understanding of rank/world_size conventions in distributed training (rank IDs, one leader role often chosen).
- Awareness that different backends (file, Redis, etc.) have different performance/consistency tradeoffs.

Key constraints and assumptions:
- The store must provide atomic add and reliable wait semantics; add must return a consistent count.
- world_size must be known and stable for the barrier lifetime; ranks are expected to be in a known range (code treats rank 0 specially).
- Unique key_prefix usage is required to avoid interference between independent barriers.
- Timeouts are used to bound blocking; store.set_timeout is temporarily changed inside the context.
- Tracing assumes a small limit on reported missing ranks and that the designated tracer (rank 0) can perform scans.

When to use it:
- When processes that cannot use native GPU/NCCL barriers (heterogeneous backends, multi‑node with a central coordinator, or elastic startups) need a portable barrier implemented on a rendezvous store.
- When you want built‑in diagnostics for stalled participants (the trace mechanism).
Not appropriate for ultra-low-latency tight GPU collectives; choose native collectives there.

mechanism.text: Track the processing state and error information for a single entry during analysis. Instances encapsulate the entry's current status (e.g., pending, in-progress, failed, succeeded), accumulated error details, and metadata needed for consistent logging. Typical use: instantiate per entry at analysis start, update status and append error/context as checks run, and then read or emit the standardized log/report when the entry completes or fails.

class EntryState:

    def __init__(self, entry: dict[str, Any], expected_ranks: set[int]) -> None:
        self.pg_name = entry['process_group'][0]
        self.desc = entry['process_group'][1]
        self.pg_desc = f'{self.pg_name}:{self.desc}' if self.desc != 'undefined' else self.pg_name
        self.profiling_name = entry['profiling_name']
        self.collective_seq_id = entry['collective_seq_id']
        self.p2p_seq_id = entry['p2p_seq_id']
        self.record_id = entry['record_id']
        self.input_sizes = entry['input_sizes']
        self.output_sizes = entry['output_sizes']
        self.collective_state = entry['state']
        self.collective_frames = entry.get('frames', [])
        self.expected_ranks = expected_ranks
        self.missing_ranks: set[int]
        self.input_numel: int
        self.output_numel: int
        self.errors: set[tuple[int, MatchInfo]]

    def log(self, logger: FlightRecorderLogger, logger_msg: str, frame_formatter: Any, total_numel: tuple[int, int] | None=None, errors: set[tuple[int, MatchInfo]] | None=None, missing_ranks: set[int] | None=None) -> None:
        logger.info(logger_msg, self.collective_seq_id)
        logger.info('internal record id: %s', self.record_id)
        logger.info('group info: %s', self.pg_desc)
        logger.info('collective: %s', self.profiling_name)
        if missing_ranks:
            self.missing_ranks = missing_ranks
            logger.info('missing ranks: %s', missing_ranks)
        if total_numel:
            self.input_numel = total_numel[0]
            self.output_numel = total_numel[1]
            logger.info('total input numel: %d', total_numel[0])
            logger.info('total output numel: %d', total_numel[1])
        logger.info('input sizes: %s', self.input_sizes)
        logger.info('output sizes: %s', self.output_sizes)
        logger.info('world size: %d', len(self.expected_ranks))
        logger.info('expected ranks: %s', str(self.expected_ranks))
        logger.info('collective state: %s', self.collective_state)
        if errors:
            self.errors = errors
            error_msg = ', '.join((f'Culprit rank {error[0]}; {str(error[1])}' for error in errors))
            logger.info('error msg: %s', error_msg)
        logger.info('collective stack trace: \n %s', frame_formatter(self.collective_frames))

    def to_collective(self, id: int, errors: set[tuple[int, MatchInfo]] | None=None, idx_map: dict[int, int] | None=None, all_entries: dict[int, list[dict[str, Any]]] | None=None) -> Collective:
        if not errors:
            return Collective(id=id, group_id=self.pg_name, record_id=self.record_id, pg_desc=self.pg_desc, pass_check=True, collective_seq_id=self.collective_seq_id, p2p_seq_id=self.p2p_seq_id, collective_name=self.profiling_name, input_sizes=self.input_sizes, output_sizes=self.output_sizes, expected_ranks=self.expected_ranks, collective_state=self.collective_state, collective_frames=self.collective_frames, missing_ranks=getattr(self, 'missing_ranks', None))
        else:
            assert idx_map is not None, 'idx_map is None'
            assert all_entries is not None, 'all_entries is None'
            mismatch_collectives = {}
            for rank, error in errors:
                idx = idx_map[rank]
                entry = all_entries[rank][idx]
                desc = entry['process_group'][1]
                pg_name = entry['process_group'][0]
                mismatch_collectives[rank] = Collective(id=id, group_id=entry['process_group'][0], record_id=entry['record_id'], pg_desc=f'{pg_name}:{desc}' if desc != 'undefined' else pg_name, pass_check=False, collective_seq_id=entry['collective_seq_id'], p2p_seq_id=entry['p2p_seq_id'], collective_name=entry['profiling_name'], input_sizes=entry['input_sizes'], output_sizes=entry['output_sizes'], expected_ranks=self.expected_ranks, collective_state=entry['state'], collective_frames=entry.get('frames', []), type_of_mismatch=error)
            return Collective(id=id, group_id=self.pg_name, record_id=self.record_id, pg_desc=self.pg_desc, pass_check=False, collective_seq_id=self.collective_seq_id, p2p_seq_id=self.p2p_seq_id, collective_name=self.profiling_name, input_sizes=self.input_sizes, output_sizes=self.output_sizes, expected_ranks=self.expected_ranks, collective_state=self.collective_state, collective_frames=self.collective_frames, input_numel=self.input_numel if hasattr(self, 'input_numel') else None, output_numel=self.output_numel if hasattr(self, 'output_numel') else None, missing_ranks=self.missing_ranks if hasattr(self, 'missing_ranks') else None, mismatch_collectives=mismatch_collectives)

    def to_nccl_call(self, all_entries: dict[int, list[dict[str, Any]]], idx_map: dict[int, int], nccl_call_id: int, collective_id: Any) -> list[NCCLCall]:
        result = []
        for i, k in idx_map.items():
            all_entries[i].pop(k)
            result.append(NCCLCall(id=nccl_call_id, collective_id=collective_id, group_id=self.pg_name, global_rank=i, traceback_id=0, collective_type=self.profiling_name, sizes=self.input_sizes))
            nccl_call_id += 1
        return result

# --- helper: torch.distributed.flight_recorder.components.types.Collective ---
class Collective(NamedTuple):
    id: int
    group_id: str
    pass_check: bool
    collective_seq_id: int
    p2p_seq_id: int
    record_id: int
    pg_desc: str
    collective_name: str
    input_sizes: list[list[int]]
    output_sizes: list[list[int]]
    expected_ranks: set[int]
    collective_state: str
    collective_frames: list[dict[str, str]]
    input_numel: int | None = None
    output_numel: int | None = None
    missing_ranks: set[int] | None = None
    mismatch_collectives: dict[int, 'Collective'] | None = None
    type_of_mismatch: MatchInfo | None = None

# --- helper: torch.distributed.flight_recorder.components.types.MatchInfo ---
class MatchInfo:

    def __init__(self, state: MatchState, culprit: str | None=None) -> None:
        self._state = state
        self.culprit = culprit

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        details = f', {self.culprit}' if getattr(self, 'culprit', None) else ''
        return f'Error type: {self._state.name}{details}'

    @property
    def state(self) -> MatchState:
        return self._state

def _stub_build_collectives_v2(

    collectives = {}
    mismatches = []
    for rank, events in all_entries.items():

            pg_id = ev.get("pg_id")
            if pg_name is None or pg_id is None:
                continue
            key = (pg_name, pg_id)
            collectives.setdefault(key, []).append(ev)
    # detect simple mismatch: expected membership size vs observed distinct ranks
    for key, evs in collectives.items():
        observed_ranks = {ev.get("rank", None) for ev in evs if ev.get("rank", None) is not None}
        expected = len(_memberships.get(key[0], set()))
        if len(observed_ranks) != expected:

def _stub_build_collectives_empty(

    _pg_guids: Dict[Tuple[str, int], str],
    version: str,
    mismatch_cap: int = 10,
):

            pg_id = ev.get("pg_id")
            if not pg or pg_id is None:

            key = (pg[0], pg_id)
            collectives.setdefault(key, []).append(ev)
            count += 1
    return {"version": version, "mismatch_cap": mismatch_cap, "collectives": collectives, "count": count}

mechanism.text:
Builds coherent collective operations and low-level call records by iteratively matching per-rank trace entries into group-wide collective events. It treats each rank’s earliest unprocessed log entry as a candidate “first” event, computes the expected participant set from process-group membership, and then tries to find matching entries across ranks. When multiple coalesced (batched or multi-op) entries exist, it expands a connectivity-aware frontier: following send/recv peer links to gather all related ranks, then runs a specialized matching routine that handles pure peer-to-peer patterns for older versions or supports non‑P2P (collective-like) patterns for newer protocol versions. Successful matches yield a Collective record and derived low-level NCCL (GPU collective) call records; non-matching or partial matches are still recorded but marked with errors. Mismatch counts per group guard against runaway failures.

Domain knowledge: understanding of distributed collective communication (ranks, process groups, sends/receives, broadcasts, NCCL semantics), trace/log formats that record per-rank operations, and how coalescing (multiple logical ops packed into one trace) and version differences affect matching are required. Familiarity with group membership, rank-to-process-group GUID mapping, and how peer links indicate cross-rank relationships is important.

Key constraints and assumptions: entries are processed in FIFO order per rank; the first collective for a group must be consistent across all its ranks; group membership and GUID mappings are correct and stable; version-dependent heuristics must reflect protocol behavior; a mismatch cap prevents infinite looping but may drop further analysis. The algorithm assumes send/recv peer info is reliable for connectivity expansion and that any coalesced entries are discoverable by scanning linked ranks.

Appropriate usage: post-processing multi-rank execution traces to reconstruct group-level collectives and their underlying NCCL calls, especially when diagnosing mismatches or visualizing collective timings. Not suitable when per-entry ordering is unreliable, membership mappings are missing, or traces lack peer/connectivity metadata.

mechanism.text:
All traces are trimmed so that every trace begins no earlier than the latest starting event seen across traces. Concretely, the algorithm finds the largest record_id among the first entries of all non-empty traces, then drops any entry whose record_id is smaller than that threshold from every trace. The computational cost is linear in the total number of traces plus the total number of entries (two simple passes: one to scan first entries, one to filter), and it uses constant extra memory beyond the input (it mutates the lists in place).

This approach is useful when working with multiple event streams or process traces that share a global sequence id (record_id) and you want to align analyses to a common “earliest agreed” starting point. Typical domains include log processing, trace comparison, distributed system debugging, or preparing traces for synchronous analysis where events before a consensus start are irrelevant or incomplete.

Key assumptions and constraints:
- Each list of dicts represents a time-ordered trace and the first element is the earliest event for that trace. If lists are not ordered, the result is undefined.
- record_id is comparable and consistent across traces (same scale and semantics). It’s usually an integer monotonically increasing with time or event order.
- The function uses >= against the maximum first-record_id: events that predate that global start are removed; events with equal record_id are kept.
- The input is mutated; if the original data must be retained, it should be copied beforehand.
- Traces can become empty after trimming; downstream code must handle that.
- If record_id semantics differ between traces (e.g., per-host counters without global synchronization), alignment is misleading.

Appropriate use cases: synchronizing multiple traces to a common observational window when record_id is a global sequence or clock and earlier data is irrelevant. Avoid this routine for aligning by relative offsets, heterogeneous clocks, or when preserving entire histories is required.

mechanism.text:
Injects a per-instance wrapper around a module method so that FSDP’s lifecycle logic runs before and after the original method call. Concretely, it replaces an instance’s method with a bound wrapper that calls the module’s FSDP state _pre_forward to prepare inputs, invokes the original implementation, then calls _post_forward to finalize outputs and restore any FSDP invariants (shard/flatten/unflatten, precision casting, communication, buffer/param state transitions, gradient hook placement, etc.).

Underlying algorithm/approach
- Method-wrapping: capture the original bound method, create a wrapper that first delegates to an FSDP-state pre-processing routine, then calls the original implementation, then delegates to an FSDP-state post-processing routine. functools.wraps preserves metadata. The wrapper is bound back onto the specific module instance using descriptor binding (__get__), so only that instance’s method is replaced.
- Lifecycle instrumentation: _pre_forward/_post_forward implement the domain logic needed to safely run forward-like computations on sharded parameters (e.g., gather shards, convert dtypes, track which params were unsharded), and then restore sharding or perform communications and bookkeeping after the forward.

Domain knowledge required
- Understanding of Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP): parameter sharding, on-demand unshard/gather, mixed precision/autocast interactions, and distributed collectives.
- Knowledge that some modules expose non-standard forward-like entry points that also need FSDP instrumentation.

Key constraints and assumptions
- module must be an FSDPModule and have a working _get_fsdp_state, _pre_forward, and _post_forward.
- The original method is expected to be a normal bound method taking self; the wrapper and binding preserve that.
- Assumes single-threaded calls or that FSDP state methods are thread-safe; calls may trigger distributed communication and device transfers.
- Replacement is per-instance (not class-level) and mutates the instance’s attribute.

When appropriate to use
- When you need to instrument a custom forward-like method (not just forward) so the module’s sharded parameters and FSDP invariants are correctly handled during that call (e.g., custom inference entry points, alternative forward variants, or testing hooks). Avoid if module is not FSDP-managed or lacks the expected FSDP state methods.

import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.distributed.fsdp.sharded_grad_scaler import ShardedGradScaler

# Minimal single-step training example on CPU with gradient scaling disabled
model = nn.Linear(4, 1)
optimizer = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)
loss_fn = nn.MSELoss()

# Use device='cpu' and disable scaling so no distributed init is necessary
scaler = ShardedGradScaler(device='cpu', enabled=False)

# Dummy input / target
x = torch.randn(2, 4)
y = torch.randn(2, 1)

optimizer.zero_grad()
output = model(x)
loss = loss_fn(output, y)

# With enabled=False, scale(...) is a no-op; call backward on returned object
scaler.scale(loss).backward()
# scaler.step will unscale (no-op when disabled) and call optimizer.step()
scaler.step(optimizer)
# update the internal scale for next iteration (no-op when disabled)
scaler.update()

# verify parameters changed
print('param norm:', torch.nn.utils.parameters_to_vector(model.parameters()).norm().item())

mechanism.text:
Manages dynamic loss-scaling state and the cross-device coordination needed for mixed-precision (AMP) training when model parameters and optimizers are sharded across processes. An instance owns the global scale tensor and growth tracker (possibly lazily initialized on first use), a per-optimizer small state machine (stage + per-device found-inf flags), and utilities to replicate the single scale/inf tensor to the particular devices that hold gradients. It also knows the process group used to all-reduce “found inf/nan” indicators across ranks.

Lifecycle and usage:
- Constructed like a GradScaler variant: it sets up internal bookkeeping and optionally disables itself. The actual scale and growth-tracker are lazily initialized the first time scale(...) is invoked on a tensor device.
- Typical use: call scale(outputs) before the backward pass; call unscale_(optimizer) before optimizer.step() to unscale grads and record per-device found-inf flags; call update() after step() to adjust the scale based on aggregated infs and to reset per-optimizer state. The class handles device-aware replication of single-element tensors so unscale and update work regardless of where gradients live.
- No explicit disposal/close API is required. Resources are ordinary tensors and Python structures; normal Python/GPU memory management applies. After update(), per-optimizer state is reset ready for the next cycle.

Key invariants and role:
- If enabled, a scale tensor and growth tracker must be initialized before unscale_/update paths assume them; scale(...) lazily establishes that invariant.
- Per-optimizer stage follows a strict protocol (READY → UNSCALED → STEPPED → READY) and unscale_ enforces ordering to avoid double-unscaling or unscaling after step.
- The class guarantees per-device bookkeeping: found-inf flags exist for every device that held gradients (it will create entries as needed), and it coordinates cross-process all-reduce of these flags so update() sees a global result.
- Architecturally, it is the coordinator for safe AMP loss-scaling in distributed sharded training: it transparently handles multi-device replication, sparsity handling for grads, device type checks, and uses low-level torch._amp helpers to perform efficient batched checks/unscales and scale updates.

mechanism.text:
Returning None serves as an explicit "no default" sentinel rather than computing or supplying a concrete NUMA policy. There is no algorithmic work: the implementation makes an unconditional, constant-time choice to provide no configuration data. Conceptually this delegates all NUMA decisions to the caller or to the environment (OS/hypervisor) instead of encoding policy in library code.

Relevant domain knowledge centers on NUMA (Non‑Uniform Memory Access) architectures and how operating systems expose and enforce locality controls: CPU/core affinity, memory allocation policies (local vs interleaved), and tools like numactl or OS syscalls (set_mempolicy, sched_setaffinity). Interpreting a None return correctly requires understanding whether the runtime or caller should apply default OS behavior, infer topology dynamically, or consult explicit configuration elsewhere.

Key constraints and assumptions:
- None is a sentinel value meaning "no default options provided," not an error. Callers must distinguish absence of defaults from explicit, empty option objects.
- There is no lazy computation; repeated calls return the same sentinel, so no caching or expensive probing occurs here.
- Thread-safety is trivial because the function is side‑effect free.
- Backwards-compatibility: consumers may rely on None to trigger legacy handling paths; changing the return type later would be a breaking change.

Appropriate usage patterns:
- Use when the library should not impose NUMA policies and wishes to leave allocation/affinity to the system or to higher-level configuration.
- Useful as a placeholder in configuration pipelines where defaults might be injected later or where explicit, caller-provided NUMA options are optional.
- Avoid when the application requires deterministic locality guarantees—there you must construct and supply concrete NUMA options or perform topology-aware setup at process start.

mechanism.text:
Fully sharding a model means partitioning each parameter and buffer across a specified device mesh and replacing standard modules with FSDP-managed wrappers so forward/backward computation happens with sharded storage and communication-aware memory management. Conceptually, the routine scans the module tree, establishes or validates a device mesh, computes pre/post-forward shard layouts (including an option to automatically reshard after forward), builds an FSDP state object, groups parameters into sharded placements (considering mixed precision and offload policies), marks managed submodules, and swaps in FSDP-wrapped modules that implement the runtime sharding, communication (all-gather / reduce-scatter), and lazy unshard/reshard behavior.

Algorithmically this is a static transformation plus runtime policy setup: it does not itself perform computation but configures per-parameter metadata and module wrappers so subsequent forward/backward passes use sharded storage and coordinated collectives to assemble full tensors only when needed (e.g., during computation or optimizer steps). Reshard-after-forward controls whether parameters stay sharded between forward and backward to reduce peak memory; mixed-precision and offload policies influence storage dtype and host-device residency.

Domain knowledge required: distributed-training concepts (collectives, topology, device meshes), memory/communication tradeoffs of sharding vs replication, PyTorch autograd lifecycle, interactions with compilation (torch.compile), and practicalities of mixed precision and CPU/GPU offload. Users should understand optimizer state placement and checkpointing implications.

Key constraints and assumptions: modules must be valid nn.Module trees; the device mesh must represent available devices; ignored parameters are respected; wrappers assume coordinated all-reduce/all-gather semantics and require compatible collective backends. Certain compilation modes (fullgraph) change how/when parameters are visible and may require different reshard settings. Some features (deepcopy, arbitrary Python-side parameter mutation) may be restricted.

Appropriate use cases: training very large models that do not fit replicated on each accelerator, reducing GPU memory footprint, or combining with mixed precision/offload for extreme-scale models. Avoid for small models where sharding overhead and communication dominate, or when application code cannot tolerate the wrapper-induced invariants (e.g., nonstandard parameter mutation or incompatible custom autograd operations).

implementation:
@contract(state_cls=FSDPState)
def fully_shard(module, *, mesh: DeviceMesh | None=None, reshard_after_forward: bool | int | None=None, shard_placement_fn: Callable[[nn.Parameter], Shard | None] | None=None, mp_policy: MixedPrecisionPolicy=MixedPrecisionPolicy(), offload_policy: OffloadPolicy=OffloadPolicy(), ignored_params: set[nn.Parameter] | None=None):
    torch._C._log_api_usage_once('torch.distributed.fsdp.fully_shard')
    _validate_module(module, 'fully_shard')
    mesh = mesh or _init_default_mesh()
    _validate_mesh(mesh)
    mesh_info = _get_mesh_info(mesh)
    device = _get_device_from_mesh(mesh)
    auto_reshard_after_forward = reshard_after_forward is None
    post_forward_mesh_info = _get_post_forward_mesh_info(reshard_after_forward if not auto_reshard_after_forward else True, mesh_info)
    arg_module, modules, managed_modules, params, buffers = _get_modules_and_states(module, device, ignored_params)
    state = fully_shard.state(modules[0])
    state.init(modules, device, mp_policy, auto_reshard_after_forward)
    _init_param_group(state, params, modules, mesh_info, post_forward_mesh_info, device, shard_placement_fn, mp_policy, offload_policy)
    for managed_module in managed_modules:
        managed_module._is_fsdp_managed_module = True
        managed_module._fsdp_use_orig_params = True
    _apply_to_module(modules, cls_to_fsdp_cls, FSDPModule, 'FSDP', _unimplemented_deepcopy)
    return arg_module

mechanism.text:
Stages are assigned to pipeline ranks in one of two deterministic patterns: a simple cyclic distribution ("loop") and a block-wise zig-zag distribution ("v"), and then the inverse mapping (rank → sorted list of stages) is produced.

1) Algorithmic approach
- The "loop" schedule uses a modulo rule: stage i is assigned to rank (i % pp_size). That cycles stages across ranks so each rank receives roughly every pp_size-th stage.
- The "v" schedule divides stages into consecutive blocks of size pp_size. Within each block, ranks are visited in one direction for the first block, then reversed for the next, and so on — effectively a zig‑zag over blocks. Concretely, a rank index increments across a block, then in the next block the assignment direction is reversed, producing a V-shaped traversal across blocks.
- After producing a stage→rank mapping, the code inverts it into rank→[stages] and sorts each rank’s stage list to ensure ascending stage order per rank.

2) Domain knowledge
- Intended for pipeline parallelism in distributed model training where a model is partitioned into ordered stages and each stage must be placed on a process (rank). Understanding what a "stage" and a "rank" mean, and why different schedules affect communication/activation flow and load balance, is necessary.
- Familiarity with how forward/backward passes flow through stages and how placement patterns influence memory, compute locality, and inter-rank communication helps choose a schedule.

3) Key constraints and assumptions
- Ranks are numbered 0..pp_size-1 and stage indices are contiguous 0..num_stages-1.
- For the "v" schedule, num_stages must be evenly divisible by pp_size (otherwise an error is raised).
- The mapping is deterministic, assumes homogeneous ranks, and does not try to rebalance by computational cost per stage—it assumes stages are comparable in cost or that the chosen schedule is acceptable.

4) When to use
- Use "loop" when a simple round-robin spread is desired (good for spreading similar-cost layers evenly).
- Use "v" when you want block-locality with alternating traversal direction (can reduce long-distance activation transfers between blocks and can be helpful when blocks are processed sequentially by microbatches).
- Appropriate for initial placement decisions in pipeline parallel training; not sufficient alone if stages have widely varying compute/memory needs or when dynamic rebalancing is required.

mechanism.text:
Computes gradients for a computational "stage" by extracting all tensors that require gradients from a (possibly nested) stage output, matching them to provided output-gradient values, calling PyTorch’s autograd.backward with those pairs, and then returning the collected gradients for the stage inputs.

1) Algorithmic approach
- Recursively traverse the stage output structure (tensors, lists/tuples, dicts) to collect output tensors that participate in autograd and their corresponding gradient tensors passed by the caller. Non-tensor leaves or tensors that do not require gradients are ignored.
- Validate structural correspondence between outputs and output-grad structures (same shapes/keys/lengths where applicable).
- Call torch.autograd.backward with the gathered output tensors and grad_tensors so the graph accumulates gradients into upstream .grad fields.
- Read .grad from each input tensor (or None for non-tensors), clear .grad to avoid retaining state, and return the list of input gradients.

2) Required domain knowledge
- Familiarity with PyTorch autograd semantics: leaf vs. non-leaf tensors, requires_grad flags, .grad storage, and how backward() accumulates gradients.
- Understanding of nested data structures and how user-supplied gradient values must mirror the output structure.
- Awareness that autograd.backward mutates .grad in-place and requires gradient tensors to match the shapes and dtypes of the corresponding outputs.

3) Key constraints and assumptions
- The provided output gradients must structurally match outputs (same containers, keys, lengths) and each gradient must be either a Tensor or None where allowed.
- Only tensors that require gradients and have a grad_fn are included; others are ignored.
- The op assumes outputs share a computation graph reachable from inputs; otherwise collected .grad may be None.
- Uses torch.autograd.backward (not torch.autograd.grad) so gradients accumulate into .grad fields; clearing .grad is done manually.
- Errors are wrapped with debug info for easier diagnosis.

4) Appropriate usage
- Useful in custom training pipelines needing manual backward across stage boundaries (e.g., pipeline/model parallelism or checkpointed segments) where outputs and their external gradients must be wired back into earlier inputs.
- Not intended for simple end-to-end training where loss.backward() suffices, nor when you need symbolic per-input gradient tuples from autograd.grad (which returns gradients directly without relying on .grad).

mechanism.text:
Replicating a PyTorch module here means wrapping it so its parameters are fully replicated (kept locally) across a 1-D device mesh and managed by a lightweight FSDP-like state object rather than being shard/partitioned. The implementation builds a DeviceMesh, validates that the mesh is 1D, gathers the module and its parameters, creates a per-module Replicate state (subclassing the FSDPState abstraction), initializes mixed-precision/offload policies and parameter groups, and replaces the original module classes with a ReplicateModule wrapper that provides the runtime semantics.

Underlying algorithmic idea
- Topology: a single-dimension DeviceMesh is used to represent the set of devices that will each hold a full copy of the model parameters. No parameter sharding is performed across that mesh dimension.
- State organization: the code leverages the same state machinery as FSDP (FSDPState) so existing mechanisms for mixed precision, offload, and per-parameter grouping can be reused, but with semantics that keep parameters replicated rather than sharded.
- Composition and wrapping: modules are inspected for existing composable-management registry; incompatible modules (already under fully_shard) are rejected. Modules are then wrapped with a ReplicateModule class to attach the new runtime behavior.

Domain knowledge required
- Distributed training basics: device meshes, data vs model parallelism, and the difference between replication (data parallel) and sharding (model parallel / FSDP).
- PyTorch module lifecycle, parameter ownership, and how wrappers can intercept parameter/state behavior.
- Mixed precision and CPU/GPU offloading trade-offs.

Key constraints and assumptions
- Mesh must be 1D; higher-dim meshes are invalid.
- Cannot compose replicate on modules already managed by fully_shard.
- The approach assumes devices can each hold a full copy of parameters (memory and bandwidth considerations).
- Uses the FSDP-style state machinery, so some FSDP semantics carry over.

When appropriate to use
- When you want data-parallel replication across multiple devices (each device runs the full model) but still want FSDP-like policies for precision/offload and parameter grouping.
- Small-to-medium models that fit in each device’s memory and where sharding would be unnecessary or harmful.
- Scenarios needing consistency with FSDP tooling without performing actual parameter sharding.

mechanism.text:
Creates a callable wrapper that binds placement/mesh metadata to a user kernel so it can be applied to sharded/localized computation paths; it supports both decorator syntax and direct creation of a pre-bound callable. The implementation uses a simple factory pattern: when no function is supplied it returns a decorator that will later capture the user function; when a function is supplied it returns a functools.partial that binds that function and the placement/mesh flags to an internal implementation (_local_map_wrapped). The partial does not execute the kernel immediately — it packages the arguments for later invocation by the runtime that understands device placements and redistribution semantics.

Algorithmically this is light-weight metadata binding and indirection rather than any data movement itself. The heavy work is deferred to _local_map_wrapped (not shown): this wrapper merely captures a closure of the kernel plus placement and redistribution policy so the execution layer can perform local mapping, input redistribution, device-aware gradient handling, and output placement management deterministically.

Domain knowledge required includes distributed/tensor-sharded computation concepts: device meshes, logical/physical placements of tensors, and how automatic differentiation should be handled across partitions. Users must understand the semantics of redistributing inputs versus assuming current placements, and how gradient propagation should interact with in-place or reshaped data on devices.

Key constraints and assumptions: the user function must conform to the calling convention expected by the internal handler; the device mesh and placement descriptors must be valid for the runtime; mutable placement objects captured by the closure can change after wrapper creation and affect behavior; thread-safety and execution ordering are governed by the downstream runtime, not this factory. Also, _local_map_wrapped must be present and accept the bound signature.

Appropriate use cases are when a computation kernel needs to be registered with consistent placement/redistribution metadata for later distributed execution — e.g., defining per-device computations that will be mapped across a mesh, or annotating layers/kernels with how their inputs and outputs should be sharded and how gradients should be treated.

import torch
from torch.distributed.tensor.experimental import register_sharding
from torch.distributed.tensor import Shard, Replicate

# Register a custom sharding strategy for aten._softmax.default
@register_sharding(torch.ops.aten._softmax.default)
def custom_softmax_sharding(x, dim, half_to_float):
    # normalize negative dim
    softmax_dim = dim if dim >= 0 else dim + x.ndim
    acceptable_shardings = []

    # fully replicated outputs and inputs
    all_replicate = ([Replicate()], [Replicate(), None, None])
    acceptable_shardings.append(all_replicate)

    # allow sharding on every dimension except the softmax dim
    for sharding_dim in range(x.ndim):
        if sharding_dim != softmax_dim:
            all_sharded = (
                [Shard(sharding_dim)],
                [Shard(sharding_dim), None, None],
            )
            acceptable_shardings.append(all_sharded)

    return acceptable_shardings

# The decorator registers the sharding function; nothing more to call here.
print('Custom softmax sharding registered for:', torch.ops.aten._softmax.default)

import torch
from torch.distributed.tensor.experimental import register_sharding
from torch.distributed.tensor import Replicate

# Register the same simple sharding strategy for multiple overloads (example: add and sub)
ops = [torch.ops.aten.add.Tensor, torch.ops.aten.sub.Tensor]

@register_sharding(ops)
def replicate_binary_op_sharding(a, b, *, alpha=1):
    # This simple strategy states: output replicated, inputs replicated (alpha is not a tensor)
    return [([Replicate()], [Replicate(), Replicate(), None])]

print('Custom sharding registered for ops:', ops)

mechanism.text:
Takes a user-supplied mapping from tensor input/output placement patterns (for a single mesh dimension) and turns it into a full set of op sharding strategies that the DTensor dispatcher can use to propagate and evaluate sharding choices across a device mesh.

Algorithm / computational approach
- The decorator wraps a user-provided "custom sharding" function that declares acceptable placements for an operation’s inputs and outputs (expressed as PlacementLists). At call time it:
  - Extracts a concise representation of the runtime argument/keyword structure (converting OpStrategy/TupleStrategy wrapper objects to their contained placement specs).
  - Calls the user custom_sharding_fn with those per-argument placement specs to get a list of acceptable (outputs, inputs) placement pairs.
  - Normalizes each pair into a flat list of placements and hands that to expand_to_full_mesh_op_strategy together with the operation’s device mesh and metadata (number of outputs, inplace flag). That expansion converts single-dimension placement patterns to full-mesh strategies (combinations across mesh dimensions) and registers them as OpStrategy choices.
- A small helper derives runtime schema info (which arguments are static integers and which kwargs are static-only) so runtime shape/pytree handling is correct.

Domain knowledge required
- Distributed tensor sharding concepts: device mesh, placement lists (Replicate/Shard), and how per-dimension sharding composes into full-mesh strategies.
- PyTorch operator schema basics (argument ordering, return counts, inplace semantics) and how DTensor’s OpStrategy and schema wrappers represent placement info.
- How to express valid sharding patterns for an op in terms of input/output placements.

Key constraints and assumptions
- The custom_sharding_fn is expected to work on the simplified spec objects and return sequences of (output_specs, input_specs) that describe a single mesh-dimension placement pattern. The expand_to_full_mesh_op_strategy is relied upon to generate cross-dimension combinations.
- Order and arity of inputs/outputs must match op_schema expectations; inplace ops and return-count are used when expanding.
- The code assumes DTensor dispatcher internals (OpStrategy, TupleStrategy, op_schema API) are available and stable.
- Integer/static-argument detection uses schema types to decide which args are runtime tensors vs static ints.

When to use it
- When automatic sharding propagation does not cover an operator or you want to supply custom, hand-crafted valid sharding patterns (e.g., for composite ops, experimental/custom kernels, or to enforce specific data-parallel/partitioning trade-offs). Use to register a sharding propagator for one or more op overloads so the DTensor planner considers your patterns when generating distributed strategies.

mechanism.text:
Manages the FSDP-specific transformations and wiring needed to treat DTensor-backed parameters like FSDP flattenable tensors: it encapsulates the logic for flattening/unflattening, chunking across ranks, and converting between DTensor and ShardedTensor representations while coordinating device streams and device meshes.

Instances hold lightweight state and coordination handles rather than heavy resources. Key state includes a device_handle (to query and enter device streams) and an optional compute_stream reference; methods use these to ensure unflattening and local conversions happen on the correct stream. The constructor wraps the post-unflatten callback with torch._dynamo.disable so it won’t be traced/optimized by Dynamo during graph capture, ensuring correct runtime side effects.

Lifecycle: created when FSDP wants to extend its parameter handling to DTensor-backed tensors; it is referenced by FSDP at model setup, checkpoint load/save, and parameter sharding/unsharding operations. Typical use: pre_flatten_transform to produce contiguous flattened buffers, chunk_tensor/chunk_dtensor to create per-rank shards, pre_load_state_dict_transform to expose local shards for checkpoint loading, and all_gather_dtensor to materialize replicated views. There is no explicit close or disposal API; the object holds no OS resources that require deterministic cleanup. The only runtime concern is that held stream references must remain valid for the device_handle’s lifetime.

Important invariants and roles:
- device_mesh consistency: when reshaping/redistributing, the tensor’s device_mesh must match expected parent_mesh; root mesh must exist and have ndim >= 2 for DTensor chunking into higher-dim meshes.
- Placement shape/semantics: methods convert placements (Replicate, DShard, TP placements) predictably so downstream FSDP code receives tensors in expected sharding/replication layouts.
- Interop contract: conversions produce either local tensors, DTensor with specific shard placements, or ShardedTensor wrappers depending on context; returned tensors have requires_grad cleared where appropriate for checkpointing.
Role in architecture: acts as an adapter between FSDP and distributed tensor abstractions (DTensor/ShardedTensor), centralizing mesh/placement-stream bookkeeping so FSDP can operate uniformly on parameters regardless of their underlying distributed representation.
